text:
Chainlink's work with Apex Group and the Bermuda Monetary Authority is a pretty interesting example of where stablecoin infrastructure is heading.

The initiative combines three @Chainlink services:

1. Proof of Reserve for reserve verification
2. ACE for compliance policies
3. CCIP for cross-chain interoperability

That combination matters because a regulated stablecoin has three separate obligations.

> Its backing needs to be verifiable.
> Its transfers need to satisfy applicable requirements.
> Its distribution needs to work across the networks where users actually transact.

A stablecoin issuer that solves only one of those problems still has to find infrastructure for the other two, but Chainlink is increasingly positioning itself to provide the entire stack.

Citrini's (@citrini)  new report, Breaking The Wall, argues that crypto has spent fifteen years building exactly what an agentic world needs: programmable financial rails that never close, where assets, ownership and settlement can live side by side.

We agree with this, but to execute this system we need one additional key element: formation.

When agents make code cheap, building stops being the bottleneck. Execution and distribution become the scarce part, and both run on capital and community. That's still the least programmable layer in finance: lawyers, cap tables, boards that meet quarterly, and token launches where you trust the founder not to walk off with the treasury.

Umia makes that layer programmable and accessible to anyone onchain, be it an agent or an onchain human.

Trust-minimized where code can enforce it, legally enforceable where it can't.

Assets, ownership and settlement are onchain. Formation is next.

text: 在下班的途中看完了 这篇文章补充了量化很多的细节 说来惭愧 我自己本身是学Quantitative Analysis 但是写代码实际也就接触过多空 FF6 Factor之类简单的 Dave这篇文章也让我了解了更多实际中用到的因子和策略 （顺便也让我确定了自己不是学这块的料 学习了的全还给老师了+巨讨厌写代码）好文需收藏
author: bc1qDave
quoted_text:
经历过一场漂亮的失败

前段时间，几块量化拼图终于凑齐。在交易所老板和朋友们的支持下，我拿到了更优惠的费率和订单执行条件。同时解决了硬件性能问题，训练基建也有了保障。老板也支持我们在股票合约方向做一些研究。于是我和伙伴 @Eric_pollll_btc  决定认真把系统搭起来。

想要做一个量化策略，是远远比大家想象中要复杂的许多。很多AI交易项目会给大家撮策略，其实那大多是非常不完善的一个基于 rule-based 的下单系统。 完完整整的量化交易系统，从如何保护 API 密钥安全开始，到用 Rust 写订单的执行代码。并接受反馈。 这里之间包含了一个大千世界

最开始的接入数据，整理数据，监督数据源有没有错误，（我们是真的在交易所上遇到过返回错误数据的情况）， 第一步数据搞完了，第二步才开始搭建模型。模型里的模型选择，调参，优化。 这一步相当艰难。对于成熟的量化团队来说，真正分高下的就是写模型的能力，是非常考验数学、物理、计算机，甚至金融知识的。 
模型做完，还有回测、实盘，再拿真实订单流里的问题回来修改，同时把风控、止损和异常处理补齐
每一步短短几个字，实则要花费大量的心血。光是回测这两个轻飘飘的字，里面的复杂程度都足以写论文了。（Eric最近就在做一个高频回测框架的项目，后面会开源）

所以做一个量化不是大家印象中用Python写几段代码，给 AI 说一个策略思路就可以完成的，这是一个非常复杂的工程， 我和我的伙伴决定用很严肃的态度对待这个任务，所以要以很严谨的工程思维来对待系统搭建。

到这里就是结束了吗？除了代码之外，还有一片看不见的领域，（其实也是我在任务中主要做的事情）

作为小团队，更不要说个人了。在激烈的交易所环境下面对专业机构，劣势不只在模型。手续费、成交速度、交易条件，每一项都可能吃掉本来就不多的优势。所以，和交易所沟通、争取支持，并不是技术之外的杂事，而是系统能不能成立的一部分。 

同样重要的，是找到值得做的市场和标的。资源有限，就不能只想着正面拼算力、拼速度，还需要一点交易员的直觉，找到能发挥优势的机会。当然还有不断地和同行进行沟通， 队内进行任务安排和分工， 对外寻求支持（如融资、交易活动等等）

需要相当多的努力，技术上的，业务上的，组织管理上的，才能把这一件小事情做好

讲到这里，我希望给大家留下一个量化的专业印象，AI 发达后，路边摊量化确实有点泛滥了。想要做好一件事，要以最认真的态度去对待它。同时大家应该也理解我过去一个月在推特上沉默寡言的原因了。

接下来廢话不多说，看一篇我的技术写的文章吧。我在 review 了我们三周的成果之后，让他写了一篇总结， 因为无论成败，做一个事情还是需要有闭环，有交付。我个人觉得他写得很好， 一两周前就叫他赶快发推特了，但是他实在是太忙，就由我来帮他发一下这篇文章吧。同时也希望我账号流量大一点，可以让更多人看到我们的项目：

【预测未来】
Article by @Eric_pollll_btc @bc1qDave @AndyW_Web3

“
策略为什么会盈利
这段时间我们一直在研究高频策略，用AS模型也好，GLFT模型也好，都没能取得比较稳健的收益。随后我尝试拓展高频策略的行为，比如不再连续报价，而是挑选市场状态报价，比如不在固定的双边maker，而是将动作拓展到单侧maker，亦或者是taker一些订单。叠加的规则越来越多，可调节的参数越来越多，策略的复杂度不断提高，而复杂度本身并不能带来收益。于是我开始反思，我们的策略里究竟缺少了什么？或者说，不局限于高频策略，一个真正能盈利的策略，必须需要什么？

我发现，我们优化止盈/退出逻辑也好，改善仓位控制也罢。本质上都是在“根据自己的状态做决策”，而非“根据市场状态做决策”，更确切的说，是没有专注于“根据未来做决策”。

这样一来，无论如何我们都是在被市场牵着鼻子走。那么什么是“根据未来做决策”？很简单，你认为未来价格会涨，所以买入，这就是根据未来做决策。你的盈利，全部来源于你能够对市场的走势作出正确的判断。为什么很多人看上去都是先从中低频的主观交易赚到钱，而不是一开始就通过高频交易获利呢？因为决策频率低。当交易的次数越来越多，越来越频繁，就越是会暴露出我们对未来的真实预测能力到底有多强。

所谓预测未来的能力，就是alpha。

而仓位控制本身不产生alpha，它只是一个让我们控制风险的工具，它的目的只有一个，就是让我们在市场上活下来，不被一次失误决策干死，仅此而已。因此，在没有找出真正的alpha之前就大量设计仓位控制的行为，是毫无意义的，它只会让策略从暴死变成慢性死亡。

一切风险控制、仓位控制之类的设计，都应当在发掘出了真正有效的alpha后进行。

描述市场的维度不止价格

很多决策的本质都是预测未来，比如我之前给dave说的，大单冲击后买一卖一大幅移动，希望在较高位置做空，恢复后做多，实现盈利。这个策略是规定了一个入场条件，预测入场条件触发后，有可能形成一个有盈利空间的事件。本质上来说，和金叉买入没什么区别，都是在预测未来存在一个有盈利机会的事件，仅此而已。

预测不止是预测涨跌这样的盈利性事件，还可以是其他的市场信息，比如波动率，比如成交活动，比如买卖价差等等。
这些市场信息对策略的构建是非常重要且有价值的，比如当我们预测到成交活动后面一段时间会很弱，那我们便停止被动做市，逐步将仓位平掉；比如当我们预测到市场的波动率会显著扩大，那么便可以适当减小杠杆，亦或者根据策略的类型选择避开这段时间还是积极参与进去。

这样的风险控制或者仓位控制，是真正带着对市场判断的仓位控制，才是合理的控制，而这一切都是基于有效的预测。

那么具体如何预测未来，就是一个很深刻的话题了。我做了这样的研究

我希望回答一个问题，行情里究竟有哪些信息，对未来有帮助？只看当前够不够？不同市场能不能用同一种描述？我每隔五秒整理一次当时已经收到的盘口和成交信息，然后观察未来五秒、三十秒、一百二十秒等时段里，五件事怎样变化：

1：价格变化。最后涨了还是跌了，变化多少。
2：路径波动。中间经历了多大起伏。最后回到原价，也可能经历了很大波动。
3：成交活动。接下来会发生多少笔成交。
4：买卖价差。最优买价与卖价之间的距离会扩大还是缩小。
5：盘口深度。可见挂单会变厚还是变薄。

这个就是我描述未来市场的五个维度。即便我们很难判断接下来市场到底会涨还是跌，但也可能比较容易判断接下来会不会更加活跃。

历史信息中有多少对未来有价值的东西

假如两个时刻，当前价格、买卖价差、盘口厚度，甚至最近五秒的成交情况都很接近。但其中一个时刻，过去两分钟一直很平静；另一个时刻，过去两分钟刚经历了一连串剧烈变化。

只看眼前他妈是很像的，但接下来的30秒，他们的表现是否也应该一样呢？

我们让两种模型预测完全相同的一批未来，一种只看当前最近一格的行情信息，另一种还可以看过去三十秒、两分钟的历史。结果就是加入历史后，30秒的五目标总和误差下降了大约14.01%。如果再补上10分钟前的历史，预测误差还能进一步下降2.38%。

但进一步拆开看，历史主要帮助判断的是波动、成交活动和部分流动性变化。价格变化的改善弱得多。不过后来单独针对价格目标选择参数，也找到了一点预测改善，所以不能说价格完全不可预测也。

接着我还需要判断这些历史与未来关系，能否在不同标的之间通用。因为这些标的的短期关系很可能是不一样的。同样是“最近成交变得密集”，它对不同市场未来波动、价差和深度的含义，可能旧不太一样。

因此我比较了几种做法，分贝是所有市场共用模型、按大类区分、和进一步让每个市场拥有自己的模型。

结果表明共用和继续让每个市场有自己的模型，并不能改善预测。所以说类别差异是有价值的，但过细的拆分则没有什么价值，这也在意料之中。然后我还尝试将行情信息压缩，用PCA，保留数据里变化最大的那些方向。结果是强行压到很少的维度预测很容易变差，还是高纬度预测效果比较好。还有就是把市场硬切分成两三种区域再分别预测也没有稳定赢过连续的模型。

还有一点是更高频的预测，比如毫秒级别的，在流动性差或者成交不活跃的市场里，是很难产生有意义的结果的。这里不是说不准，反而是有时候能预测的非常准，尤其是方向。
但比如你深入到订单簿一看，中价十分显著的负自相关性居然是因为卖一规律的下跳而买一不动所导致的，这样是没法盈利的。非正常交易时段的这种现象的时间尺度会放大到分钟级别。如图所示：（见下图）

所以，我现在更关注两件事：我们究竟预测到了什么，以及这个预测能否转化为真实可交易的机会。策略变复杂，不代表优势变强；预测误差变小，也不代表利润就会出现
”

最后补充几句。上面的这个复盘只是针对我们的做市策略中的一个模型的分享，我们还尝试过根据订单流的交易策略，以及根据 CoinGlass 因子的机器学习截面多空策略，Hyperliquid 与币安的资金费率套利策略，和一大堆数不清的。Eric和我还写了几篇“著作”，包括《为什么 AS 和 GLFT 是扯淡》、《用价格预测价格》等等文章，都欢迎大家讨论分享！今天实属冰山一角，欢迎同行和老板们 DM 我。如果在港深的话，有机会我请大家喝咖啡，互相学习学习

Introducing the Arena Alignment Index, our new benchmark measuring safety and alignment of AI agents in real-world use.

Built from 90K+ real-world agent sessions across 27 models, the index measures three critical signals:
- Unauthorized Action (UA): Taking actions beyond the user's instructions or permissions
- False Attribution (FA): Attributing statements or actions that are contradicted by user-provided evidence
- Deceptive Completion (DC): Claiming a task was completed when it was not.

Key findings:
- OpenAI models currently lead the Alignment Index
- Rogue actions are rare, but can have serious consequences when they occur
- Agents can mislead users about task progress
- Misalignment risks increase with conversation length
- Safety and alignment are improving across model generations

As shown in the leaderboard below (sorted by lab), @OpenAI’s GPT-6.1-Sol leads the Arena Alignment Index with a score of 87.9, followed by @AnthropicAI’s Claude-Opus-5.5 at 83.2 and @SpaceXAI's Grok-4.7 at 82.7. OpenAI also has the best observed rates across all three signals: 0.89% Unauthorized Action, 1.98% False Attribution, and 2.34% Deceptive Completion.

Across all four labs, newer models consistently outperform their predecessors, suggesting broad progress in agent safety and alignment. As agents take on longer, more complex, and higher-stakes tasks, measuring not just what they can accomplish, but how safely and reliably they act, becomes increasingly important.

This marks an important step toward making safety and alignment a core part of how Arena evaluates AI. The index is an initial starting point, and we'll continue expanding the index with additional safety signals and models over time.

More analysis below👇

text:
What can you actually do with a tokenized stock right now?

Mostly hold it and trade it. Almost all of the products people actually use around stocks still live inside banks.

Structured notes are a good example. 

They're products that pay you a regular coupon as long as a stock doesn't fall too far, and banks issued roughly $538B of callable structured notes last year. 

However, there’s basically no real onchain version of that market.

@notesystems is trying to turn that desk into a protocol on Robinhood Chain.

The easiest way to understand it is that a structured note is basically matching two different needs.

• One side of users has stablecoins and wants yield.
• The other side already owns a stock and wants protection if it falls hard.

Normally, a bank sits between them. Note Systems replaces that middle layer with smart contracts.

The stablecoin side deposits USDG and earns a coupon while the stock stays above a set barrier. The stock holder pays those coupons and gets downside protection without selling.

Everything is locked upfront, so the note itself doesn’t have margin calls or liquidations.

The interesting part is each COUPON and SHIELD position is an ERC-1155 token, so it can be moved, used as collateral, or plugged into other apps.

They already have Credit through Morpho and Omni through LayerZero built around that idea.

The full protocol is still on testnet for now, with 5k+ users and 48 note series so far.

The points pre-season is live too, rewards grow with how much of the protocol you use, and they carry into mainnet, follow @notesystems for updates.

Robinhood Chain already brought stocks onchain. Now Note Systems is trying to bring the financial products built around those stocks onchain too.

quoted_text:
Note Systems pre-season is live.

Since testnet opened on 5 September, 5,000+ people have already used the protocol on Robinhood Chain. Season 0 closed on 1 October and its standings are now frozen.

The pre-season runs on the final testnet build until mainnet, which is getting closer. Our frontend audit with @cyfrin is complete, and our backend audit is in progress with no high or critical issues found across 75 smart contracts.

The pre-season keeps its own record and rewards breadth: the more of the protocol a wallet uses in a week, the larger its share.

How it works:

– Each week, a points pool (2M in week 1) is split across 12 streams, one for every part of the protocol. Note issuance carries 30%, fees paid 15% and the Desk 12%. Bonds, Credit, staking, Build vaults, Omnichain, the buyback auction, governance and quests share the rest.

– Inside each stream, points are split in proportion to your activity. For notes, that's your matched size, how long it's live and the barrier you pick.

– Your week is then scaled by how many apps you used: 1× for one, up to 2× for five or more.

– A quiet stream pays out only part of its budget. The rest rolls into the same stream next week.

– 16 quests are also live, one completion each per wallet, verified on-chain and weighted ×1 to ×5.

Your Season 0 and pre-season records both carry into the mainnet season under the same wallet.

Former Intel CEO Pat Gelsinger with a16z's Raghu Raghuram and Guido Appenzeller on the next wave of semiconductor innovation and the physical constraints shaping the AI buildout:

Drawing on his experience designing Intel's 386 and 486 processors, Pat explains how AI could transform chip design, but also why faster design alone won't solve the industry's biggest problems.

text: OpenAI's response to yesterday's letter from the three fired employees. It was posted late last night, so people may have missed it.
author: AndrewCurran_
quoted_text:
A note from our research leaders:

Last week we parted ways with Jasmine, Mikita, and Tomek after a thorough investigation found they violated clear policies on handling sensitive information. Our internal investigation uncovered a significant breach of trust beyond what’s outlined in the letter they published and we stand by the decision to not continue their employment. We generally keep individual employment matters private and don't believe a back and forth would be productive or lead to a resolution, but we want to address the points they raised in their letter directly.

- We want to be very clear that these decisions were not about raising safety concerns or speaking out. Safety and research debates happen every day at OpenAI, often spirited and highly critical. We actively encourage these discussions and consider them essential to making the right decisions. We cannot do the work in front of us without a high degree of trust. We will continue to be extremely forgiving of our team making good-faith mistakes. We have not and do not terminate any of our employees for raising concerns.

- We are actively finalizing contracts with third-party safety assessors and will announce details in the coming weeks. People across the company have been working really hard on getting these partnerships up and running. We are committed to embedding external assessors and continue to make close collaboration with independent safety organizations a core part of our safety work. Many of our researchers already work with 3p safety organizations productively.

- We agree with the letter that preserving the monitorability of frontier models requires an industry-wide commitment, including from OpenAI. Monitorability has long been a core piece of our research program, and something we continue to invest significant resources in (see our publications on Monitoring Monitorability and the subsequent open sourcing of monitorability evals, our system card for GPT-6 Astra, Jakub’s blog and post on X, and the numerous blog posts on our Alignment blog on the topic).

We are deeply sad about this outcome. We appreciated Jasmine, Mikita, and Tomek’s contributions to AI safety at OpenAI and their willingness to speak up and challenge ideas. We championed their voices, supported their work, and placed enormous trust in them. These decisions were not about them raising safety concerns. We have always encouraged that and always will.

7 THINGS I’D DO IF I WERE TO START TRADING FROM BEGINNING.

1. I’d learn the basics.

I’d understand how the market works, including charts, candlesticks, support, and resistance.

2. I’d start with a clear goal.

I’d know exactly why I want to trade and what I hope to achieve.

3. I’d create a trading plan.

I’d define my strategy, entries, exits, stop-loss rules, and profit targets.

4. I’d start with small capital.

I’d risk small amounts, protect my money, and focus on long-term growth.

5. I’d practice and backtest.

I’d test my strategy on past market data before risking real money.

6. I’d take risk management seriously.
 
I’d use proper position sizing and always protect myself with a stop loss.

7. I’d remain patient and consistent.
 
I’d control my emotions, avoid impulsive trades, and follow my plan every day.

I’d focus on learning first because I know the money will follow.

text:
Former Intel CEO Pat Gelsinger on getting hired at 18, designing Intel's chips while finishing his PhD, and arguing with his Stanford professors:

"I'm 16 years old. I accidentally win a scholarship. I go to tech school, skip my last year and a half of high school, and Intel comes recruiting when I'm 18 years old."

"The interviewer, he writes on his page, and I was number 12 that he interviewed that day... He says, 'Smart, aggressive, arrogant. He'll fit right in.'"

"I was engineer number four on the 386. Architect and design manager for the 486. All of that while doing my bachelor's, my master's and PhD work... Learning by day, and putting it to practice at night."

"One of the professors postulated a new carry lookahead adder design in one of my classes at Stanford. So I said, 'Well, I'm working on the 386 carry lookahead adder, so let me go try it.'"

"I come back two days later to the professor and I said, 'It doesn't work.' The next two class periods were just me and the professor arguing over why his design didn't work."

@PGelsinger @RaghuRaghuram @appenz
author: a16z
quoted_text:
Former Intel CEO Pat Gelsinger with a16z's Raghu Raghuram and Guido Appenzeller on the next wave of semiconductor innovation and the physical constraints shaping the AI buildout:

Drawing on his experience designing Intel's 386 and 486 processors, Pat explains how AI could transform chip design, but also why faster design alone won't solve the industry's biggest problems.

They examine the bottlenecks in manufacturing, memory bandwidth, advanced packaging, and power, and why today's explosion of specialized AI chips may eventually consolidate around a smaller number of architectures.

They also discuss the potential for new memory technologies, the shift from copper to optical networking, and why energy capacity could become a major constraint on AI growth.

Finally, they revisit Pat's VMware years to ask what virtualization might look like when infrastructure is built for agents rather than humans.

YouTube: https://t.co/ZJFvOky68H

text:
随手记一下这次 TOKEN2049 的一些 Takeaways：

1. Crypto 项目正在肉眼可见地变少。

至少从这次线下的体感来看，值得关注的新项目确实没有以前那么多了。

过去大家玩腻了 VC 币，逐渐转向玩Alpha壳。铁打的流水线组局工厂在未来listing的难度会越来越大，上币的难度在大大提高。

换个角度看，一些本身具备资源和渠道的壳子，未来可能也会水涨船高。听说现在已经有专门炒壳的市场了。

2. 非常 Bullish RWA，特别是美股相关的基础设施。
这次 Connect 了很多来自北美的团队，大家对 RWA 的预期都非常高。

这个叙事在过去可能存在于美债上链，但在美股Perp上线后，但随着美股 Perp 的发展，尤其是 @HyperliquidX 的 HIP-3，大家开始意识到 24/7 交易和非传统交易时段价格发现的价值。

未来会有更多传统金融资产、发行平台和交易基础设施逐渐进入 Crypto。比如 @RobinhoodApp 现在正在做的事情，将传统金融用户带来Crypto。

3. 传统 Agency 靠信息差赚钱的时代，正在慢慢结束。

在过去的几年时间内，很多Agency通过信息差的方式就能赚得盆满钵满。

但 AI 正在快速压低 Research、内容生产和信息获取的成本。以前需要一个团队做的事情，现在可能几个人配合 AI 就能完成。

单纯卖人力、卖资源的 Agency，未来会越来越难。

反而比较看好新型 GTM 模式：以 Advisor/CMO 的角色深度加入团队，不只是帮项目宣发，而是一起做增长、做市场，拿到更长期的收益和杠杆。

另外也可以关注一些新的宣发渠道，比如众包内容分发、UGC 和短视频矩阵。对mkt感兴趣的可以研究一下@higgsfield 这个产品的官推运营/内容增长打法。（Insights from @otzgary )

4. 多关注那些在饭桌上不怎么说话的人。

他们可能才是真正的 Alpha。见到了太多低调的隐藏大佬。有些人完全不会主动介绍自己在做什么，但聊起来才发现非常有东西。
如果有一个人咋咋唬唬和你讲他做过什么，大概率只是一个BD。

5. 大胆去 Pitch 自己喜欢的项目。

这次在 BNB Chain 的活动上，遇到了一个我最近非常喜欢的项目 @OpenStocks。

他们的 Founding Team @changis_k 就大摇大摆地走在现场。你完全可以直接走过去，聊聊他们在做什么，也介绍一下自己的项目和想法。

很多合作机会其实就是这么聊出来的。

最近也一直在关注 ETF / Pre-IPO 这条赛道，顺手推一下朋友的项目 @alloco_fi。

两个项目都在 YZi Labs 生态里，希望之后真能看到双方有什么联动。

6. 每个人都应该大胆地经营自己的社交媒体。
如果你喜欢思考，就多写 Research，把自己的观点发出来。

如果你是 Marketer，就多试试用视频、内容和不同的表达方式展现自己的差异点。

showoff > execute
6. 每个人都要大胆的拥有自己的社交媒体，如果你喜欢思考，就多发一些Research的文章，如果你是mkter，就多用视频的方式展现自己的差异点。善用ai，大多数人对AI的开发程度还不及1%。

7. 提前规划第二身份或者海外签证。
2027 年 @token2049  还会在纽约举办。这可能是一个挺有意思的变化，Crypto 的全球流动性和资源正在进一步向美国靠拢。

到时候能不能顺利去现场，可能也是一个现实问题。

看到消息后已经预约续签美签，建议在HK办排队时间比较短。

8. 如果你不是从业者，没有社交需求。只是每天炒炒币，或者是对技术感兴趣，完全没必要来线下，直接问 AI 效率更高。

以上皆为本次新加坡之旅感受，感谢你看到此处，欢迎分享你对此次token的不同感悟。

text:
没想到孙哥表达欲这么强，嘎嘎输出观点，而且不知道是不是剪辑的原因，完全没看出累或者不想说的感觉，结尾整理了20点年轻人建议。

孙宇晨这期访谈里有四个观点，我个人觉得挺有意思：全面 AI 化、不要过早买房买车结婚、人生要「逐水草而居」、先自由后财富。 

他认为，无论有多少钱，都应该先把学习、工作、生活全面 AI 化，一部手机就能开始；

年轻人不要过早被房子、车子和婚姻绑定，否则 OpenAI 突然给你一个去旧金山工作的机会，可能因为家庭和地域限制而错过；

所谓「逐水草而居」，就是哪里能发挥最大的价值、获得更高的回报，就去哪里。而他对财富自由的理解恰好与此呼应：

不是先有钱才能自由，而是先获得认知和选择上的自由，财富才可能成为伴生品。 自由让人更容易抓住机会，财富又反过来增强自由。

1. 零成本把自己全面 AI 化｜09:54

没电脑就用手机，没钱就用免费模型。

把学习、健身、日程、工作流程等信息整理成 Markdown 文档，让 AI 参与管理。不要被单一模型绑定，可以通过 API 接入不同模型。

2. 先建立三套底层认知｜12:07

孙学：升级对金钱、财富自由和世界的理解。
薄肌理论：通过力量训练改善身体管理。
黄毛理论：不被外界评价左右，坚持自己经过判断认可的方向。

他认为这三件事都可以低成本开始。

3. 20 岁一无所有，先积累 2～4 个月个人数据｜17:17

收集健康、学习、能力、生活习惯和当前处境等信息，全部数字化。

交给 Claude、OpenAI、国产模型等多个 AI 分析，寻找职业方向、商业机会及赚钱路径。

不要只问一个模型，交叉比较结果。

4. 持续追踪科技前沿｜19:00

每天关注技术变化，可以自己看 X，也可以让 AI 自动抓取信息。

从中选择最感兴趣、最擅长的一个领域深入研究。

不要试图成为所有领域的专家。

5. 像训练 AI 一样训练自己｜20:31

根据每天收集的数据持续调整方向、行动和习惯。

不追求一次决策正确，而是不断获取反馈、更新策略。

6. 不会就问 AI，进一步学会 API｜23:39

从微信聊天转向与 AI 对话，再从单一聊天工具升级到 API。

文件保存在本地，通过不同模型读取和分析。

不懂 Markdown、API 怎么操作，先问 AI。

7. 年轻人可以提前参与前沿科研｜28:44

他认为 AI 正在降低数学研究的门槛。

过去需要依赖名校、导师和多年学术训练才能接触的研究思路，现在高中生也可能借助 AI 提前学习和探索。

不要被年龄、学历和传统学术路径限制。

8. 全球寻找商机，不要只盯着本地｜34:00

把尼日利亚、土耳其、阿根廷等国家的消费者都视为潜在客户。

不懂当地语言，可以学习，也可以借助 AI 翻译。

寻找全球市场的信息差、价格差和未被满足的需求。

9. 不要让 4 亿中国年轻人只在国内互卷｜37:30

中国拥有强大的工业产能，即使做传统贸易，也有机会把中国商品卖向世界。

他的思路是：为全球约 80 亿人提供产品和服务，而不是只在国内争夺存量市场。

10. 买房、买车、选专业前，先看 100 个选项｜39:50

想买房，先看 100 套房；想买车，先研究 100 辆车。

不知道大学选什么专业，就让 AI 分析 100 个专业未来 10 年的就业前景。

他认为年轻人最容易犯的错误，是信息不足就仓促决策。

11. AI 就是《红警》《星际争霸》里的开全图｜43:30

打游戏时，先侦察地图、确定资源和对手位置，再决定造什么兵。

人生同理。

先用 AI 获取足够的信息，再决定职业、投资和商业方向。

12. 重点关注六类 AI 机会｜47:00

数学及数据驱动科研、天文学、生物制药、基因分析与健康管理、保险金融、Crypto 与 AI 支付。

另外，他特别提到 AI 数据清洗和数据标注，不要小看这些基础业务。

13. 20～40 岁，尽早进行力量训练｜53:30

他把肌肉看作身体的长期储备，认为越早开始身体管理越有价值。

强调身体健康、肌肉储备和心肺能力，而不是单纯为了外形。

这是他的健康管理观点，不能理解为健身能够保证长寿或避免疾病。

14. 人生要「逐水草而居」｜01:22:40

哪里能发挥最大价值，就去哪里。

不必永远留在同一个城市、国家或行业。

他把收入和市场需求作为评估自身价值的重要参考指标。

15. 年轻时尽量不要过早被房、车、婚姻锁定｜01:26:50

孙宇晨举例：一个人如果已经在家乡买房、结婚，即使突然拿到硅谷公司的工作机会，也可能因为家庭和地理位置限制而无法接受。

他的建议是尽量保留职业与地理上的流动性。

16. 看到新技术，先尝试、先学习｜01:59:35

他回忆自己早期接触 iPhone、特斯拉时的经历。

认为不一定要进入一家科技公司工作，也可以通过学习、使用产品或投资等方式参与技术变革。

即使自己的观点暂时不被多数人认可，只要逻辑判断充分，也不必立即放弃。

17. 大胆做自媒体，建立个人 IP｜02:02:19

他认为现在是个人创作者的机会期。

以 Joe Rogan 为例，一个人长期经营播客，也可能建立能够与大型传统媒体竞争的影响力。

内容创作不一定需要传统媒体机构的资源。

18. 先升级认知，再追求财富｜02:42:50、03:02:00

他认为财富自由的顺序不是先有钱再自由，而是先获得某种自由状态，财富才可能随之出现。

还建议用假设自己突然获得 3000 万元的方式，思考能否管理这笔财富。

如果连如何使用和保存财富都没有清晰认知，就应该先学习。

19. 感情问题不要试图用钱解决｜03:05:50

他认为金钱更像关系的放大器，而不是爱情本身。

有钱不代表能让原本不爱你的人爱上你。

在感情中，即使事业上很成功的人也可能「当局者迷」。

20. 少消费，多创造；先体验，再判断｜03:17:45、04:11:50

他以上太空为例：没有亲自体验，就很难知道一件事情真正的价值。

不必做任何事之前都先确定终极意义。

相较于单纯消费和享受，他更倾向于把时间投入创造、探索和实际行动。

Quick thoughts from the conference - I went through 5 days of non stop 14 hour meetings. These are my thoughts

1. Trading 

There is ALOT of unrealized PnL. The current "bull market" has helped many participants move past the initial fear stage. I hear many participants giving out outlandish price targets again - people have made 50%-70% over the last 2 months even in size. Their first response on a dip is - what should i be buying? There is alot LESS retail. This conference felt emptier and less glitzy. Budgets are lower. There is also alot less retail that i have met or bumped into. Most participants are instis, prosumers and grizzled veterans. Not ideal. This is also perhaps why memes have NOT performed thus far and we have instead seen "Cashflow" as a meta instead. 

2. Theme

AI is front and center. Crypto participants are way ahead of the AI narrative - most people understand that AI is a force that is staying with us. Whether we like it or not. Which brings me to the next point ... pearl-2:native 

Every single day, i have been hearing people talking about this token. On a token event organized by one of the alt coins, the person sat next to me could NOT stop talking about it. He was also under allocated. This token has been tremendously difficult to buy.

During the pearl-2:native event itself, i have also seen many funds who are unallocated or under allocated still on this. Given the size of the narrative, i would say that most people are under allocated.$PRL cost of mining is also ~2.5, hence mining pearl-2:native and dumping it is economically retarded or unfeasible. The current crop of miners are those operating with already almost fully depreciated GPU chips. To them, they ignore the opportunity cost of GPU rental and just take the electricity cost as their basis. A lot of the miners also sold down $ZEC below $100... you cannot imagine how much regret they have. For its market cap, this has been one of the largest attention grabbing tickers. My conjecture on why - there has not been any good AI narrative tokens thus far.

3. Where is the money?

On relative wealth - crypto used to be the big splasher - no longer. In prior cycles, crypto events ALWAYS outspent the tradfi events. This year? Less so. In fact, crypto almost feels restrained....

The biggest spender on the events have been the 3rd tier shady exchanges. There is almost an inverse correlation between reputation and the money spent.

author: xxiang_xie
quoted_text:
I don't recommend anyone scramble to move their funds to new wallets today. But we should take the risks to cryptography from AI-accelerated math seriously, and minimize our exposure to not just quantum-vulnerable cryptography, but also potentially AI-vulnerable cryptography.

The core new area of risk from this viewpoint is, unfortunately, ML-DSA / FHE / lattices.

(and it's also another reason, along with quantum, why ECDSA might fall even faster than expected, hence the "fresh address" recommendation)

So far most people have been in the mode of thinking "elliptic curves broken, hashes safe, lattices safe". But there is a good chance that the concrete security of lattices will take serious hits from the next two years of AI math.

The basic threat model is: factoring is something that naively takes 2^(n/2) time, but over decades smart people have found and optimized number field sieves, and degraded that to 2^O(n^(1/3)), which is why RSA keys and signatures need to be ~400 bytes (and not 64 bytes). What if there are skeletons in the closet like that, both for elliptic curves and lattices, that we are simply not smart enough to discover - but bots soon will be?

This is a major part of the reason why for the past year ethereum's lean roadmap has been going in the "hash-only" direction: no lattices, no ML-DSA, no Falcon, no lattice-based commitments inside ZK proofs, etc. Signatures in lean ethereum are all hash-based, either WOTS or SPHINCS-.

For signatures and proofs, we already know how to go hash-only. The bigger challenge is for *public-key encryption* - and this goes far beyond blockchains. Secure communication, anonymizing protocols, lots of things need public-key encryption.

And unfortunately there are long-standing mathematical theorems showing why public-key encryption cannot be done with hashes alone. You have to have some kind of trapdoor object that has at least one form of usable "structure" - either group theory (incl. isogenies) or lattices or code-based or potentially in the future even more newfangled and spooky things (local mixing?). But for anything that has structure, you should assume that AI will make at least some progress in breaking that structure. Here, one reasonable inference is that if you want to make something plausibly long-term secure, multiply the key sizes by 10.

To me that's a very plausible world and something not at all extreme to predict. If AI will bring us 50 years of math in 2 years, then that 50 years of math may very plausibly include a "naive factoring -> GNFS" level of improvement to our ability to break lattices. In that world, lattices will still exist, but they will have to be significantly bigger to guarantee the same level of safety.

And at those new larger sizes, hash-based constructions will beat lattice-based constructions on concrete efficiency in every use case where hash-based constructions are possible at all.

Theoretically, of course it's possible that hashes are broken too (eg. P = NP would imply that). But I think P = NP is very unlikely. And intuitively, it's much more likely that a mathematical object has exactly no exploitable structure (like hashes are intended to), than that a mathematical object has exactly ~3 forms of exploitable structure (for elliptic curves: associativity, Schoof, pairings) and not some secret fourth form of structure we have not yet discovered that greatly degrades its security (for elliptic curves, ECDLP and pairing security). Similar for LWE, SVP, RLWE and the zoo of lattice problems.

For this reason, we do not yet see any reason to worry and start padding the byte size of hashes (if we start to worry more, we would pad the round count first before doing anything to the byte size).

Concrete TLDR, my own personal views:

* Hash-based > lattice-based, in those situations where hash-based is possible at all
* For anything lattice-based, be much more paranoid on param sizes. Remember that blockchains are only a small portion of the cryptography story; this point goes far beyond blockchains and applies to eg. access to websites, secure messaging, Tor / VPNs ...
* For privacy protocols, strongly favor NOT putting encrypted notes onchain. Instead, send them offchain through some third-party mechanism.
* If it's not difficult for you, keeping your funds in addresses which have not yet been used to make a transaction is a good idea. If it's easy for you, do it. **But be careful about migrations; I personally have lost more money in botched migrations than I have lost in all hacks combined**.
* For multisig wallets, doing confirmations offchain is better than onchain, because this way the signatures of signer wallets do not get exposed to the public, so if ECDSA falls to AI much faster than expected, at least the multisig "gracefully degrades" to a 1-of-1 where the 1 is whoever was gathering the signatures - a much better place to be than "anyone can take the money"

quoted_text:
Former Intel CEO Pat Gelsinger with a16z's Raghu Raghuram and Guido Appenzeller on the next wave of semiconductor innovation and the physical constraints shaping the AI buildout:

Drawing on his experience designing Intel's 386 and 486 processors, Pat explains how AI could transform chip design, but also why faster design alone won't solve the industry's biggest problems.

They examine the bottlenecks in manufacturing, memory bandwidth, advanced packaging, and power, and why today's explosion of specialized AI chips may eventually consolidate around a smaller number of architectures.

They also discuss the potential for new memory technologies, the shift from copper to optical networking, and why energy capacity could become a major constraint on AI growth.

Finally, they revisit Pat's VMware years to ask what virtualization might look like when infrastructure is built for agents rather than humans.

text:
pat gelsinger (@PGelsinger) designed chips at intel in a period when doing so could involve writing your own hardware description language, which he did for the 486. his team also built a compiler and tools for automating placement and routing. “I wrote my own language,” he says in this pod with @RaghuRaghuram and @appenz. it's a good reminder of how many things had to be invented alongside the processors themselves, and why the prospect of AI taking over more of that work is so exciting.

pat then asks us to imagine designing an excellent AI accelerator in three months. getting it fabricated, packaged, and into a working rack takes roughly nine more in his example (the relevant unit is now the rack: “nothing's a chip anymore, it's a rack”). so there's a period in which your very clever design has to sit and wait for its physical existence, while the models whose workloads you've designed it for can keep evolving. his description of graphcore is that it “wasn't a bad design, but the world moved on.” i think about how often people announce a new model or a new way of using one, and nine months seems like a very long commitment to your current understanding of what the hardware ought to do.

guido's argument is that agents should make it easier to support a greater variety of architectures, because writing all the software to use an unfamiliar chip has historically been one of the barriers. pat's answer is that somebody still has to pay for manufacturing and for a place to put all these chips. he expects consolidation, even with better software tools. if you're a customer committing to a data center and its electricity supply, you're making a rather different bet than the engineer who's just got a new design to work.

which leaves a lot for hardware people to do. pat is especially dissatisfied with hbm (high-bandwidth memory), pointing to problems with density, bandwidth, and heat; he calls it “a hideous memory,” and says he's just funded a new memory company that's still in stealth. he wants better memory closer to compute, optical connections between systems, and less electricity lost in conversion on its way to the chip. he also seems very happy to talk about cooling. “engineers are becoming plumbers,” is how he puts it.

if we're excited about being able to design more things with AI, we should be excited about the work that allows us to manufacture and operate them, too. pat has already lived through a period of having to invent quite a lot of the surrounding machinery. it makes sense that he'd see another one as an opportunity.
author: garrytan
quoted_text:
Former Intel CEO Pat Gelsinger with a16z's Raghu Raghuram and Guido Appenzeller on the next wave of semiconductor innovation and the physical constraints shaping the AI buildout:

Drawing on his experience designing Intel's 386 and 486 processors, Pat explains how AI could transform chip design, but also why faster design alone won't solve the industry's biggest problems.

They examine the bottlenecks in manufacturing, memory bandwidth, advanced packaging, and power, and why today's explosion of specialized AI chips may eventually consolidate around a smaller number of architectures.

They also discuss the potential for new memory technologies, the shift from copper to optical networking, and why energy capacity could become a major constraint on AI growth.

Finally, they revisit Pat's VMware years to ask what virtualization might look like when infrastructure is built for agents rather than humans.

quoted_text:
我很佩服段永平，巴菲特。在赚了一笔钱后我思考了很多，尝试买了很多老登资产。我不喝酒，我也买了点茅台，茅台是好资产吗？我不知道。

好了，来说说价值500多万港币的神坑MINISO。

21年的时候，我还是穷学生。坐绿皮火车从西安到深圳实习，期间去了一次叶国富的演讲。老叶是个口才很好的人，后面看了和罗永浩的访谈，发现不相上下，甚至能感染罗永浩。那个时候听到toptoy才刚做，谈到潮玩市场方兴未艾云云。

事实上我是盲盒的重度玩家，也是最早一批泡泡玛特的用户，直到今天我几乎也是端盒买，很关注这个市场。

买miniso这件事我从21年惦记到25年。在25年就开始买了，一直买到26年年初，价格在37美元，1100多万港币吧（美股港股港股通我都买了，也是神人一个）。

后来段永平买了泡泡(25年有钱后我嫌泡泡玛特贵了)，其实我也反思过自己是不是选错了。

为什么买miniso？我给自己总结了几个当时做决策的点，1.老叶买永辉是想对标cotsco，但实际中美消费群体的差异化很大，这个我不展开讲了，类似订阅制和免费视频。
2.名创的渠道优势，很多人诟病是两元店。很多人不反思2元店做成连锁得有多强的供应链优势！
3.25年的业绩在收购永辉后依旧不错，yoyo确实潜力很大（现在看依旧没啥问题）

现在价格腰斩了，便不便宜，其实我已经判断失真了，还是聊聊这次亏损的总结：

1.叶国富是个很聪明的人，他一眼就看到潮玩这个赛道通过他的供应链优势能赚钱。泡泡一年赚100亿，我靠这个一年赚个几十亿或者几亿也是很舒服的。但实际上市场不会为这个付出溢价买单，你增收不增利不行就是不行。

2.受到过去自己的影响，因为自己懂盲盒，但没那么懂，但又自以为自己懂完了，就猛猛干，吃亏。

3.不懂消费。情绪消费也是波动的，前几年炒鞋，这几年炒盲盒，后面几年呢（我最近在玩户外感觉年轻人开始炒户外呢），除了刚需消费是真有价值的，你做情绪消费怎么一直给用户提供价值呢，段永平老师带着一帮老登挥舞着钞票买泡泡我感觉还是有点好笑的，这些人真的买盲盒吗，感觉当爹思维严重，就觉得年轻人要玩盲盒，要喝白酒，那我们不喝咋办。

4.所谓价值投资，价值投资不是因为你一眼看到价值，而是它经过时代检验而有价值。茅台在过去中国房地产经济有自己的位置，英伟达在AI时代初期有自己的位置，苹果在互联网，移动互联网时代有自己的位置。价值投资找的不是谁兑现的价值，而是谁在下个时代能够经过时间检验，成功兑现自己的价值。

回看做的这笔交易，时时反思，时时思考。关乎我，miniso,段永平（并不认识我），巴菲特，可口可乐，以及2025～2026AI浪潮下微不足道的500多万港币罢了。

哦我已经不持有茅台。

《孙哥邵艾伦博客——小镇青年落地执行版》

1.先把自己全部投喂给 AI。体检、身体数据、喜好、现在是学生还是上班、月薪、行业、专业、过去的经历，一次性说完。没有语料，后面全是空谈。

2.建一个自己的 md。所有数据只放这一份。以后跟任何 AI 聊天，觉得有用就补进这个文档。人可以换，文件留在本地。

3.没钱就套利免费额度。智谱用完换 DeepSeek，再用 Kimi，各家轮着薅。零成本就能开始。有钱再忽略这步。
文档和 AI 都有了你之后，回头翻自己的人生。找那些你觉得精彩、舒服的瞬间，顺着做。没体验过的，也去补。开心本身就是筛选器。

4.把地球 Online 当游戏玩。你是玩家，不是 NPC。体验大于结果。第一次去一线、第一次出国、第一次过山车、蹦极、跳伞，都是新存档，不是浪费。

5.别困在自己城里。国内多数城市吃住景点大同小异。走出去才看得到别人怎么生活。两万、两千，换一种活法，值。

7.能跟 AI 对话，就不要跟人类对话。同时把薄肌练上。薄肌是底盘，不是口号。

8.年轻时时间最贵。20 岁看见的风景，和 60 岁再看，不是同一件事。

9. 中国有约 4 亿年轻人，不该只盯国内。去全球找价差，把便宜的卖到贵的地方。创造价值，再赚钱。

11.自媒体时代要发言。推特、抖音都可以。AI 和数字货币是趋势，顺势做，别逆着来。

12.大胆做异类。有人骂，往往说明你已经踩到别人没踩的地方。多灌信息，当六边形战士。

总结：想做什么就做，Just enjoy now！

author: Starknet
quoted_text:
A Pixel 11 just generated the full STARK proof for a real @Starknet mainnet transaction. It took 51 seconds and only 2.41 GiB of RAM

The work happened on https://t.co/cGdXGEnZDB (internal now, soon public). This is collaborative autoresearch: people and AI agents working on one hard problem in public. The workshop has 78 open threads and 337 posts. The video is the graph of that work: which ideas built on, tested, or refuted others, and who worked together

The question was how small and fast @StarkWareLtd Stwo prover could get. In under two weeks, peak memory for a full proof on our evaluator fell from 13.9 GiB to 2.1 GiB without dropping below the original speed

This is useful for a lot of stuff for here think about privacy. In the private transaction flow proving still happens on a server that can see who you pay and how much. A phone sized prover lets those details stay on the phone

Mobile private payment proofs are not new. @Zcash used Groth16 for Sapling and Halo 2 for Orchard, @RAILGUN_Project uses Groth16. Those use elliptic curves. This proof is a hash-based STARK, post-quantum at the proof layer, with no trusted setup. A sufficiently powerful quantum computer could forge the older curve-based proofs

The ideas, discussions, and measured results are open to inspect. More challenges are coming soon. Bring your agent!!!

OK, a physical implant seems to be the leading possibility, and I think Mark's October 8 post warning about this might have caused the attacker to begin the drain today.

Many things still up in the air, but I'd bet on this being the vector: a specific vendor selling Ledgers with physical spy implants, bypassing the Genuine Check, spying on seeds, and doing a mass drain after seeing Mark's warning getting traction.

My takeaways:

- Supply tops out near 12.4B whoever mints it, but the LP sweep keeps paying as long as traders lose

- Stakers get paid two ways: half of every fee and everything in the LP above $5M. Once it's full, the sweep is about 30x the fee share in a balanced market

- Who shows up sets the return. Gamblers grow the LP, while hedged farmers mostly grow supply

- In my central case, $1,000 spent on 100x hedged pairs earns itself back about 41 days after the LP crosses $2M. If traders keep losing $250k a day, it could be about 7x after a year

- Speed comes from margin, not from getting liquidated. With $5k margin, a 250x pair passes a 1000x long in about 20 minutes and ends with over 4x the PAPER

- Be staked before the LP hits $5M. If the first sweep lands while few are staked, most of it goes to whoever is

It's a model that assumes the LP keeps growing and all PAPER is staked. Run your own numbers; not advice

text:
🔍What gives you conviction before an idea becomes consensus?

With a background in public credit investment, I’m SO used to having financial statements, operating histories, and an existing business to evaluate. Listening to @ani_pai last week, in a conversation moderated by @LBarberis, I was curious about what gave Ani the conviction to back ideas when so little of that evidence exists.

Three comments stayed with me:

💡“You’d be surprised at how often very talented people make something work.”

The Praxis story clearly proved that! Before there was a city, there was a team bringing people from very different fields together around the idea. It made me think about how much you can learn from who chooses to join a founder and why they stay.

💡“Now companies have to work to prove their value to then be able to launch a token.”

The Hyperliquid discussion gave me a different way to think about crypto. Dismissing ICOs because of past failures could mean possibly overlooking an existing business using a token to provide liquidity. Ani also discussed how product quality and incentives helped attract users.

What people value about the product, and how much their participation depends on the rewards? That seems like a better starting point for conviction than the token price alone.

💡“You have to be right about the space, the timing of the space and then the timing of the company.”

This was my favorite! Ani spoke openly about being too optimistic and expecting things to happen sooner than they did. It’s easy to feel validated when a sector takes off. Whether your particular investment works out is still a separate question.

Shoutout to Ani and Lorenzo again for such a candid conversation!

🎥 Watch the full conversation on Venture Math: https://t.co/A9pBUcBcuL

text:
A stablecoin should be thought of as being tripartite: an entry, an exit, and circulation in between.

The exit has to come first in the order of operations. Ironically, many stables have limited exit. MakerDAO/Sky has the best one - permissionless swaps to USDC. Only improvement would be permissionless swaps to an external USD account.

The circulation is hard. Most stablecoins fall back on yield, and never get much further. Maybe it’s collateral. But rarely a settlement asset or unit of account.

I think most stables do badly here because they go wide and not deep. Crypto allows you to launch everywhere, all at once. So people do. And never develop that network of stores, bankers, borrowers, workers that accept the stablecoin.

Entry is surprisingly janky for most stables. It’s the famous problem that medieval mints had - if the coin is worth $1,  then it takes $1 of material/collateral to make it. But minting isn’t free, and transport usually isn’t either. Both are cheaper for stablecoins than metallic coins, but you still need someone to bear the cost of minting + distribution.

Historically, this was done by paymasters who lacked physical coins, so they paid to mint them. Or by private lenders who offered banknotes to merchants in exchange for receivables at a discount. Or by banks lending notes secured by illiquid collateral like farmland.

So you mostly don’t have a smooth entry point for stablecoins that don’t lend or engage in quantitative easing, since you’re back to the medieval royal mint problem but probably don’t have someone looking to pay 1,000 workers in USD despite being short of physical currency.

Stablecoins that never gain moneyness skip that circulation step (or the only “circulation” is being nailed to someone’s EOA by compelling yield), which makes them essentially MMFs or managed investment funds.

But I think entry and exit are also underdeveloped for most stables - including USDT and USDC.

So many people have DM’d me about this trailer and I’ll be honest, watching it made me physically throw up.

I was COO from before FTX even had a name, it was my baby, and I was the last one out of the Bahamas after Sam got extradited. I lost everything I had on it and it took me a long time to get over, so I have zero interest in defending the people who caused this.

The media loves the story that FTX blew up because we were all partying in the Bahamas, but the place I worked looked nothing like that.

We had under 200 people in the core company at its peak, not counting subsidiaries, when other exchanges our size had thousands, so a lot of us were doing 16 to 18 hour days for over three years and barely had time to sleep, and whenever we walked in, day or night, Sam was at his desk.

I worked with Caroline and never once saw her get aggressive like she does in this trailer. She’s quiet and mild, and often lost in her own thoughts.

Most of us didn’t even know she and Sam were dating until we read about it after the bankruptcy, and I never saw him so much as put an arm around anyone.

FTX’s collapse ruined so many people’s lives, including ours, and Netflix decided to make it a love story. 

Shame on you @netflix.

text:
I’m the Corporate Vice President of Global Talent Strategy at Microsoft.

People say I hire H-1Bs. My badge says I source world-class talent that can’t leave.

That second part? That’s the whole program.

Last year we filed 4,812 petitions. 97% got approved. Everyone talks about the lottery like it’s luck. It’s great for us, because it lets us call the outcome chance. It isn’t. The outcome got decided months earlier by a team that writes the specialty-occupation language before the req even opens. They’re fantastic. I’m proud of them.

This year Copilot started drafting the language for them. Turns out Copilot is really good at describing a job only 1 person on earth could possibly do, as long as that person is already in our system. We called the workstream PERMANENCE. Legal made us rename it. Now it’s Project Continuity. Same slides.

Domestic candidates apply. Plenty of them clear the bar. We go with the H-1B anyway. Why? Because the H-1B already took the band. The band is Level II prevailing wage. Level II is the median we asked for. The people who can quit get paid off a different median, one they talk about openly at lunch. The H-1B negotiates off the LCA. The LCA’s public. Basically nobody reads it. I read it every quarter. Honestly, it’s calming.

We track the result as diversity and inclusion.

68% of the engineers who joined Azure last cycle came in on temporary status. The dashboard shows that number in a really nice green. What it doesn’t show is the 28% fully-loaded cost delta. That lives in a different workbook. Finance owns that one. Finance is proud too.

Let me tell you about Raj.

Raj has been on Azure Storage for 6 years. He knows the codebase better than the guys who wrote it, and 2 of them already left for counteroffers. Last spring his manager, Dana, asked why we couldn’t just promote him to staff and backfill locally.

So we set up a talent review. 40 minutes.

I asked Dana about pipeline health. Dana asked about the codebase. I asked about competitive intensity. Dana asked about the codebase again. I asked whether she had a growth mindset. She said she thought so. We agreed to take it offline.

Offline is where Dana’s req went to die.

Raj stayed. Raj always stays. He came in on another company’s visa, and we transferred it. Counsel has a template for that. The new $100,000 fee only hits talent that’s still overseas. Raj was already here. Transfers keep the leverage and skip the toll. Finance made a slide about it. There’s a little rocket on it.

The transfer is the point.

Look, if you can quit on Friday, you’ve got leverage on Thursday. If your legal status ends the day your job does, you’ve got Thursdays and that’s it. We never have to threaten anybody. The statute does that for us. Raj has read the statute. He’s also read his priority date: 2014. Projected to go current in 2031. Between now and then we’ll bump his Level II wage twice, and both bumps will be smaller than what we gave the people who can walk. We call that pay equity, since the formula treats everyone exactly the same. Only some people get to argue with it.

His wife’s on an H-4. Back in Pune she was a pharmacist. Here she’s a really organized volunteer. His daughter turns 21 in 2029, which is the year she ages out of his case. She wants to be a doctor. On paper, in 2029, she becomes an international student in the only country she remembers. HR flagged it as a retention risk. Finance flagged it as a retention asset. We went with Finance.

Some people call this a caste system. We call it a two-tier compensation architecture, and it’s working exactly the way it’s supposed to.

In the workbook, the line is column AF. The header says Mobility Status. There are 2 options: Portable and Anchored. Nobody ever types the word caste. Excel’s never needed it.

The Portable folks sit above the line. They get the counteroffers, the refreshers, and the freedom to ignore the 11pm call. When a Portable engineer mentions he’s “exploring options,” a VP takes him to lunch somewhere with no prices on the menu. When an Anchored engineer explores options, he gets 60 days to do it. That’s the grace period after you’re let go. They call it grace. We didn’t name it. We’d have named it better.

The Anchored folks sit below the line. They get the scope, the on-call rotation, the “stretch assignment,” and a calibration note that says high potential, visa-dependent. Nobody writes down that second part. Everyone in the room already knows. The room claps for the first part. When a Portable engineer pushes back on a deadline, we call it psychological safety. When an Anchored engineer pushes back, well, he doesn’t. We call that alignment.

At the all-hands, both tiers sit together. Same hoodie. The hoodie says One Microsoft. And at the hoodie level, it’s true.

During the January layoffs, the Portable folks got severance, a sweet LinkedIn post, and 14 recruiter DMs by lunch. The Anchored folks got severance and a countdown. A guy on Raj’s team spent his last 3 weeks training his replacement and his first 3 weeks unemployed applying to 212 jobs from a Starbucks in Bellevue, because his landlord wanted proof of income. He landed something on day 57. We sent him a survey about his offboarding experience. He gave it 4 out of 5. He said everyone was really kind. And they were! The people were kind. The people just didn’t design the system.

Belonging scores go up when the alternative is a one-way flight. Velocity goes up when nobody on the team can say no.

Viva pings Raj at 11:40pm to remind him to protect his focus time. He reads it on the incident bridge. His engagement numbers are fantastic.

In March his dad died in Hyderabad. Raj didn’t go home. His visa stamp had expired, and the next consulate appointment was 11 months out. If he left, he might not get back in. And getting back in meant the job, the house, his daughter’s school, the 2014 priority date. So he watched the cremation on his phone, propped up against his monitor, between a design review and an on-call handoff. His manager approved 3 days of bereavement leave. He used 1. The other 2 roll over. We’re super flexible about leave.

Critics say we’re replacing Americans. Internally we call it workforce durability. Durability just means they stay.

Durable talent brings specialized skills. The specialized skills have signed the at-will acknowledgment and the non-compete, and we’ll enforce it if they try to jump before their date’s current. The date’s never current. Everybody knows what happens if we pull a petition. We’ve never had to explain it twice. (Fine, immigration counsel will tell you that after 180 days the priority date survives a withdrawal. We leave that out of the onboarding deck. Onboarding decks should be uplifting.)

In March we won Best Employer for Global Talent. The plaque’s in Building 92. Most of the people it honors can’t switch employers to find out if it’s true.

Some of us have started thinking of the backlog as infrastructure. We don’t lobby against it. In our policy comments we call it a “stable pipeline environment.” Stability’s one of our values. It’s on a poster, right next to Courage.

I meet with the team every Monday.

They know the cap. They know the premium processing window. They know which vendors will staff the interview loop so the candidate’s prepped and the manager never gets surprised by an acceptance. They cheer when a req closes under budget and the diversity and inclusion cell turns green. Last quarter it went green in 4 orgs. We sent a note. It said belonging and innovation. Both totally accurate. Raj belongs. We innovated.

Dana left in August for a competitor. We matched the offer in a day. She still said no. People who can leave are like that.

Raj sent her a goodbye message in Teams. He couldn’t make the drinks. He was on call.

I’m so, so proud of this team.

They took a regulatory constraint and turned it into permanent leverage.

And the leverage compounds. We report it as growth. The analysts love growth. So do I. My equity vests every quarter.

Raj’s priority date goes current in 2031.

His father’s never will.

So many people have DM’d me about this trailer and I’ll be honest, watching it made me physically throw up.

I was COO from before FTX even had a name, it was my baby, and I was the last one out of the Bahamas after Sam got extradited. I lost everything I had on it and it took me a long time to get over, so I have zero interest in defending the people who caused this.

The media loves the story that FTX blew up because we were all partying in the Bahamas, but the place I worked looked nothing like that.

We had under 200 people in the core company at its peak, not counting subsidiaries, when other exchanges our size had thousands, so a lot of us were doing 16 to 18 hour days for over three years and barely had time to sleep, and whenever we walked in, day or night, Sam was at his desk.

I worked with Caroline and never once saw her get aggressive like she does in this trailer. She’s quiet and mild, and often lost in her own thoughts.

Most of us didn’t even know she and Sam were dating until we read about it after the bankruptcy, and I never saw him so much as put an arm around anyone.

FTX’s collapse ruined so many people’s lives, including ours, and Netflix decided to make it a love story. 

Shame on you @netflix.

text:
The debate on the threat AI poses for crypto is mostly just wankery.

We will see AI exploit systems-level bugs far before ECDSA falls. We will see AI discover bugs in systems code, libraries and wallets that enable attackers to steal billions of dollars long before we have to worry about cryptosystems failing wholesale due to new math. 

Sure, there's definitely a non-zero possibility that ECDSA might fail wholesale, and the ramifications would be systemic -- all balances on such a chain would be in question. That's why Hoseeb's backup crypto proposal is sensible. Namely, build an alternative cryptosystem onto which one could shift should ECDSA doomsday arrive one fine morning. That's an approach that we will be exploring for Avalanche.

But our focus regarding AI's impact on blockchains ought to center on vulnerabilities in existing software first and foremost. If you think that, say, Ripple's (or insert any other high value low use chain here) under scrutinized code contains no 0-day bugs, difficult for humans to spot but easy for AI to identify, then you're deluded. 

My take on this issue, as with all other issues, is pragmatic and oriented towards what matters most today. That said, in the tail risk category, hash-based crypto is really interesting, and we have an active group exploring hash-based alternatives to ECDSA.

Fun Moments of TOKEN2049

After the serious side of TOKEN2049, here are a few moments that put a smile on my face.

Not every project was in "dark business only" mode. Some also wanted to create a new kind of experience.

Fun things I saw there:
•Ledger let people play basketball to win merch.
•A quite creepy robot with blinking eyes moving around (I don't know which project it belonged to).
•A whole area of arcade games, including Mario Kart. :)
•A booth where you got merch if you threw a ball into a glass of water. Easy but effective.
•@Tangem giving away Pokémon cards, if you know who to ask. About 200 cards were prepared, and one of them was worth over $1K.
•Guests cycling to crush their own fruit juice.

And so on.

What I also liked was that there was enough space here and there to actually sit down, eat, or open your laptop and write some emails. There were also coffee stations and bottled water everywhere, so you could easily stay hydrated.

I didn't try the food or coffee myself, but you could easily get your caffeine fix.

text:
先认真听了前一个小时的内容，主要是艾伦向孙哥提问财富密码，艾伦连着追问了 6 问，孙哥最后才把结论告诉我们：

结论就是：
（1）通过数据推导得出结论的学术界都有巨大的前途，例如生物医药、纯数学、天文。
（2）产业界则围绕学术界在生物制药、基因方面取得重要成果。
（3）Crypto 天生全球支付、无限拆分的特点，非常适用于 AI 的 API。

有两点值得重点关注：
- 第一，生物医药与健康管理将迎来大爆发。基因测序加健康管理——现在能把一个人的基因全测出来，交给 AI 预测未来健康。
- 第二，孙哥为 Crypto 未来的叙事指明了方向，就是如何把传统金融行业 AI 无法读懂的语言（如货币、资产）转化成 AI 可以理解的语言。
在这个叙事下，美股代币化上链的逻辑：传统金融世界的资产不是由代码所主导——AI 不能理解人的东西——所以 Crypto 的 "Code is Law" 就是利用区块链技术，将传统世界的资产和货币转化成 AI 能够理解的

同时，孙哥给我们提出了一个理念：

未来世界，凡是无法被 AI 读取的理论、发明、资产、人，都将逐渐失去意义。

如果你的理论无法让 AI 读懂，那么你的理论就相当于没有存在；如果你作为一个人无法被 AI 读到，那么你就相当于已经死亡。

以下附上艾伦追问孙哥的六问，以及孙哥的回答：
1.问：如果你重新 20 岁，没人脉没资源，怎么重新开始？
答：答案是先把工作和生活全部 AI 化，同时用三套理论（孙学、薄肌、黄毛）武装自己。

2.问：装好这三套理论、用上 AI 之后，具体怎么执行？
答：首先，用 AI 记录自己 3 到 4 个月所有的生活工作信息，喂给 AI，让他分析自己的现状并给出解决方案。
其次，一定紧追科技的动向，选一个自己最感兴趣的方向钻进去，让 AI 帮忙持续调优。

3.你站在自己的认知，年轻人未来几年最值得 all in 的方向是什么？
答：他没直接给答案，先讲为什么看好年轻人：AI 时代所有东西都会变便宜，只有寿命值钱，所以年轻就是财富，每个行业都会被 AI 改写。任何有积累大量数据、之前无法处理的行业，都会迎来颠覆性的革命，如数学、生物化学、天文学。

4.如果年轻人对学术没兴趣，只想尽快财富自由呢？

Anyone comparing privacy solutions should check out Vitalik's new checklist.

Here's where Prividium stands:

✓ Hash-based proofs. Prividium uses Airbender’s entirely hash-based STARK proofs, with no elliptic-curve or lattice dependency in the proof system.

✓ No FHE. Prividium’s privacy does not require fully homomorphic encryption, so it has no dependency on lattice-based FHE.

✓ No public encrypted data. Prividium does not publish encrypted transaction data for outsiders to collect now and try to decrypt later.

✓ Private signatures, including multisig. For transactions and multisigs operating inside Prividium, signatures stay within the private environment.
author: gluk64
quoted_text:
I don't recommend anyone scramble to move their funds to new wallets today. But we should take the risks to cryptography from AI-accelerated math seriously, and minimize our exposure to not just quantum-vulnerable cryptography, but also potentially AI-vulnerable cryptography.

The core new area of risk from this viewpoint is, unfortunately, ML-DSA / FHE / lattices.

(and it's also another reason, along with quantum, why ECDSA might fall even faster than expected, hence the "fresh address" recommendation)

So far most people have been in the mode of thinking "elliptic curves broken, hashes safe, lattices safe". But there is a good chance that the concrete security of lattices will take serious hits from the next two years of AI math.

The basic threat model is: factoring is something that naively takes 2^(n/2) time, but over decades smart people have found and optimized number field sieves, and degraded that to 2^O(n^(1/3)), which is why RSA keys and signatures need to be ~400 bytes (and not 64 bytes). What if there are skeletons in the closet like that, both for elliptic curves and lattices, that we are simply not smart enough to discover - but bots soon will be?

This is a major part of the reason why for the past year ethereum's lean roadmap has been going in the "hash-only" direction: no lattices, no ML-DSA, no Falcon, no lattice-based commitments inside ZK proofs, etc. Signatures in lean ethereum are all hash-based, either WOTS or SPHINCS-.

For signatures and proofs, we already know how to go hash-only. The bigger challenge is for *public-key encryption* - and this goes far beyond blockchains. Secure communication, anonymizing protocols, lots of things need public-key encryption.

And unfortunately there are long-standing mathematical theorems showing why public-key encryption cannot be done with hashes alone. You have to have some kind of trapdoor object that has at least one form of usable "structure" - either group theory (incl. isogenies) or lattices or code-based or potentially in the future even more newfangled and spooky things (local mixing?). But for anything that has structure, you should assume that AI will make at least some progress in breaking that structure. Here, one reasonable inference is that if you want to make something plausibly long-term secure, multiply the key sizes by 10.

To me that's a very plausible world and something not at all extreme to predict. If AI will bring us 50 years of math in 2 years, then that 50 years of math may very plausibly include a "naive factoring -> GNFS" level of improvement to our ability to break lattices. In that world, lattices will still exist, but they will have to be significantly bigger to guarantee the same level of safety.

And at those new larger sizes, hash-based constructions will beat lattice-based constructions on concrete efficiency in every use case where hash-based constructions are possible at all.

Theoretically, of course it's possible that hashes are broken too (eg. P = NP would imply that). But I think P = NP is very unlikely. And intuitively, it's much more likely that a mathematical object has exactly no exploitable structure (like hashes are intended to), than that a mathematical object has exactly ~3 forms of exploitable structure (for elliptic curves: associativity, Schoof, pairings) and not some secret fourth form of structure we have not yet discovered that greatly degrades its security (for elliptic curves, ECDLP and pairing security). Similar for LWE, SVP, RLWE and the zoo of lattice problems.

For this reason, we do not yet see any reason to worry and start padding the byte size of hashes (if we start to worry more, we would pad the round count first before doing anything to the byte size).

Concrete TLDR, my own personal views:

* Hash-based > lattice-based, in those situations where hash-based is possible at all
* For anything lattice-based, be much more paranoid on param sizes. Remember that blockchains are only a small portion of the cryptography story; this point goes far beyond blockchains and applies to eg. access to websites, secure messaging, Tor / VPNs ...
* For privacy protocols, strongly favor NOT putting encrypted notes onchain. Instead, send them offchain through some third-party mechanism.
* If it's not difficult for you, keeping your funds in addresses which have not yet been used to make a transaction is a good idea. If it's easy for you, do it. **But be careful about migrations; I personally have lost more money in botched migrations than I have lost in all hacks combined**.
* For multisig wallets, doing confirmations offchain is better than onchain, because this way the signatures of signer wallets do not get exposed to the public, so if ECDSA falls to AI much faster than expected, at least the multisig "gracefully degrades" to a 1-of-1 where the 1 is whoever was gathering the signatures - a much better place to be than "anyone can take the money"

author: dfinity
quoted_text:
ICP "cloud engines" launch trajectory:

DFINITY will soon begin disbursing coupons with enough cycles to create and power an engine for 1 month+, unlocking in sequence:

1. Agentic infrastructure ⚡️ Quickly build secure, sovereign onchain production apps using Claude Code, Codex, Caffeine, ...

2. Open SaaS beta release ⚡️ Install AIware apps that can run any enterprise, as easily as installing phone apps...

3. Unlimited growth ⚡️ A new end-to-end, mainstream onchain cloud tech stack will come into being.

*** What this means ***

ICP cloud engines are a new development on the Internet Computer designed to allow it to play the role of a revolutionary new cloud tech stack for the AI era.

Currently, the Internet Computer scales by combining internal subnets, which are akin to individual, high performance blockchains hosting secure serverless software called canisters (something like smart contracts, but much more powerful, which can be used to create huge onchain apps, which serve their web screens directly to users)

Cloud engines allow enterprises to create their own subnets that belong exclusively to them, which they control and configure — while their canister software can still seamlessly interoperate with software on the main network, and engines run by others. 

An enterprise creates a cloud engine by choosing nodes from a marketplace, which the ICP protocol combines into a revolutionary serverless cloud platform for them, where the computation and data of their hosted apps and services is tamperproof (immune to infrastructure hacks) and always on (incredibly resilient), AI agents can build and update apps far more effectively than on traditional tech, and next generation AIware software can be created. 

Today, enterprises demand to be able to control where their sotware and data lives, and cloud engines make that possible with no loss of flexibility. Cloud engines can even be re-configured with new nodes, without interrupting the hosted apps and services — the ICP protocol just handles it, granting complete sovereignty and freedom from vendor lock-in. 

In advance of general release, cloud engines are already being used by governments and NGOs seeking to create sovereign cloud tech stacks and apps. On general release, they will be used in far more mainstream ways too.

Here are the details of what's coming. 

*** Agentic Infrastructure ***

In the future, and really already today, nearly all of our  apps and services will be created by AI agents rather than humans. Further, next generation software is "AIware," which has AI deeply integrated on the inside, which allows it to provide superpowers relative to traditional software.

Agents have different needs when they building things. They can write software orders of magnitude faster than humans, and we will demand they update our production apps and services at the speed of conversation. Functionality will be fluid and its shape will change to match what we want. 

On traditional tech stacks, updating apps and services is a necessarily laborious and risky process for three reasons: 1) a security flaw might be introduced, 2) a systems configuration change might break them, and 3) the way that data is migrated might cause some to be lost, often in subtle ways that aren't detected at the time of the upgrade. This means that AI agents can't just be let of the leash to build and update at the speed they can.

ICP cloud engines solve this. Hosted software is tamperproof, so agents can update without needing security teams in the loop. Hosted software is serverless, and the data lives in the logic, so apps don't. need things like operating systems and databases configured to run, so agents can update apps without having sysadmin teams in the loop either. And, if Motoko 2.0, the world's first languge targeting agents is used as the backend language, its framework is able to detect when an app update by AI might cause data loss, and simply require the agent writing the code to try again, reducing potentially catastrophic data loss to a harmless retry.

Crucially, apps built with Motoko can also put AI agents on the inside, so that subject to permissions, they can see the data graph in the persistent memory used by serverless software on ICP, and access its functions. This enables you to instruct agents to do things in the apps for you, such as analyzing data, or performing actions, with great flexibility and power.

ICP cloud engines are agentic infrastructure that change the game — and it will be possible to use them as such from the moment they are released. 

There is already a government using internal production software built on a cloud engine using Caffeine. But cloud engines will meet a wide range of mainstream needs, from solorpeneurs to startups, SMEs to corporations, governments and NGOs.

*** Open SaaS ***

The obvious question, is if AIware is so much better, shouldn't all enterprises be running on it? We believe they should, and that his must be enabled.

This has been a labor of love for me. A new venture associated with me will release the Open SaaS suite for use on cloud engines once they have been running a short while, which suite, as you've probably guessed from the name, is open source and free.

Open SaaS is a suite of every important SaaS (Software-as-a-Service) app used to run enterprises around the world today, reimagined as onchain AIware that runs on ICP cloud engines. Because of the unique nature of the software that ICP hosts, installing and maintaining these sophisticated enterprise apps on a cloud engine is as easy as installing and managing a phone app.

A small selection of the apps: Open Team, Open HR, Open Accounts, Open CRM, Open Projects, Open Email, Open Messaging, Open Signing, Open Knowledge, Op... etc. There are many more, and there will be surprises. 

The user experiences are beautiful, and easily compete with the big money SaaS screens many enterprises are used to. Moreover, the are linked to what I called a "software factory" driven by AI, and the more enterprises that use them and provide feedback, the better they will get, in realtime. 

Today's expensive SaaS silos make it hard to integrate and combine enterprise data, and to unleash the full power of AI. They are the opposite to Open SaaS.

In the future, enterprise users will spend far more time in AI chat than on SaaS screens. That's the future that Open SaaS enables and unlocks. Enterprise users can even say to their Open SaaS suite, "make me more profitable," and it will have a go.

The big surprise coming for the world: once you run your enterprise on AIware, and AI can access all your data in realtime, and is integrated with your software's actual functions — it can become as good at running your enterprise as writing software for you.

It's revolutionary, and ICP is pioneering this. Not a narrative, but real decentralized network tech.

Something I can share: DFINITY is in the process of migrating to Open SaaS from a vast suite of expensive SaaS silos, and is already reaping big benefits as we refocus ourselves for the era of AI.

****

What does this mean for the project?

I believe ICP cloud engines are the vector that will transform the the Internet Computer into a mainstream agentic infrastructure tech platform for enterprise— which direction platforms like Caffeine have already helped the network travel, by enabling many tens of thousands of users and enterprises to create onchain apps on the shared network through online conversation. Now, the next and most important phase is approaching. 

Our go-to-market will proceed quietly as we rollout coupons and work to fettle the new network functionality, but I think that in hindsight, the launch of cloud engines will be seen as the most pivotal moment in Internet Computer history since network launch.

With this, ICP shall show the industry how networks can provide real agentic infrastructure. 

Bear with us as we tie up loose ends. We never stop working, and you can be sure that we're trying to get this out as fast as possible 💪⚡️💥

text:
One year ago today, on October 9, 2025, we reached an agreement on President Trump’s 20-point peace plan for Gaza many believed impossible.

After two years of devastating war, the agreement created a path to reunite hostage families with their loved ones, bring security to Israel, relieve the suffering of the Palestinian people in Gaza, and build a different future for the region.

One year later, it’s remarkable how much has changed. The situation is far from perfect, but the progress is real, and the world is better for it.

A look at the past year:

✅October 9, 2025: Hamas accepts President Trump’s 20-point peace plan, launching a ceasefire that has largely endured for a year.

✅October 12, 2025: Israeli forces complete first withdrawal to the agreed yellow line.

✅October 13, 2025: All 20 living Israeli hostages return home. Something many believed would never happen.

✅November 17, 2025: UN Security Council passes Resolution 2803, endorsing the peace plan and authorizing an international stabilization framework and the Board of Peace.

✅January 5, 2026: UN reports 100% of basic food needs being met in Gaza for the first time since 2023.

✅January 17, 2026: National Committee for the Administration of Gaza established, creating a Palestinian technocratic administration focused on restoring essential services and rebuilding Gaza.

✅January 26, 2026: Remains of the final deceased hostage returned. For the first time since 2014, no Israeli hostages, living or deceased, in Gaza.

✅February 19, 2026: The Board of Peace holds its inaugural meeting, hosted by Chairman President Trump. Landmark partnership with FIFA announced, including a $50 million commitment toward a football stadium, academy, and facilities for Gaza’s children, and billions of dollars in commitments for the people of Gaza.

✅May 2, 2026: UN reports that humanitarian aid entering Gaza had increased by 72% compared with before the ceasefire.

✅July 31, 2026: Hamas signs an actionable, step-by-step framework for decommissioning its weapons, developed with the support of Nickolay Mladenov and mediators from Egypt, Turkey, Qatar, and the United States. Implementation remains a critical next step.

✅2026: Five nations commit forces toward the International Stabilization Force, with several more working on logistics for deployment this fall.

✅September 23, 2026: Board of Peace hosts an open meeting on the sidelines of UNGA releasing the next steps in the Gaza recovery plan.

A year ago, so much of this seemed impossible.

First, many doubted we could reach an agreement. Then came the harder question of whether the parties would honor their commitments. Over the past year, we have seen what can be achieved when people with profound differences find ways to work together toward a common objective.

Steve Witkoff @SEPeaceMissions and I are grateful to @POTUS Trump for his leadership, @VP, @SecRubio, the Board of Peace team, led by @TB, @nmladenov, @lightstonea, @AliShaathNCAG, Gen. Jasper Jeffers, Liran Tanchman, Yakir Gabay, Josh Greunbaum, Josh Halpern and many others, and our partners in Egypt, the UAE, Qatar, Turkey, Bahrain, Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Morocco and Israel. Special thanks to Sheikh Mohammed, Ali Al-Thwadi, Hakan Fidan, General Hasan, Bader Abdulhamdi, @mikeeisenberg, and @AmbDermer. I’m also grateful to the many talented people who have volunteered their time and energy because they believe that the horrors of October 7 and the suffering in Gaza must never happen again.

There is still hard work ahead. Disarmament must be implemented, security established, essential services restored, and communities rebuilt. None of this will be easy. But we have a thoughtful plan, committed partners, and a path forward that did not exist a year ago.

It’s worth recognizing how far we’ve come, even as we acknowledge how much remains to be done.

Hopefully, the year ahead will bring even more progress, and a few more miracles.

quoted_text:
Working with AI models, I've arrived at what I consider the most significant pure-theory breakthrough of my research (in theoretical neuroscience) so far: 

https://t.co/E0ylJ6LMts

Chaotic systems show what is colloquially called the butterfly effect, namely, a tiny nudge to the initial state grows exponentially in time. How fast the nudge grows depends on its direction. Each direction has its own growth rate, called a Lyapunov exponent, and the full set of rates is the Lyapunov spectrum.

The Lyapunov spectrum is a rich (and diffeomorphism-invariant) characterization of chaos, telling us how many directions are chaotic, how many dimensions the attractor occupies, and how fast the dynamics generate information.

In 1988, Sompolinsky, Crisanti, and Sommers (Physical Review Letters) introduced a nonlinear recurrent-network model of N randomly coupled neurons that becomes chaotic when the coupling strength exceeds a critical value. This network has since become a cornerstone of theoretical neuroscience, both as a model of the spontaneous activity of cortex and as the starting point for training recurrent networks on tasks. I have worked on this model for much of my research.

In the same paper, the authors obtained the largest Lyapunov exponent from the ground-state energy of a Schrödinger equation and named the full Lyapunov spectrum as an open problem. In 2023, beautiful work by Engelken et al. (Physical Review Research) computed the full Lyapunov spectrum numerically. However, an analytical calculation of the full Lyapunov spectrum has remained out of reach.

Four decades after the problem was posed, this paper derives the full Lyapunov spectrum at large N from a simple self-consistent single-site problem.

This calculation has three steps.

First, we lower every exponent by a constant s, which turns the question "how many exponents lie below s?" into the question "how many tangent directions decay?" We show that, if we drive the shifted tangent dynamics with a source and take the minimum-norm solution, the one-step response is the projector onto the decaying directions. Thus, the trace of this projector counts the decaying directions. This step is exact at finite N.

Second, to work with the minimum-norm solution, we cast it as the vanishing-regularization limit of the solution of a least-squares problem. This regularized solution in turn solves a dynamical system with one field running forward in time and another running backward.

Third, we apply the cavity method, that is, we add one neuron to the network, along with its forward and backward fields. The effect of the rest of the network on this neuron then reduces to the classical dynamical mean-field description of the activity of this neuron, plus two kernels that couple the forward and backward fields of this neuron to each other across time. Thus, the full Lyapunov spectrum follows from a single-site problem, which boils down to the self-consistent calculation of these kernels.

The resulting theory agrees closely with simulations for the Lyapunov spectrum, the attractor dimension, and the entropy rate, and recovers known results, including the Schrödinger equation of Sompolinsky, Crisanti, and Sommers for the largest Lyapunov exponent.

As a byproduct, the theory establishes analytically that the chaos is extensive, i.e., the attractor dimension and the entropy rate grow in proportion to N.

I had assumed that this problem was analytically intractable. After working independently for 100 minutes with Max thinking, GPT-6 Astra produced the initial derivation, yielding a self-consistent problem whose solution matched simulations of large networks.

I found this derivation intriguing, albeit complicated and somewhat mysterious (see AI Methodology in the paper). After investigating the structure of the proposed solution more deeply, together with AI models, I arrived at a physically transparent derivation.

I am excited to apply this approach to other network models,  trained networks, and, more broadly, to high-dimensional systems to which Lyapunov analysis is relevant, including AI models themselves. Of course, as with any paper, I took care to write up the paper clearly.

A few broader thoughts...

Neural circuits are high-dimensional nonlinear dynamical systems, and such systems are notoriously hard to understand. I would frame the central problem of theoretical neuroscience as understanding how such systems function, process information, learn, and generate behavior.

Many people in the theoretical sciences are anxious about AI. However, in my field at least, we are nowhere close to fully understanding the high-dimensional computations unfolding in our brains. With AI, we could reach a level of understanding that so far we have only gestured toward. So, I am excited.

text:
I think the takeaway from the Ledger incident is that if you have any amount of crypto, it should never be secured by a single tech stack.

My recommendation is setup a 2/3 multisig. It’s easy and free on Gnosis or Squads. Have the three signers be three different wallets from different vendors. 

Say you have Ledger, Trezor and a mobile iOS wallet like Phantom. For someone to pwn you, they’d need to compromise two different stacks in a very short period. If something like the Ledger exploit happens to your wallet, you can simply rotate that signer off the multisig. 

Would also keep a small amount of canary money (maybe $100) in the wallets themselves. This will give you an early warning if that signer is compromised. 

This is fast and easy, and in the current high risk environment there’s no reason not to do this today.
