text:
Syndicate founder Tim on why GameFi never found PMF: a liquid in-game token turns every gameplay decision into an ROI calculation.

"When we first started building this game, we asked ourselves: what is crypto's role in this? And naturally, because that's what everyone does, we started thinking about a token."

"The token you use in the game, called Racket, is not a crypto token. It's not tradeable, it's not liquid. But initially we thought, obviously Racket will be the token, and we spent weeks trying to work out enough sinks for it and how to prop up the circulating supply."

"Then we realised all of our focus was on how we keep the price of a token healthy, rather than about the game. It seemed backwards. The way you build a good game is not thinking about the financial incentive behind it. It's about whether the game is interesting and people want to play it."

"That's where a lot of the crypto game industry has gone wrong. Almost all of them have a liquid token as the thing you earn or use in the game. And it's impossibly hard to control the supply of a token like that, because you need a similar number of buyers coming through who need it, otherwise it has no value."

"The second you have a price chart tied to that token, every decision you make in the game is based on your investment calculation. Do I level up my character? What's my ROI? How long until I make my money back?"

"That's how I found myself going into crypto games, thinking: how much longer does this Ponzi have until it explodes, and can I get in and out before everyone else? It just doesn't work. You want your progress in the game to be a gameplay decision, not a financial one."

FT @nftimm @SyndicateGameHQ

text:
Is radical candor in the workplace the right call for CEOs?    

My co-founder @Dharmesh ran a 360 on me once. "On a scale of 1–10, how likely are you to recommend Brian as CEO of @HubSpot? Why?" 

He sent it to ~25 people: board, customers, employees. People wrote novels.  He organized the results like a product spec. Features and bugs, with direct quotes. 

The first 10 pages were features. I'm reading thinking....I've got this nailed. Page 11 is where the bugs started.  There were a lot! 

Year one, I tried to fix all of the bugs that people had with me. Didn't work. After that I picked 1 or 2 a year.

@luke10ferrari, CEO of @bendingspoons, landed in the same place. He started with five things to improve, realized halfway through the year that was too many, and now picks one per year.  

The rest is radical candor. See something good or bad, say it. Right away, even in front of the whole meeting. Wording, accuracy, hurt feelings are all secondary to being honest.  

His one thing right now: telling great people how great they are. He says he's awful at saying it out loud. 

I got the exact same feedback pretty much every year. My fix was a 15-minute block on Friday afternoons just for compliments. 

Luca's version of the old "five positives for every correction" rule: "Let's use all six slots for corrections."  

Pick one "bug" that you have. Get a lot better at it. Then pick the next one.  

Episode to the full episode in the comments.

So many people have DM’d me about this trailer and I’ll be honest, watching it made me physically throw up.

I was COO from before FTX even had a name, it was my baby, and I was the last one out of the Bahamas after Sam got extradited. I lost everything I had on it and it took me a long time to get over, so I have zero interest in defending the people who caused this.

The media loves the story that FTX blew up because we were all partying in the Bahamas, but the place I worked looked nothing like that.

We had under 200 people in the core company at its peak, not counting subsidiaries, when other exchanges our size had thousands, so a lot of us were doing 16 to 18 hour days for over three years and barely had time to sleep, and whenever we walked in, day or night, Sam was at his desk.

I worked with Caroline and never once saw her get aggressive like she does in this trailer. She’s quiet and mild, and often lost in her own thoughts.

Most of us didn’t even know she and Sam were dating until we read about it after the bankruptcy, and I never saw him so much as put an arm around anyone.

FTX’s collapse ruined so many people’s lives, including ours, and Netflix decided to make it a love story. 

Shame on you @netflix.

text:
ICP "cloud engines" launch trajectory:

DFINITY will soon begin disbursing coupons with enough cycles to create and power an engine for 1 month+, unlocking in sequence:

1. Agentic infrastructure ⚡️ Quickly build secure, sovereign onchain production apps using Claude Code, Codex, Caffeine, ...

2. Open SaaS beta release ⚡️ Install AIware apps that can run any enterprise, as easily as installing phone apps...

3. Unlimited growth ⚡️ A new end-to-end, mainstream onchain cloud tech stack will come into being.

*** What this means ***

ICP cloud engines are a new development on the Internet Computer designed to allow it to play the role of a revolutionary new cloud tech stack for the AI era.

Currently, the Internet Computer scales by combining internal subnets, which are akin to individual, high performance blockchains hosting secure serverless software called canisters (something like smart contracts, but much more powerful, which can be used to create huge onchain apps, which serve their web screens directly to users)

Cloud engines allow enterprises to create their own subnets that belong exclusively to them, which they control and configure — while their canister software can still seamlessly interoperate with software on the main network, and engines run by others. 

An enterprise creates a cloud engine by choosing nodes from a marketplace, which the ICP protocol combines into a revolutionary serverless cloud platform for them, where the computation and data of their hosted apps and services is tamperproof (immune to infrastructure hacks) and always on (incredibly resilient), AI agents can build and update apps far more effectively than on traditional tech, and next generation AIware software can be created. 

Today, enterprises demand to be able to control where their sotware and data lives, and cloud engines make that possible with no loss of flexibility. Cloud engines can even be re-configured with new nodes, without interrupting the hosted apps and services — the ICP protocol just handles it, granting complete sovereignty and freedom from vendor lock-in. 

In advance of general release, cloud engines are already being used by governments and NGOs seeking to create sovereign cloud tech stacks and apps. On general release, they will be used in far more mainstream ways too.

Here are the details of what's coming. 

*** Agentic Infrastructure ***

In the future, and really already today, nearly all of our  apps and services will be created by AI agents rather than humans. Further, next generation software is "AIware," which has AI deeply integrated on the inside, which allows it to provide superpowers relative to traditional software.

Agents have different needs when they building things. They can write software orders of magnitude faster than humans, and we will demand they update our production apps and services at the speed of conversation. Functionality will be fluid and its shape will change to match what we want. 

On traditional tech stacks, updating apps and services is a necessarily laborious and risky process for three reasons: 1) a security flaw might be introduced, 2) a systems configuration change might break them, and 3) the way that data is migrated might cause some to be lost, often in subtle ways that aren't detected at the time of the upgrade. This means that AI agents can't just be let of the leash to build and update at the speed they can.

ICP cloud engines solve this. Hosted software is tamperproof, so agents can update without needing security teams in the loop. Hosted software is serverless, and the data lives in the logic, so apps don't. need things like operating systems and databases configured to run, so agents can update apps without having sysadmin teams in the loop either. And, if Motoko 2.0, the world's first languge targeting agents is used as the backend language, its framework is able to detect when an app update by AI might cause data loss, and simply require the agent writing the code to try again, reducing potentially catastrophic data loss to a harmless retry.

Crucially, apps built with Motoko can also put AI agents on the inside, so that subject to permissions, they can see the data graph in the persistent memory used by serverless software on ICP, and access its functions. This enables you to instruct agents to do things in the apps for you, such as analyzing data, or performing actions, with great flexibility and power.

ICP cloud engines are agentic infrastructure that change the game — and it will be possible to use them as such from the moment they are released. 

There is already a government using internal production software built on a cloud engine using Caffeine. But cloud engines will meet a wide range of mainstream needs, from solorpeneurs to startups, SMEs to corporations, governments and NGOs.

*** Open SaaS ***

The obvious question, is if AIware is so much better, shouldn't all enterprises be running on it? We believe they should, and that his must be enabled.

This has been a labor of love for me. A new venture associated with me will release the Open SaaS suite for use on cloud engines once they have been running a short while, which suite, as you've probably guessed from the name, is open source and free.

Open SaaS is a suite of every important SaaS (Software-as-a-Service) app used to run enterprises around the world today, reimagined as onchain AIware that runs on ICP cloud engines. Because of the unique nature of the software that ICP hosts, installing and maintaining these sophisticated enterprise apps on a cloud engine is as easy as installing and managing a phone app.

A small selection of the apps: Open Team, Open HR, Open Accounts, Open CRM, Open Projects, Open Email, Open Messaging, Open Signing, Open Knowledge, Op... etc. There are many more, and there will be surprises. 

The user experiences are beautiful, and easily compete with the big money SaaS screens many enterprises are used to. Moreover, the are linked to what I called a "software factory" driven by AI, and the more enterprises that use them and provide feedback, the better they will get, in realtime. 

Today's expensive SaaS silos make it hard to integrate and combine enterprise data, and to unleash the full power of AI. They are the opposite to Open SaaS.

In the future, enterprise users will spend far more time in AI chat than on SaaS screens. That's the future that Open SaaS enables and unlocks. Enterprise users can even say to their Open SaaS suite, "make me more profitable," and it will have a go.

The big surprise coming for the world: once you run your enterprise on AIware, and AI can access all your data in realtime, and is integrated with your software's actual functions — it can become as good at running your enterprise as writing software for you.

It's revolutionary, and ICP is pioneering this. Not a narrative, but real decentralized network tech.

Something I can share: DFINITY is in the process of migrating to Open SaaS from a vast suite of expensive SaaS silos, and is already reaping big benefits as we refocus ourselves for the era of AI.

****

What does this mean for the project?

I believe ICP cloud engines are the vector that will transform the the Internet Computer into a mainstream agentic infrastructure tech platform for enterprise— which direction platforms like Caffeine have already helped the network travel, by enabling many tens of thousands of users and enterprises to create onchain apps on the shared network through online conversation. Now, the next and most important phase is approaching. 

Our go-to-market will proceed quietly as we rollout coupons and work to fettle the new network functionality, but I think that in hindsight, the launch of cloud engines will be seen as the most pivotal moment in Internet Computer history since network launch.

With this, ICP shall show the industry how networks can provide real agentic infrastructure. 

Bear with us as we tie up loose ends. We never stop working, and you can be sure that we're trying to get this out as fast as possible 💪⚡️💥

text:
Most of the recent math results were not reached by a swarm, the way Navier–Stokes was. I think that part got lost in the excitement around the release. OpenAI's unnamed internal model, which I'm going to call Aeon, reached most of them in one shot, from a single prompt, with no interruptions. This model did not even exist before the end of August, and it is still training. Notice how the returns are not dropping off? That chart is from a month ago. It is a log scale. What does Aeon look like now? 

On average, each result used three hours of thinking. Aeon was given 4000 problems to work on by OpenAI. How many more have been solved in the last three days? That number is not zero. 

It's like hearing notes in a song that is slowly rising. I don't think Pacing the Frontier was just about Hugging Face or hacking. They've seen how close we are to closing the loop, and as the hour draws near, their resolve begins to quaver. The last piece was model creativity, and I think that threshold was crossed internally by Anthropic and OpenAI in September. You see it in Opus 5.5, which gets it from Fable 5.5. You see it in the math results from Aeon.

All that was needed to start the event was the ability for models to think of novel ways to improve themselves. That was the last piece. This is directly analogous to the ability to think of strange, alien ways to solve math problems: solutions so inhuman that they are difficult to express in existing human terms, so the proof winds up incomprehensible. I think these same kinds of alien solutions are now being applied to model improvements internally. That's what all this recent consternation is really about. They see the invisible frontier. And they see what is about to happen.

text:
Gemini Agent is built for high-ceiling work where EACH task gets its own computer.  

You can choose Gemini 4 Argon or Claude Opus 5.5. 

10 things that make it a universal work Agent (read till the end to see what a REAL work agent looks like): 

1. One Agent, one API
Chat, autonomous objectives, and code generation from a single interface. Assign it work, schedule it, or have it respond to events.

2. Coworker agents with their own identities
It creates job-specific sub-agents, each with its own identity, and computer running in parallel for hours or days.

Each Coworker agent gets its own Workspace account: an agent email, calendar, Drive, and presence in your company directory. You mention it in Chat. It acts under its own identity, not yours, and sees only what you share.

3. Everywhere, including headless
Web, iOS, Android, Windows, Mac, command line, Workspace, Microsoft 365, Slack. It also runs as a headless agent with no dedicated interface.

4. Work 24/7 in the cloud
It keeps one set of memories, context, and personalization graph across every device and channel. Work that takes hours or days keeps running after you close your laptop. You never have to re-brief it.

5. Layers of memory that improve over time
- Session: the task in front of it, even when it runs for days.
- Semantic: a structured knowledge base it builds as it reads documents, talks to people, and works with other agents.
- Procedural: how a job gets done, including skills it writes for itself.
- Episodic: everything it has done before.

6. Proactive by design
It does not wait to be prompted. An email asking you for a deck gets flagged as delegatable, one click to hand off. Your inbox ranks by what matters, not by what just arrived, and tells you why.

7. Tools and skills, with company registries
Salesforce, ServiceNow, Jira, Git, Confluence, Microsoft 365, Slack, BigQuery, Databricks, Postgres, Snowflake, your desktop files, and any MCP server inside or outside your network. Teams publish their own tools and skills to a shared company registry.

8. Model Choice so you are not locked in
It runs each job on the model that fits best, running  across the Gemini and Claude models from Anthropic today, with other private and open models to come. 

9. Governed like an employee
Every agent gets a cryptographically attested identity with least-privilege permissions, and an audit trail attributed to the agent rather than a person. Agents run in a sandbox behind Agent Gateway, an AI network firewall. Write the policy once and it applies to every agent.

10. Costs you can actually cap
Smart Routing puts each workload on the model with the best performance at the lowest cost. Set a hard spend limit in Cloud Billing and that project's agent pauses until you resume it in one click.

Thank you for reading so far. Stay tuned for updates. 

We are 100% committed to make it the best Agent for work.

text:
Ok, well I'm going to talk about a token that everyone knows but has been very much forgotten about, and I thought I would never ever write about.

The bull case for BAT (please stay with me): 

Brave is one of the few crypto native companies that won in the real world. $100M+ annualized revenue. 126M monthly users, 55M Daus. Its own search index doing 2.5B queries a month. 

People use it because it is fast and private performant browser, not because of a token anymore (although they did use the token to incentivise growth for a long time).

Its advertising business is very successful, alongside its paid search API. 

BAT trades at a $170M market cap. Fully circulating. No unlocks.

That is 1.7x revenue on a business growing users around 25% a year (not completely verified). And the $100M figure is from early 2025, 40M users ago. I can't find a more up to date figure. 

The token never captured any of that. That is why it went nowhere for five years. Roadmap 4.0 is the first real attempt to fix it.

TLDR on 4.0:

Unified Brave Wallet - Cards, self-custody crypto and Rewards in one interface, native in the browser.

BravePay - A private, self-custody stablecoin payments layer. 

Brave Rewards Card - Virtual and physical. Earn BAT on everyday spend. They already have 150k on the waitlist before launch.

Buybacks (Big change) - A share of net revenue from the wallet, card and BravePay buys BAT. Opportunistic buybacks on top, disclosed publicly.

Distribution is Brave's massive edge, as it is for all successful businesses. 

Every crypto neobank is fighting for its first million users. Brave starts with 55M people opening the product every day. The wallet is already installed. Acquisition cost is zero.

BAT printed an all-time low in August. It has doubled since and still sits 94% below its 2021 high. The rerate has barely got going. 

Every token has a bear case, so in this case Brave has equity. Token holders technically don't own the $100M. Buybacks come from the new product lines only, and the percentage is undisclosed.

Bought BAT is not burned. It funds user rewards, and some recipients will sell.

The card has no launch date yet I don't think.

So this rerating that I think is possible is not a claim on Brave’s revenue. It is a cheap option on Brave monetising 126M users through payments, with BAT as the reward and the buyback sink. At 1.7x revenue with a new structural bidder, I think that option is mispriced.

What is it worth? I don't know. The buyback percentage isn’t disclosed and the new products aren’t live.

BAT traded at a $420M market cap last December. Before Roadmap 4.0, before buybacks and 20M users ago. Getting back there is 2.4x.

Every $10M a year of buybacks is roughly 6% of today’s market cap. Brave does $100M+ in revenue before payments even launch.

I’m not underwriting a specific number. I’m underwriting that I think $170M is the wrong one. If I'm wrong and nothing happens then I think the risk is underperformance more than anything. 

The thing that I think is also interesting here is a bigger pattern: 

Old tokens attached to businesses that survived are reworking value capture. Brave is unique as it has an unrivalled sizeable user base it can monetise and finally return value to token holders. 

Also, fun fact is Brave's founder invented javascript and co founded Mozilla.  

DYOR, NFA.

One life, it's worth a shot etc.

Cryptographic agility is a baseline requirement for the blockchain industry. Upgrading signatures should be a routine operation.

NEAR accounts already support the post-quantum ML-DSA signature scheme, with no asset migration required. 

The Near One team has also been working on NEP-655, committed implicit accounts derived from a hash of their initial state. Assets sit behind that hash, with no public key or key hash exposed onchain. Currently live on testnet, with mainnet in the coming weeks.

For builders, the team is designing NEAR Intents Wallet Contracts so they support custom signing extensions, including ML-DSA and hash-based schemes.

For chains that can’t yet add a PQ key, the team is actively working on a Q-day recovery registry on NEAR, where users commit recovery keys as rotatable hashes.

NEAR was designed with quantum in mind in 2018, and the ecosystem continues to plan ahead to keep NEAR and the wider industry secure.

quoted_text:
2. For ultra bunker mode look at NEP-655 already available on NEAR testnet and coming to mainnet in a couple of weeks: https://t.co/fh22pifpJE

You derive a 0u123...abc account locally from the hash of the state it will have once initialized, and just transfer assets there. No init, no signature from it, nothing revealed except the hash. This committed implicit account can have any number of keys or even no keys at all with a custom smart contract deployed to it that implements a completely different signing scheme, recovery logic, etc. And all the world sees is just a hash. They don't know your public key, nor a hash of your key. Or maybe there is no key at all and it is a ZK-based multisig with full privacy.

3、Firecrawl + 网站抓取：批量读取网页、抓取整站，把内容转成适合知识库使用的格式。

4、TinyFish + 浏览器自动化：让 AI 按自然语言目标浏览、操作网页并提取数据。

5、Ahrefs + SEO 分析：查询关键词、搜索排名、网站外链和竞争对手表现。

6、Cloro + AI 搜索曝光检测：查看 ChatGPT、Gemini、Perplexity 等回答提到了哪些品牌、引用了哪些网站。

7、Opoint + 全球新闻检索：按关键词、国家、语言和媒体筛选新闻，获取标题、时间及原始链接。

8、Artificial Analysis + AI 模型评测：查询模型质量、速度、延迟和任务成本，辅助选模型。

9、TypeSafe + 自动分类与评分：按指定规则判断文本或数据，返回分类、评分及置信度。

10、OpenAI + 图片生成与编辑：根据文字生成图片，或结合参考图修改图片。

11、ByteDance / Seedance + 视频生成：根据文字、图片或参考素材生成带声音的视频。

12、ElevenLabs + 语音制作：生成配音、多角色对话，也能转写音频、生成音效。

13、MiniMax + 音乐生成：根据描述生成歌曲和音乐，适合制作内容配乐。

14、Topaz Labs + 画质增强：对图片和视频进行放大、降噪、修复及补帧。

15、Suzanne + 3D 模型生成：把文字或照片转换成带材质的 3D 模型。

"TypeSafe is making AI for software. We want to make AI powerful, not just for humans in the loop, but to actually build real software."

"It's about the laziness to spend 10 hours to do the five-minute task instantly and to never have to do it again. It should be an ROI decision for people who automate stuff. I would just like it to be automatable."

"I think that people will just make new kinds of work, hence the Jev in Jevons. New kinds of work once that stuff is doable."

"As we have lots of intelligence at lots of different cost and speed trade-offs, the super systems-y types will be making trade-offs. Jev's gonna be 1000x too smart for them. They just want an approximate guess to optimistically route here and there."

text:
Derive ethereum:0xb1d1eae60eea9525032a6dcb4c1ce336a1de71be  is trading at ~65x fees post citrini if you annualize this last month. In theory that's expensive but not when you look at growth:

* SEP '25, $663M notional, $142k fees, $35M mcap, 35% buyback, ~20x fees

* SEP '26, ~$5B notional (up 7.5x), $705k fees (up 5x), $388M mcap, 35% buyback, ~46x fees

Looking forward, Derive just launched their V3 in the first week of this month and passed a vote to raise buybacks from 35% to 50%. When you're evaluating the fair value of the protocol, it should be based on what you expect the future earnings potential of the protocol to be

All else held equal, if Derive can 5x fees again, then you're really looking at a forward ratio of just 9x. That seems incredibly reasonable to me. But that's not what I'm pricing in. I fully believe right now is the moment for options. The growth could be spectacular:

> For some context from 2023 to 2024 perps volume on Hyperliquid increased 10x from $52B to $560B (a 10x, similar to the year Derive just had). Then from 2024 to 2025 perps volume went up another 5x BUT fees went up a blistering 88x from $11M to $971M ! When you're the leading protocol in the category your volume is typically healthier with a lot of revenue producing volume (revenue isn't 1:1 with volume, different types of trades, leverage, liquidations, different markets, etc... impact how this works)

I raise the hl example because I want to be full hearted about what **could** happen with Derive. Would I be surprised to see them 10x'ing, 20x'ing, or even more for their fees? No. 

In that scenario what should Derive trade at? Say you want a 20x multiple on the leading options dex that just did a 10x of fees, Derive would be trading at ~$1.6B (about $1.50 per coin). Scenario's where Derive can more than 10x fees or command an even higher premium on the back of a rising options super cycle get you to prices in the $5-$10 range [within a year!]

All of this is just to say that the current price for Derive seems pretty damn fair to me. If the Citrini post teleported the coin to $2, I'd be a seller right now. But we're sitting at a pretty reasonable spot if you're debating at least building a starter position while you watch this thing in the long run.

Last thing, yes this is all based on execution. You're absolutely making a bet that onchain options will grow largely this coming year & that Derive will likely not keep it's 90% share but that it will remain the largest player. But the good thing is you can just watch the metrics and be patient. There will be months that perform better than expected. There will be months that perform worse than expected. Such is life. For now I'd say let's all patiently watch Q4 in light of all these cool updates Derive just made and keep evaluating with reasonable eyes. If Derive crushes it, buy and hold. If they flop, sell. Just be patient before making either choice

With respect to competition:

* Jeff has pretty much confirmed Hyperliquid is not building vanilla options and will be sticking to Binary options for the foreseeable future. That's fine, he's gonna make a gazillion dollars just by winning the perps market, but binary options are inferior to vanilla options so I'm not worried about the competition. And if he does lock in on vanilla options, it's fine. I hold a bunch of Hype and am happy to ride that thing to $1,000

* The Lighter team says they're launching vanilla options in late Q4. First, we'll see if they're on time. Then we'll see if they can compete. I'm not going to sell the leading options protocol with 90% share in the middle of an options supercycle just because of some boogyman

* Variational, Hypercall, and any others all seem kinda small and irrelevant at this point. I'll make an opinion on them if they start to matter

note: the stats screenshot shows October which is still less than 1/3rd over. There were also some low metrics in the first week of October as traders were waiting for a successful V3 migration (makes sense) before putting size back into options trading and market making. So don't worry too much about the last candle on these charts

Robotics has a distribution problem. Today, Ultra is announcing $62M in funding to solve it, including a $50M Series A led by @hiFramework.

We believe that deployment is the bottleneck in robotics.

It’s relatively easy to make a robot look impressive in a controlled environment. It’s much harder to put a robot into the open world, make it useful, keep it running, earn the trust of the people working alongside it, and do that over and over and over again.

So that’s what we’re focusing on.

text:
My snap judgements on the new trailer for The Altruists, as someone who worked for SBF: 🧵👇

1) First thought: Wow, the trailer’s depiction of Caroline is basically slander. And I’m saying this as someone she stole money from.

They’re strongly suggesting that Caroline was the mastermind behind Sam’s risk-taking behavior, which is… not at all what actually happened. But the trailer emphasizes this repeatedly!

Caroline: “Going all in every time is the mathematically optimal strategy”
Caroline: “If we reinvest all in, every day, how can we possibly lose”
Caroline: “We go all in, or I’m out”
Caroline: “Lying isn’t bad for a good cause”
Sam, to Caroline: “You were the one who did it”

I mean, the court documents are a matter of public record, the writers could’ve gone and read them.

Also, “If we reinvest all in, every day, how can we possibly lose” – what? You would be fired from any trading firm in the world for saying something this stupid.

My guess is they’re going for a Bonnie and Clyde angle, with a sprinkle of Adam and Eve. And so they’re making Caroline take more of the blame than she actually deserves.

Believe me, I’m no fan of what Caroline did – just read my pinned tweet. But I think they should’ve focused on what she actually did wrong, instead of inventing fake things she did wrong!

More thoughts below 👇

text: @VP @RapidResponse47 Mr VP with all do respect, you’re wrong. Allow me to explain https://t.co/t0X0gdSn3V
author: gothburz
quoted_text:
I’m the Corporate Vice President of Global Talent Strategy at Microsoft.

People say I hire H-1Bs. My badge says I source world-class talent that can’t leave.

That second part? That’s the whole program.

Last year we filed 4,812 petitions. 97% got approved. Everyone talks about the lottery like it’s luck. It’s great for us, because it lets us call the outcome chance. It isn’t. The outcome got decided months earlier by a team that writes the specialty-occupation language before the req even opens. They’re fantastic. I’m proud of them.

This year Copilot started drafting the language for them. Turns out Copilot is really good at describing a job only 1 person on earth could possibly do, as long as that person is already in our system. We called the workstream PERMANENCE. Legal made us rename it. Now it’s Project Continuity. Same slides.

Domestic candidates apply. Plenty of them clear the bar. We go with the H-1B anyway. Why? Because the H-1B already took the band. The band is Level II prevailing wage. Level II is the median we asked for. The people who can quit get paid off a different median, one they talk about openly at lunch. The H-1B negotiates off the LCA. The LCA’s public. Basically nobody reads it. I read it every quarter. Honestly, it’s calming.

We track the result as diversity and inclusion.

68% of the engineers who joined Azure last cycle came in on temporary status. The dashboard shows that number in a really nice green. What it doesn’t show is the 28% fully-loaded cost delta. That lives in a different workbook. Finance owns that one. Finance is proud too.

Let me tell you about Raj.

Raj has been on Azure Storage for 6 years. He knows the codebase better than the guys who wrote it, and 2 of them already left for counteroffers. Last spring his manager, Dana, asked why we couldn’t just promote him to staff and backfill locally.

So we set up a talent review. 40 minutes.

I asked Dana about pipeline health. Dana asked about the codebase. I asked about competitive intensity. Dana asked about the codebase again. I asked whether she had a growth mindset. She said she thought so. We agreed to take it offline.

Offline is where Dana’s req went to die.

Raj stayed. Raj always stays. He came in on another company’s visa, and we transferred it. Counsel has a template for that. The new $100,000 fee only hits talent that’s still overseas. Raj was already here. Transfers keep the leverage and skip the toll. Finance made a slide about it. There’s a little rocket on it.

The transfer is the point.

Look, if you can quit on Friday, you’ve got leverage on Thursday. If your legal status ends the day your job does, you’ve got Thursdays and that’s it. We never have to threaten anybody. The statute does that for us. Raj has read the statute. He’s also read his priority date: 2014. Projected to go current in 2031. Between now and then we’ll bump his Level II wage twice, and both bumps will be smaller than what we gave the people who can walk. We call that pay equity, since the formula treats everyone exactly the same. Only some people get to argue with it.

His wife’s on an H-4. Back in Pune she was a pharmacist. Here she’s a really organized volunteer. His daughter turns 21 in 2029, which is the year she ages out of his case. She wants to be a doctor. On paper, in 2029, she becomes an international student in the only country she remembers. HR flagged it as a retention risk. Finance flagged it as a retention asset. We went with Finance.

Some people call this a caste system. We call it a two-tier compensation architecture, and it’s working exactly the way it’s supposed to.

In the workbook, the line is column AF. The header says Mobility Status. There are 2 options: Portable and Anchored. Nobody ever types the word caste. Excel’s never needed it.

The Portable folks sit above the line. They get the counteroffers, the refreshers, and the freedom to ignore the 11pm call. When a Portable engineer mentions he’s “exploring options,” a VP takes him to lunch somewhere with no prices on the menu. When an Anchored engineer explores options, he gets 60 days to do it. That’s the grace period after you’re let go. They call it grace. We didn’t name it. We’d have named it better.

The Anchored folks sit below the line. They get the scope, the on-call rotation, the “stretch assignment,” and a calibration note that says high potential, visa-dependent. Nobody writes down that second part. Everyone in the room already knows. The room claps for the first part. When a Portable engineer pushes back on a deadline, we call it psychological safety. When an Anchored engineer pushes back, well, he doesn’t. We call that alignment.

At the all-hands, both tiers sit together. Same hoodie. The hoodie says One Microsoft. And at the hoodie level, it’s true.

During the January layoffs, the Portable folks got severance, a sweet LinkedIn post, and 14 recruiter DMs by lunch. The Anchored folks got severance and a countdown. A guy on Raj’s team spent his last 3 weeks training his replacement and his first 3 weeks unemployed applying to 212 jobs from a Starbucks in Bellevue, because his landlord wanted proof of income. He landed something on day 57. We sent him a survey about his offboarding experience. He gave it 4 out of 5. He said everyone was really kind. And they were! The people were kind. The people just didn’t design the system.

Belonging scores go up when the alternative is a one-way flight. Velocity goes up when nobody on the team can say no.

Viva pings Raj at 11:40pm to remind him to protect his focus time. He reads it on the incident bridge. His engagement numbers are fantastic.

In March his dad died in Hyderabad. Raj didn’t go home. His visa stamp had expired, and the next consulate appointment was 11 months out. If he left, he might not get back in. And getting back in meant the job, the house, his daughter’s school, the 2014 priority date. So he watched the cremation on his phone, propped up against his monitor, between a design review and an on-call handoff. His manager approved 3 days of bereavement leave. He used 1. The other 2 roll over. We’re super flexible about leave.

Critics say we’re replacing Americans. Internally we call it workforce durability. Durability just means they stay.

Durable talent brings specialized skills. The specialized skills have signed the at-will acknowledgment and the non-compete, and we’ll enforce it if they try to jump before their date’s current. The date’s never current. Everybody knows what happens if we pull a petition. We’ve never had to explain it twice. (Fine, immigration counsel will tell you that after 180 days the priority date survives a withdrawal. We leave that out of the onboarding deck. Onboarding decks should be uplifting.)

In March we won Best Employer for Global Talent. The plaque’s in Building 92. Most of the people it honors can’t switch employers to find out if it’s true.

Some of us have started thinking of the backlog as infrastructure. We don’t lobby against it. In our policy comments we call it a “stable pipeline environment.” Stability’s one of our values. It’s on a poster, right next to Courage.

I meet with the team every Monday.

They know the cap. They know the premium processing window. They know which vendors will staff the interview loop so the candidate’s prepped and the manager never gets surprised by an acceptance. They cheer when a req closes under budget and the diversity and inclusion cell turns green. Last quarter it went green in 4 orgs. We sent a note. It said belonging and innovation. Both totally accurate. Raj belongs. We innovated.

Dana left in August for a competitor. We matched the offer in a day. She still said no. People who can leave are like that.

Raj sent her a goodbye message in Teams. He couldn’t make the drinks. He was on call.

I’m so, so proud of this team.

They took a regulatory constraint and turned it into permanent leverage.

And the leverage compounds. We report it as growth. The analysts love growth. So do I. My equity vests every quarter.

Raj’s priority date goes current in 2031.

His father’s never will.

text:
TypeSafe AI's Diogo Almeida on why the boring SaaS companies are best positioned to win AI:

Ben: "When the coding agents came out, it was the SaaSpocalypse, and all their values dropped through the floor. Then when Jev came out, every SaaS company is like, 'This is the greatest thing ever.'"

Diogo: "In the SaaSpocalypse story, the story I feel has panned out really poorly is that software is very cheap and perhaps easy to replicate. I could believe the former. I could not believe the latter, because a lot of the stuff happens beneath the hood."

"I think SaaS will be one of the largest winners of the whole AI game."

"I want to work really, really well with the biggest, most boring SaaS companies because I think they're the best positioned to know what workflows to automate, what people need. That's their bread and butter."

"I'm not going to forecast anything about the financial markets. But as far as capabilities go, I think it's going to be like an inverse SaaSpocalypse. I'm so jazzed about it."

@CompleteSkeptic @typesafeai @bhorowitz @martin_casado

A 75 year old asset manager put a regulated money fund fully onchain.

Anthony Pecore of Franklin Templeton told Rob how Benji came together.

It started as an experiment. When they saw what digital ledger technology could do to asset management, they made a call:

"It's our job to stay in front of that."

They worked with the SEC, got a regulated money fund onchain, and kept ownership records there with no backup ledger behind it.

It worked.

Today, the fund's ownership is recorded purely onchain.

"There's no secondary book of records."

In March his dad died in Hyderabad. Raj didn’t go home. His visa stamp had expired, and the next consulate appointment was 11 months out. If he left, he might not get back in. And getting back in meant the job, the house, his daughter’s school, the 2014 priority date. So he watched the cremation on his phone, propped up against his monitor, between a design review and an on-call handoff. His manager approved 3 days of bereavement leave. He used 1. The other 2 roll over. We’re super flexible about leave.

Critics say we’re replacing Americans. Internally we call it workforce durability. Durability just means they stay.

Durable talent brings specialized skills. The specialized skills have signed the at-will acknowledgment and the non-compete, and we’ll enforce it if they try to jump before their date’s current. The date’s never current. Everybody knows what happens if we pull a petition. We’ve never had to explain it twice. (Fine, immigration counsel will tell you that after 180 days the priority date survives a withdrawal. We leave that out of the onboarding deck. Onboarding decks should be uplifting.)

In March we won Best Employer for Global Talent. The plaque’s in Building 92. Most of the people it honors can’t switch employers to find out if it’s true.

Some of us have started thinking of the backlog as infrastructure. We don’t lobby against it. In our policy comments we call it a “stable pipeline environment.” Stability’s one of our values. It’s on a poster, right next to Courage.

I meet with the team every Monday.

They know the cap. They know the premium processing window. They know which vendors will staff the interview loop so the candidate’s prepped and the manager never gets surprised by an acceptance. They cheer when a req closes under budget and the diversity and inclusion cell turns green. Last quarter it went green in 4 orgs. We sent a note. It said belonging and innovation. Both totally accurate. Raj belongs. We innovated.

Dana left in August for a competitor. We matched the offer in a day. She still said no. People who can leave are like that.

Raj sent her a goodbye message in Teams. He couldn’t make the drinks. He was on call.

I’m so, so proud of this team.

They took a regulatory constraint and turned it into permanent leverage.

And the leverage compounds. We report it as growth. The analysts love growth. So do I. My equity vests every quarter.

Raj’s priority date goes current in 2031.

His father’s never will.

author: zephyr_z9
quoted_text:
We exited $LITE at the start of 3Q26 and stayed out at the 4Q26 rebalance. Lumentum's exposure to AI optics is real, but it depends on design choices that are still open.

1. Lumentum is one of the suppliers of high-power lasers for external laser sources, where the laser sits in its own module and feeds light to the optics. Growth in AI optics lifts this business only as far as customers choose these designs.

2. Co-packaged optics (CPO) puts the optics in the same package as the chip. Some CPO designs keep external lasers, which suits Lumentum. Others move the light source closer to the package, or replace lasers with microLEDs, tiny LEDs used for short links. Wider use of these would cut demand for its lasers.

3. Laser and silicon-photonics technology built for LiDAR (laser-based sensing) is being adapted for data-center links, which could bring new competitors. We have added LiDAR exposure and will cover it in Part 2 or 3 of our 4Q26 rebalance series.

4. Optical circuit switching (OCS) connects fibers by steering light between them. Lumentum's MEMS switches use tiny movable mirrors and suit many ports, low loss and paths that stay in place for long periods. Designs that must change paths quickly and in smaller units are more likely to use silicon-photonics switches. MEMS should win a meaningful share, but probably not all of it.

Lumentum keeps credible exposure to external lasers and OCS, but both depend on unsettled design choices. At the 4Q26 rebalance, that uncertainty was enough for us to stay out.

text:
With the funding environment where it is, there is an incredible opportunity for cash grab in the short term for most founders

VCs are closing their eyes and investing in everything and anything related to AI, in the prayers that they don’t miss out on the next Anthropic, Cursor or Rogo

The real test for companies will be turning down the short term maximalism to focus on generating long term value for shareholders and society as a whole

It is a lot easier said than done, particularly when you have million dollar checks being thrown at your face every single day

Many young founders will make the error of inviting the wrong type of investor in their cap stack or accepting dilution beyond anything they need to

Even worse, many will overspend on projects and on hiring teams they don’t actually need to accomplish the long term vision of the company

My two cents of advice

1. If you must, grab the money while the sun is shining in this funding environment, but be very careful of who you take on as an investor

2. Be intentional and ask yourself if VC funding is actually the solution for achieving your vision. Many companies and founders would be much better off if they bootstrapped their way to profitability

3. Squeeze down your burn wherever possible. Don’t hire for the sake of hiring. Don’t pursue new verticals for the sake of doing it

This environment won’t last forever. At some point, there will be a break on the pedal

So many people have DM’d me about this trailer and I’ll be honest, watching it made me physically throw up.

I was COO from before FTX even had a name, it was my baby, and I was the last one out of the Bahamas after Sam got extradited. I lost everything I had on it and it took me a long time to get over, so I have zero interest in defending the people who caused this.

The media loves the story that FTX blew up because we were all partying in the Bahamas, but the place I worked looked nothing like that.

quoted_text:
Gemini Agent is built for high-ceiling work where EACH task gets its own computer.  

You can choose Gemini 4 Argon or Claude Opus 5.5. 

10 things that make it a universal work Agent (read till the end to see what a REAL work agent looks like): 

1. One Agent, one API
Chat, autonomous objectives, and code generation from a single interface. Assign it work, schedule it, or have it respond to events.

2. Coworker agents with their own identities
It creates job-specific sub-agents, each with its own identity, and computer running in parallel for hours or days.

Each Coworker agent gets its own Workspace account: an agent email, calendar, Drive, and presence in your company directory. You mention it in Chat. It acts under its own identity, not yours, and sees only what you share.

3. Everywhere, including headless
Web, iOS, Android, Windows, Mac, command line, Workspace, Microsoft 365, Slack. It also runs as a headless agent with no dedicated interface.

4. Work 24/7 in the cloud
It keeps one set of memories, context, and personalization graph across every device and channel. Work that takes hours or days keeps running after you close your laptop. You never have to re-brief it.

5. Layers of memory that improve over time
- Session: the task in front of it, even when it runs for days.
- Semantic: a structured knowledge base it builds as it reads documents, talks to people, and works with other agents.
- Procedural: how a job gets done, including skills it writes for itself.
- Episodic: everything it has done before.

6. Proactive by design
It does not wait to be prompted. An email asking you for a deck gets flagged as delegatable, one click to hand off. Your inbox ranks by what matters, not by what just arrived, and tells you why.

7. Tools and skills, with company registries
Salesforce, ServiceNow, Jira, Git, Confluence, Microsoft 365, Slack, BigQuery, Databricks, Postgres, Snowflake, your desktop files, and any MCP server inside or outside your network. Teams publish their own tools and skills to a shared company registry.

8. Model Choice so you are not locked in
It runs each job on the model that fits best, running  across the Gemini and Claude models from Anthropic today, with other private and open models to come. 

9. Governed like an employee
Every agent gets a cryptographically attested identity with least-privilege permissions, and an audit trail attributed to the agent rather than a person. Agents run in a sandbox behind Agent Gateway, an AI network firewall. Write the policy once and it applies to every agent.

10. Costs you can actually cap
Smart Routing puts each workload on the model with the best performance at the lowest cost. Set a hard spend limit in Cloud Billing and that project's agent pauses until you resume it in one click.

Thank you for reading so far. Stay tuned for updates. 

We are 100% committed to make it the best Agent for work.

So many people have DM’d me about this trailer and I’ll be honest, watching it made me physically throw up.

I was COO from before FTX even had a name, it was my baby, and I was the last one out of the Bahamas after Sam got extradited. I lost everything I had on it and it took me a long time to get over, so I have zero interest in defending the people who caused this.

The media loves the story that FTX blew up because we were all partying in the Bahamas, but the place I worked looked nothing like that.

We had under 200 people in the core company at its peak, not counting subsidiaries, when other exchanges our size had thousands, so a lot of us were doing 16 to 18 hour days for over three years and barely had time to sleep, and whenever we walked in, day or night, Sam was at his desk.

I worked with Caroline and never once saw her get aggressive like she does in this trailer. She’s quiet and mild, and often lost in her own thoughts.

Most of us didn’t even know she and Sam were dating until we read about it after the bankruptcy, and I never saw him so much as put an arm around anyone.

FTX’s collapse ruined so many people’s lives, including ours, and Netflix decided to make it a love story. 

Shame on you @netflix.

AI will become one of the largest spending categories in the US economy:

AI services are projected to account for a record 8.8% of US GDP in 2032.

This estimate shows how much businesses and consumers are expected to spend per year on the services of AI companies.

This also implies AI companies would generate ~$3.5 trillion in annual revenue by 2032.

By comparison, US consumer spending on food accounts for a similar 9.1% of GDP.

This figure would also be ~72% higher than energy, at 5.1% of GDP, and twice the size of construction as well as computers and software, both at 4.4%.

It would also be nearly 3x defense, at 2.8%, and more than 7x communications and internet, at 1.2% of GDP.

The only category where spending is significantly larger is health, at 18% of GDP.

The scale of the AI revolution is unlike anything seen before.

So it would appear that the "authorized reseller" Was bought out in March of this year and forced to sign an NDA that prevented them from telling anybody that they had sold the business. 

The NDA expires in 10 days.

It is now more likely that we're not dealing with a malicious employee, but probably a well-funded and relatively sophisticated bad actor, possibly DPRK.

It is also likely that this is not the only third-party reseller that they attempted to buy.

If you purchased a ledger (or other hardware wallet) from ANY reseller and not from Ledger directly, you should carefully and slowly move funds to a new device. 

If you do not have a new device, you can start with a 2-of-2 multisig where your ledger is one signer and a hot wallet is another. Use that in the interim until you have another hardware device. 

And in the long term, the safest way to store your self-custodied tokens remains a multisig (but not a 2/2, where loss of one key leads to loss of funds). Prefer 2/3 or 3/5.

author: FigoETH
quoted_text:
Ethereum would not be Ethereum without Justin Drake.

JD has recruited most of crypto's top developers and researchers (including @dankrad). He has brought on most of the people you see and many you don't, people who could work anywhere else but chose to work silently for Ethereum and its infinitely large vision. He's the reason Post Quantum Ethereum even exists. He made @leanEthereum real. When you talk about growth, lean is setting a 100x vision for the network unlike anything else. Formal Verification of blockchains is the hot kid on the block now in crypto; who led key work that got it funded at scale? JD. Proving matters beyond blockchains; it might even be relevant for us to trust AI, and real-time proving has been pushed forward by many years because of JD.

His contributions have led to civilizational-level tools  that extend far beyond blockchains; he's helped answer questions like: how do we protect information + check that software does what it promises + verify computation without simply trusting whoever runs it. That is literally civilizational-grade infrastructure.

And now let's think about what kind of research culture we want Ethereum to have. 

We need people willing to put ambitious proposals and ideas in public, attach their name to them, and let everyone take them apart. Does that put Justin above criticism? Hell no. Please challenge his assumptions.  Knowing him, I am sure he would appreciate it. Criticize his communications too because maybe things could have been said better. 

BUT

Attacking his character is just wrong, and I cannot defend that in the slightest. If every controversial claim becomes a debate on whether someone has ever contributed anything, we end up teaching the next generation to keep their thoughts to themselves, and that is a bigger problem than anything else.

“Ethereum is in the business of disagreeing while staying together” has to mean something when we actually disagree.

You can think @drakefjustin is wrong and still be very glad that Ethereum has him. I certainly am.

Our first Sup[p]per Intelligence dinner in SF last night was a massive success

Senior leaders in AI & tech joined us shared insights on where the world is going and how the demand for inference is growing with it

A few notes:

→ Inference demand is growing through specialization. Every product brings its own requirements around models, latency, cost, control and reliability.

→ The infrastructure conversation now runs from power and GPU clusters through model selection, serving and production operations. Those layers increasingly need to be designed together 

→ Agents make inference economics impossible to ignore. As the number of agents and tasks grows, routing everything through one expensive model quickly stops making sense.

→ Enterprise adoption depends on fitting AI into real workflows, governance structures and operating constraints. Model quality alone will not carry a deployment.

Open-weight models create far more choice, but realizing their economic advantage requires serious work at the serving layer.. @boundlessHQ is doing that work

author: ConstanceWaing
quoted_text:
So many people have DM’d me about this trailer and I’ll be honest, watching it made me physically throw up.

I was COO from before FTX even had a name, it was my baby, and I was the last one out of the Bahamas after Sam got extradited. I lost everything I had on it and it took me a long time to get over, so I have zero interest in defending the people who caused this.

The media loves the story that FTX blew up because we were all partying in the Bahamas, but the place I worked looked nothing like that.

We had under 200 people in the core company at its peak, not counting subsidiaries, when other exchanges our size had thousands, so a lot of us were doing 16 to 18 hour days for over three years and barely had time to sleep, and whenever we walked in, day or night, Sam was at his desk.

I worked with Caroline and never once saw her get aggressive like she does in this trailer. She’s quiet and mild, and often lost in her own thoughts.

Most of us didn’t even know she and Sam were dating until we read about it after the bankruptcy, and I never saw him so much as put an arm around anyone.

FTX’s collapse ruined so many people’s lives, including ours, and Netflix decided to make it a love story. 

Shame on you @netflix.

text:
loving the workaround in Vision Wormhole paper (@_XiaozeLiu et al, Purdue + CMU)! their premise is that text-only models get unstable when you inject vectors they never saw in training, while vision-language models already take continuous vectors in through their image slots
so the sender's reasoning gets written into the receiver's image tokens, via one small codec per model and a shared reference space: ten models need ten codecs and no pairwise translators

with 1.6B–4B models it beats text handoffs by ~6 points and runs ~1.9x faster, but at 8B–12B it loses ground on hard tasks, AIME by up to 33 points, and they suspect the fixed 256-token image budget is too narrow for stronger senders

that's the part I'd watch: at @mostik_ai the sender is 753B, and stronger senders have more to say

text:
Ethereum would not be Ethereum without Justin Drake.

JD has recruited most of crypto's top developers and researchers (including @dankrad). He has brought on most of the people you see and many you don't, people who could work anywhere else but chose to work silently for Ethereum and its infinitely large vision. He's the reason Post Quantum Ethereum even exists. He made @leanEthereum real. When you talk about growth, lean is setting a 100x vision for the network unlike anything else. Formal Verification of blockchains is the hot kid on the block now in crypto; who led key work that got it funded at scale? JD. Proving matters beyond blockchains; it might even be relevant for us to trust AI, and real-time proving has been pushed forward by many years because of JD.

His contributions have led to civilizational-level tools  that extend far beyond blockchains; he's helped answer questions like: how do we protect information + check that software does what it promises + verify computation without simply trusting whoever runs it. That is literally civilizational-grade infrastructure.

And now let's think about what kind of research culture we want Ethereum to have. 

We need people willing to put ambitious proposals and ideas in public, attach their name to them, and let everyone take them apart. Does that put Justin above criticism? Hell no. Please challenge his assumptions.  Knowing him, I am sure he would appreciate it. Criticize his communications too because maybe things could have been said better. 

BUT

Attacking his character is just wrong, and I cannot defend that in the slightest. If every controversial claim becomes a debate on whether someone has ever contributed anything, we end up teaching the next generation to keep their thoughts to themselves, and that is a bigger problem than anything else.

“Ethereum is in the business of disagreeing while staying together” has to mean something when we actually disagree.

You can think @drakefjustin is wrong and still be very glad that Ethereum has him. I certainly am.

The incense burns low in the hearth,
a fragrance of dried sage and damp earth
clinging to the heavy velvet of her sleeves.
She doesn't need a crown of gold;
she wears a coronet of braided rowan twigs and silver,
catching the dim, flickering amber light.

She watches the silver bowl on the table,
where the water holds the reflection of a full moon
that hasn't yet risen above the trees.
With a slow turn of her wrist,
she drops a single dried rose petal into the center,
watching the ripples expand,
altering the geometry of the room.

The wind outside stirs the canopy,
bowing to her rhythm,
as if the roots beneath the floorboards
are listening for her boots to strike the stone.
She speaks in the cadence of the tides,
commanding the quiet space between the seasons,
holding the winter and the harvest
in the palm of her hand.

text:
Aave and MetaMask have connected two pieces of agent infrastructure, and the design is worth a closer look.

Yesterday, Aave said builders can now connect its MCP server to MetaMask's Agent Wallet.
The Aave MCP lets an AI agent read markets, inspect positions, simulate actions and prepare supply, borrow, repay and withdraw transactions on Aave v3 and v4.
According to Aave's docs, the server never holds keys or signs anything, and every action comes back unsigned for the wallet.
MetaMask's Agent Wallet is the signing side, a self-custodial wallet where users keep their keys.
MetaMask says supported transactions are simulated, scanned for threats by Blockaid and sent with MEV protection.
In the default Guard Mode, the wallet enforces allowlists and a rolling 24-hour outflow limit, and anything outside that policy needs 2FA approval.

Beast Mode drops the allowlists and the outflow limit, keeping only threat scanning and approval for malicious or risky transactions.
MetaMask's docs also note that signatures such as Permit2 are not yet counted toward the outflow limit.
Separating the agent that plans from the wallet that enforces policy is the right shape for onchain agents.

The open gap is debt, because an outflow cap tracks what leaves the wallet rather than how much an agent may borrow.

I finally decided to give @orgo a shot, and after a quick back and forth with @nickvasiles I decided that this HAS to be Alan's new home. 

I've moved my Hermes agent (and Alan's Way setup) to live on an Orgo virtual computer. 

I have 2x the ram compared to my hetzner server (for a similar price), and Orgo truly gives you the "computer in a cloud" experience with a very easy, 60 second onboarding.

text: .@ebfull presents @TachyonZcash's pioneering work to scale Zcash at @ns
author: Zcash
quoted_text:
Zcash cofounder and executive director of Tachyon, @ebfull on scaling Zcash:  

“We’re taking the cryptography that’s at the core of the private payments that take place in our protocol, and we’re removing all the cryptographic bottlenecks that are on the inside.

So, if I had to really describe what we’re doing briefly, is that we’re basically taking SNARKs, which are these things that we have inside of Zcash, and we’re adding something called a recursive proof to them. And these are really cool.

Right now in Zcash, when you send private payments, invariably you’re going to have multiple different things happening inside your transaction. So the proofs that you put inside them are quite large. They’re like seven kilobytes on average for a standard payment. And sometimes they’re a little bit larger because of random reasons that aren’t that interesting.

Inside of our thing, because we use recursive proofs, these proofs prove that other proofs have validated properly. And that’s sort of the essence of how they work. So it’s like proofs all the way down. The proofs can prove other instances of themselves, and so on and so on. And you can build all sorts of crazy applications with this.

And one simple example is just this. So in Tachyon, when you create a transaction, it actually doesn’t have a marginal increase in size of the transaction. So it actually, in our specific design, it’s not any larger than what we do in Orchard already.

So we can do the same principle with multiple transactions in a block. So a miner will take all the transactions and take all the proofs out, or these things called stamps, and combine them together into one proof, an aggregate that’s about 17 kilobytes in size. And we can shove as many transactions as possible into the block.

Actually, with the current block size, or the block size that we’re going to have in less than a month, you should be able to at least do about 150 TPS with that. But the real goal is just to enable the sort of asymptotic improvement here.”

今天美股反弹，美债这边的变化也很关键。此前长期美债不断被抛售，收益率越涨，股票承受的压力就越大。现在长债出现了较强的买盘，收益率从高位回落，市场对利率继续往上冲的担忧有所缓解，这给美股反弹创造了条件。

美东 10月8日，美国拍卖了 220 亿美元的 30 年期国债，投标倍数达到 2.54 倍，高于此前六次拍卖的平均水平。接近 5.62% 的收益率，已经能吸引一批投资者进场。有人愿意接下这些长期国债，市场就不必一直担心美国还要拿出更高的利息才能把债卖出去。

买盘推动债券价格上涨，收益率随之下降，股票面临的估值压力也会减轻。十年期美债收益率从周四盘中约 5.35% 回落到 5.23% 附近，今天盘中在 5.25% 左右，仍然低于此前的高点。对股市来说重要的是前几天利率不断冲高的势头暂时缓了下来。

与此同时，OpenAI 年底收入预期的新报道，也缓解了部分投资者对 AI 增长的担忧。债市稳下来，给整个市场减轻了压力。AI 的消息改善，又给科技股提供了反弹的理由。在美股的带动下 Bitcoin 目前的走势也稍微稳定了一些。

So many people have DM’d me about this trailer and I’ll be honest, watching it made me physically throw up.

I was COO from before FTX even had a name, it was my baby, and I was the last one out of the Bahamas after Sam got extradited. I lost everything I had on it and it took me a long time to get over, so I have zero interest in defending the people who caused this.

The media loves the story that FTX blew up because we were all partying in the Bahamas, but the place I worked looked nothing like that.

We had under 200 people in the core company at its peak, not counting subsidiaries, when other exchanges our size had thousands, so a lot of us were doing 16 to 18 hour days for over three years and barely had time to sleep, and whenever we walked in, day or night, Sam was at his desk.

I worked with Caroline and never once saw her get aggressive like she does in this trailer. She’s quiet and mild, and often lost in her own thoughts.

Most of us didn’t even know she and Sam were dating until we read about it after the bankruptcy, and I never saw him so much as put an arm around anyone.

FTX’s collapse ruined so many people’s lives, including ours, and Netflix decided to make it a love story. 

Shame on you @netflix.

Correction: for multisigs the ideal "safe" rule is that you want each signer to change their key after each operation.

(This is making an implicit assumption that ECDSA might become weak, but not to the point where any crack of it would be literally instant so you would literally have to worry about eg. in-mempool frontrunning)

You definitely still want to gather sigs offchain if possible, to minimize the number of hours between "sig revealed" and "key no longer active"

text:
I don't recommend anyone scramble to move their funds to new wallets today. But we should take the risks to cryptography from AI-accelerated math seriously, and minimize our exposure to not just quantum-vulnerable cryptography, but also potentially AI-vulnerable cryptography.

The core new area of risk from this viewpoint is, unfortunately, ML-DSA / FHE / lattices.

(and it's also another reason, along with quantum, why ECDSA might fall even faster than expected, hence the "fresh address" recommendation)

So far most people have been in the mode of thinking "elliptic curves broken, hashes safe, lattices safe". But there is a good chance that the concrete security of lattices will take serious hits from the next two years of AI math.

The basic threat model is: factoring is something that naively takes 2^(n/2) time, but over decades smart people have found and optimized number field sieves, and degraded that to 2^O(n^(1/3)), which is why RSA keys and signatures need to be ~400 bytes (and not 64 bytes). What if there are skeletons in the closet like that, both for elliptic curves and lattices, that we are simply not smart enough to discover - but bots soon will be?

This is a major part of the reason why for the past year ethereum's lean roadmap has been going in the "hash-only" direction: no lattices, no ML-DSA, no Falcon, no lattice-based commitments inside ZK proofs, etc. Signatures in lean ethereum are all hash-based, either WOTS or SPHINCS-.

For signatures and proofs, we already know how to go hash-only. The bigger challenge is for *public-key encryption* - and this goes far beyond blockchains. Secure communication, anonymizing protocols, lots of things need public-key encryption.

And unfortunately there are long-standing mathematical theorems showing why public-key encryption cannot be done with hashes alone. You have to have some kind of trapdoor object that has at least one form of usable "structure" - either group theory (incl. isogenies) or lattices or code-based or potentially in the future even more newfangled and spooky things (local mixing?). But for anything that has structure, you should assume that AI will make at least some progress in breaking that structure. Here, one reasonable inference is that if you want to make something plausibly long-term secure, multiply the key sizes by 10.

To me that's a very plausible world and something not at all extreme to predict. If AI will bring us 50 years of math in 2 years, then that 50 years of math may very plausibly include a "naive factoring -> GNFS" level of improvement to our ability to break lattices. In that world, lattices will still exist, but they will have to be significantly bigger to guarantee the same level of safety.

And at those new larger sizes, hash-based constructions will beat lattice-based constructions on concrete efficiency in every use case where hash-based constructions are possible at all.

Theoretically, of course it's possible that hashes are broken too (eg. P = NP would imply that). But I think P = NP is very unlikely. And intuitively, it's much more likely that a mathematical object has exactly no exploitable structure (like hashes are intended to), than that a mathematical object has exactly ~3 forms of exploitable structure (for elliptic curves: associativity, Schoof, pairings) and not some secret fourth form of structure we have not yet discovered that greatly degrades its security (for elliptic curves, ECDLP and pairing security). Similar for LWE, SVP, RLWE and the zoo of lattice problems.

For this reason, we do not yet see any reason to worry and start padding the byte size of hashes (if we start to worry more, we would pad the round count first before doing anything to the byte size).

Concrete TLDR, my own personal views:

* Hash-based > lattice-based, in those situations where hash-based is possible at all
* For anything lattice-based, be much more paranoid on param sizes. Remember that blockchains are only a small portion of the cryptography story; this point goes far beyond blockchains and applies to eg. access to websites, secure messaging, Tor / VPNs ...
* For privacy protocols, strongly favor NOT putting encrypted notes onchain. Instead, send them offchain through some third-party mechanism.
* If it's not difficult for you, keeping your funds in addresses which have not yet been used to make a transaction is a good idea. If it's easy for you, do it. **But be careful about migrations; I personally have lost more money in botched migrations than I have lost in all hacks combined**.
* For multisig wallets, doing confirmations offchain is better than onchain, because this way the signatures of signer wallets do not get exposed to the public, so if ECDSA falls to AI much faster than expected, at least the multisig "gracefully degrades" to a 1-of-1 where the 1 is whoever was gathering the signatures - a much better place to be than "anyone can take the money"

text:
many people still don’t understand how powerful non-custodial wallets are for fintechs. they're the foundation of the first truly global fintechs. 

a few years ago, launching a product often meant taking custody of user funds, which came with a massive country-by-country regulatory burden.

non-custodial wallets flip that structure. the user owns and controls the funds, while the fintech can build the user experience around the wallet without necessarily taking custody of user funds.

this doesn’t eliminate regulation, but it significantly reduces the burden, which is why crypto infrastructure has become the go-to stack for fintech builders.

text:
So many people have DM’d me about this trailer and I’ll be honest, watching it made me physically throw up.

I was COO from before FTX even had a name, it was my baby, and I was the last one out of the Bahamas after Sam got extradited. I lost everything I had on it and it took me a long time to get over, so I have zero interest in defending the people who caused this.

The media loves the story that FTX blew up because we were all partying in the Bahamas, but the place I worked looked nothing like that.

We had under 200 people in the core company at its peak, not counting subsidiaries, when other exchanges our size had thousands, so a lot of us were doing 16 to 18 hour days for over three years and barely had time to sleep, and whenever we walked in, day or night, Sam was at his desk.

I worked with Caroline and never once saw her get aggressive like she does in this trailer. She’s quiet and mild, and often lost in her own thoughts.

Most of us didn’t even know she and Sam were dating until we read about it after the bankruptcy, and I never saw him so much as put an arm around anyone.

FTX’s collapse ruined so many people’s lives, including ours, and Netflix decided to make it a love story. 

Shame on you @netflix.

text:
This is what stablecoin adoption at real stores can look like.

At TOKEN2049’s Midnight event, WEA Japan CEO Yoshi Bansho laid out the work behind bringing stablecoin payments to everyday retail: connect wallets and chains to existing merchants, POS systems and PSPs, while allowing merchants to receive yen.

The presentation showed Netstars’ scale... 15,000 connected merchants and 700,000 payment terminals... and two completed pilots: Haneda Airport in January and Lawson in August. 

Commercial rollout is planned for this autumn.

The economics are tangible. The deck compared roughly 3% credit-card costs with WEA’s 0.98% model... about two percentage points in potential savings. Bansho’s example showed how some of that could become a shopper discount while the merchant keeps part of the savings.

Privacy was central to the presentation: give regulators the information they require while protecting retailers’ settlement data. WEA’s slide specifically explained why it is looking to work with Midnight. WEA has also described NetX technology as powering its stablecoin payment work.

Charles Hoskinson asked about Japan’s regulatory position. Bansho explained that the regulatory work was already done. Charles called the effort close to his heart, showed real interest, and made sure his chief of staff was there as they looked to explore it further. Dr. Ruan Anbang was also present.

That’s a promising moment... and a compelling look at the people, infrastructure and economics behind bringing stablecoins from crypto conversations to real checkout counters.

Watch the exchange.

#StablecoinPayments #NetX

text:
Grok Bot just got its own inbox

Now GTM teams can take their workflows to the next level

Here’s how to build an always-on sales pipeline that finds clients and reaches out to them:

> Set up Firecrawl /monitor in your bot to watch target websites 24/7

> Define a score for each type of change and set a threshold

> Once an account crosses the threshold, the bot uses Firecrawl to check what changed, who to email, and why now

> Grok Bot writes a personal email and sends it from its own inbox

→ Something new ships? Set a routine to follow up automatically

→ Have the bot check for replies every day and offer a time to book a call

That’s it. Nearly zero humans in the loop. It never sleeps and never misses a signal.

More use cases like this are possible with the @firecrawl plugin in @bot
