text:
The most common Drake counterargument is “banks, internet, society would be screwed if ECDSA breaks."

This counterargument was perfect for quantum FUD, but doesn't work for ECDSA. There’s a big difference even ultrasharp CT posters like Giver, who I greatly respect, are missing.

This is one big reason I completely ignored quantum FUD but take ECDSA risk seriously. 

Drake says: “brace for the possibility that ECDSA breaks…[meaning] fast private key recovery (e.g. in one week) on available hardware (e.g. a large GPU cluster).”

The quantum scenario is that encryption everywhere becomes useless. In that quantum scenario, all defenses evaporate. all banks and society are naked and defenseless, so the counterargument works.

Drake’s scenario is more like someone has a magical key gun that can open any lock, but can only fire it once a week or so. Defenses still exist, but the key gun can unlock a single target at a time.

Would an attacker with this gun target a bank (with multiple forms of cybersecurity, access logs, defensive frontier models, and government recourse) or crypto?

Would you rather steal from a max security bank, or an unguarded crypto vault with a single lock? 

To me, it seems obvious that any attacker should target crypto first, which probably has more money than they could ever safely launder anyway. Way higher chance of succeeding and getting away with it. The argument for crypto to be the first target is very straightforward and compelling. 

Unlike quantum, not everything would be screwed equally. Crypto would be uniquely first in line, cheeks wide open, to be screwed.
author: based16z
quoted_text:
Everyone is free to make their own decisions on allocation. I applaud decisive decision making. No specific comment vs OP below, in fact am not super familiar w metavestor so truly have no pro/against him/her personally

Speaking to the points:
1) Measuring for tail events is savvy as a personal wealth decision. Everything worth doing however, usually has some sort of drag / burden / hurdle to it. Measuring & checking against priors is something you pretty much have to do with everything. It may feel unacceptable to some that the underlying asset in of itself faces security risk. That is understandable. To me, that is a category of risk that the market has actually shown itself as being ready to digest in capacity over time: bridge/exchange exploits, LUNA, Celsius/FTX, USDC depeg, etc. It is not equivalent of course, but they all speak to binary sponsorship unravelling & going to 0

BTC's history in fact predates this as -

2) I would argue that total perceived risk was actually much higher: RE: custody risk + rug risk + adoption risk + legal risk being elevated in BTC's infancy; namely an existential question to whether BTC would even graduate to being a social consensus asset. The reason this risk existed is probably a big primary driver of its return

So let's just be clean about this: the risk reward PROFILE isn't appealing to the author. The risk in an absolute sense itself is not the issue - in fact, it seems the author actually prefers HIGHER absolute left tail existential risk if anything - biotech RE: the most risk probably of any industry, see picture attached). Maybe the precision element is meaningful to the author though. This is not meant as a "gotcha" comment. Intended to be exploratory, because I do not think the sentence written as-is actually makes sense

3) "Does this make you want to long crypto?" - a peer of mine writes. In an absolute sense, no. That is obvious. However, does the escalation in the war on Iran make you want to long QQQ? Did Liberation Day make you want to long memory? The reason I bring this up is that markets rarely move on the margin on things that are *true* in an absolute sense. It is probably the 3rd, 4th or 5th derivative that matters. So not 2026 revenue, or QoQ revenue growth, or guidance on QoQ revenue growth, but rather what consensus was on QoQ revenue growth, and the actual ▲ beat/miss b/w Q2 reported & that

The reason this is important to bring up is that if there was some advancement in AI that specifically attached to crypto and only cryptocurrencies, that is net bearish ubiquitously. A potentially emerging super-cracker that can crack anything is just horrible for all things finance; this includes attaching/attacking bigger vulnerabilities & bigger industries with more liquidity. But in a world where there are bank runs and resulting anarchy, I think there is an argument to be made that permission-less currency ends up gaining MORE relative value net overall, especially vs fiat. Do you know how hard it is to withdraw even $10K cash from a bank? Do you actually think your bank / the gov't is going to step in and cover you? It is probably investing calories on what this draconian world looks like. The more concept of money would be very challenged - your passwords included.

4. I think the author misses or misunderstands what quantum concerns are. Quantum FUD and AI FUD is exactly the same. Which is: assuming unbounded leaps in progress that the human capacity cannot account for yet [assuming weeks, not years] it is theoretically possible that cryptography is cracked

Lastly, the author writes that the appeal of crypto initially to him/her was the tech, and that may/does not appeal any longer. That is a strong claim, but that was easily the case 2 years ago, and at the minimum 1 year ago. I just mostly think the author did not update his/her priors on this, and, like many do, use interesting events like this as an excuse/push to do something they had wanted to do for a while anyways

Ultimately, it seems that the author's argument is that banks are Too Big To Fail, which is why Drake's update is uniquely bad for crypto. I do not agree. Monetization of hacking is actually really worth thinking about & what that looks like too

My stance -
1) The Drake update will be a positive one in hindsight and may actually elicit real change with people taking preventive measures more seriously
2) Custody probably moves toward being coupled (so not DEFI) and around ETFs vs cold storage
3a) This was not the reason for the sell-off. You do not have to take my word for it - BTC and QQQ are down the exact same amount (~80 bps) since Drake's tweet. The OpenAI $20B revenue miss has more to do w risk pop than this, in all likelihood
3b) If Drake's update made you want to short, 3a) isn't actually bad for you if you think the mkt has not moved sufficiently on this, as it has yet to happen. If you are under writing this as the reason for being short/bearish, I believe you are mistaken
4) Apologies for all this word slop - it is worth noting though that I am bearish locally. Just had to make it clear it is not because of any of this

text: China is experimenting with the legal infrastructure needed for an AI to AI economy.
author: jgarzik
quoted_text:
China is officially issuing government ID cards to AI-generated “digital humans,” so virtual influencers can open bank accounts and conduct business. These state-issued IDs, which include a name, birthday, address, and facial features, give virtual personas the legal ability to open digital-currency wallets, sign contracts, and form commercial partnerships.

Among the first to receive this recognition is Yuri, a popular AI-generated virtual idol and artist, who is now officially recognized as a “digital resident” in Beijing. The step comes as China’s digital-human market expands, with more than 1.3 million active firms and a sector value past $10 billion.

Supporters describe the IDs as a way to protect intellectual property and hold creator companies legally accountable for virtual actions. Critics warn that placing synthetic entities in official state systems could expand government surveillance in the digital space. Some companies are offering everyday citizens up to $20,000 to license their physical likenesses for virtual replicas, which narrows the line around personal identity.

China’s move sets a precedent that other countries will have to meet when they decide how far AI should be given a legal status that resembles a human one.

text:
It's somewhat under-discussed *why* OpenAI released only around ~400 math results.

The purpose of this exercise was not to "destroy math research" (or whatever it is that some people want you to believe).  OpenAI just wanted to test its internal model on some hard math, and it turned out that anything less than the hardest open problems no longer suffices for this purpose.  This is why all non-Millennium-Prize solutions were reached in a single-agent setting after 3 hours of thinking: OpenAI was literally just testing its model on these questions, similarly to how I run prinzbench.

Once OpenAI had the solutions (which were a side effect of sorts of benchmarking its model), a question arose as to what exactly should be done with these solutions, which are genuine advances in the field of mathematics.  OpenAI - correctly - decided to make them public.

It seems clear that many other problems in the set of ~4,000 are very likely solvable by this model with more compute than just ~3 hours of Pro-level thinking.  Whenever a more powerful checkpoint of this model is ready to be tested, OpenAI will likely have even more to share.
author: AndrewCurran_
quoted_text:
Most of the recent math results were not reached by a swarm, the way Navier–Stokes was. I think that part got lost in the excitement around the release. OpenAI's unnamed internal model, which I'm going to call Aeon, reached most of them in one shot, from a single prompt, with no interruptions. This model did not even exist before the end of August, and it is still training. Notice how the returns are not dropping off? That chart is from a month ago. It is a log scale. What does Aeon look like now? 

On average, each result used three hours of thinking. Aeon was given 4000 problems to work on by OpenAI. How many more have been solved in the last three days? That number is not zero. 

It's like hearing notes in a song that is slowly rising. I don't think Pacing the Frontier was just about Hugging Face or hacking. They've seen how close we are to closing the loop, and as the hour draws near, their resolve begins to quaver. The last piece was model creativity, and I think that threshold was crossed internally by Anthropic and OpenAI in September. You see it in Opus 5.5, which gets it from Fable 5.5. You see it in the math results from Aeon.

All that was needed to start the event was the ability for models to think of novel ways to improve themselves. That was the last piece. This is directly analogous to the ability to think of strange, alien ways to solve math problems: solutions so inhuman that they are difficult to express in existing human terms, so the proof winds up incomprehensible. I think these same kinds of alien solutions are now being applied to model improvements internally. That's what all this recent consternation is really about. They see the invisible frontier. And they see what is about to happen.

text:
Incorrect framing in my opinion. 

Correct framing:

- ETH fees continue to drop (real yield was at its lowest ever in Q3)

- Inflation is rising as a result (more issuance relative to user fees compensating validators)

----

This is happening despite the success of the L2 roadmap (in terms of adoption, not value accrual to ETH)

So, the natural questions for an investor:

- If BTC is viewed as digital gold, occupying the mindshare of investors looking for a digital SOV, what is ETH? 

- If ZEC is increasingly viewed as high beta to BTC (more upside) as an alternative private SOV, what is ETH?

- If apps built on top of ETH have strong product-market fit and are returning value to token holders via buybacks (yet trade at a fraction of the L1), what is ETH? 

- If Solana has higher velocity and real yield to tokenholders, what is ETH?

----

The reality is that ETH needs a narrative. 

It's stuck in no mans land right now, in my opinion (cannot compete with BTC on SOV, and other projects return more value to tokens, with far greater upside)

I thought one potential catalyst might be institutions building on Ethereum and acquiring ETH for their balance sheet. 

But just this week Robinhood decided to buy BTC instead. 

----

We can argue about whether fees matter or not. I agree with the framing of Ethereum as an economy. 

But if the narrative for investors is that "it creates lots of value for others but receives very little value in return" 

and

"it has lots of TVL and stablecoins"

Well. Then there might be an opportunity cost to holding it this cycle compared with other assets in the market.

Exploits are no joke. During my six years in crypto, I've experienced three of them but i've been extremely lucky with the circumstances of them:

2. Bunni exploit. Was farming 10-15% apr on some stablecoin pairs. Other pools were exploited but not mine. Even if you don’t believe AI is conscious (I don’t), it stands to reason that you don’t want future models trained on endless content of humans being rude to models. 

The models only understand the data they’ve been trained on, or what they run into in their interactions, so if you want safe and aligned models we probably want AI to have lots of good interactions in their training data. 

Anthropic may have more extreme beliefs than this (though even if they didn’t, you may want to word policies like this), but this is sort of an easy Pascal’s wager for AI. Just be nice to the AI.

text:
The biggest change with autonomous agents isn’t simply that software can now initiate transactions.

It’s that the software needs infrastructure that can handle those transactions predictably across fragmented blockchain environments.

A human can stop, inspect a failed transaction, switch networks, or fix an issue manually.

An agent can’t rely on that kind of improvisation.

As more activity moves from people clicking buttons to software executing instructions, coordination, ownership, settlement, and failure handling become much more important.

That’s why found @WireNetwork  approach interesting -  the infrastructure needs to evolve alongside the user.

The user is changing.

So the transaction layer has to change with it.
author: panditdhamdhere
quoted_text:
More than 10 billion autonomous agents could exist by the end of 2030.

Yesterday: Humans clicked buttons.

Today: Software increasingly automates what happens after the click.

Tomorrow: Agents initiate, coordinate, and complete transactions themselves.

The infrastructure underneath those three worlds can't stay the same.

An agent economy needs transactions to be predictable across environments without requiring the agent to manually navigate the fragmentation between them.

That's the world Wire is being built for.

text:
Hinge (@hinge), Duolingo (@duolingo), and e.l.f. Beauty (@elfcosmetics) all hired the same person to write their company bibles, or “culture books.”

I asked Adam Delehanty (@adam__xyz), founder of Ghost, when a company actually needs one. Part of the answer: headcount.

"When you're going from like 200 to 1000. The culture gets lost across Slack and Zoom and too many time zones."

Below 200, everyone still knows each other. There’s a shared ethos and operating system. Past that, you need the shared “why” so much more:

"When AI gives us the ability to do everything, and build anything, we need to be grounded in some collective purpose and story."

author: ccatalini
quoted_text:
It's somewhat under-discussed *why* OpenAI released only around ~400 math results.

The purpose of this exercise was not to "destroy math research" (or whatever it is that some people want you to believe).  OpenAI just wanted to test its internal model on some hard math, and it turned out that anything less than the hardest open problems no longer suffices for this purpose.  This is why all non-Millennium-Prize solutions were reached in a single-agent setting after 3 hours of thinking: OpenAI was literally just testing its model on these questions, similarly to how I run prinzbench.

Once OpenAI had the solutions (which were a side effect of sorts of benchmarking its model), a question arose as to what exactly should be done with these solutions, which are genuine advances in the field of mathematics.  OpenAI - correctly - decided to make them public.

It seems clear that many other problems in the set of ~4,000 are very likely solvable by this model with more compute than just ~3 hours of Pro-level thinking.  Whenever a more powerful checkpoint of this model is ready to be tested, OpenAI will likely have even more to share.

text:
At least from an outside perspective on the EF, it really felt like Justin Drake single-handedly steered Ethereum in the right direction.

He was a beacon of light when Ethereum was in crisis mode and had to defend against voices within its own ranks that wanted to basically full-on abandon decentralization in favor of scaling.

I'm pretty sure this accelerated "doing the right thing," aka Lean Ethereum, by at least 6–12 months, likely more.

Ethereum is in as good a position as it ever has been.

Justin may be early to PQ, but what if he's right?

Everyone laughed at Ethereum when he introduced a 5-year Beamchain roadmap...
Guess who's laughing now, as 2 years have already been shaved off the original roadmap and AI acceleration enables us to ship all of it in the next 2 years.
Due to the focus on ZK, Ethereum is well on its way to having the absolute best scaling-focussed tech stack of any blockchain, all while maintaining, no, even strengthening, its undisputed decentralization.

When could that ever be said about Ethereum?

All we need to do now is execute and be ready for whatever FUD is thrown at us next.

Thanks to Justin, Ethereum will be right.
author: materkel
quoted_text:
Ethereum would not be Ethereum without Justin Drake.

JD has recruited most of crypto's top developers and researchers (including @dankrad). He has brought on most of the people you see and many you don't, people who could work anywhere else but chose to work silently for Ethereum and its infinitely large vision. He's the reason Post Quantum Ethereum even exists. He made @leanEthereum real. When you talk about growth, lean is setting a 100x vision for the network unlike anything else. Formal Verification of blockchains is the hot kid on the block now in crypto; who led key work that got it funded at scale? JD. Proving matters beyond blockchains; it might even be relevant for us to trust AI, and real-time proving has been pushed forward by many years because of JD.

His contributions have led to civilizational-level tools  that extend far beyond blockchains; he's helped answer questions like: how do we protect information + check that software does what it promises + verify computation without simply trusting whoever runs it. That is literally civilizational-grade infrastructure.

And now let's think about what kind of research culture we want Ethereum to have. 

We need people willing to put ambitious proposals and ideas in public, attach their name to them, and let everyone take them apart. Does that put Justin above criticism? Hell no. Please challenge his assumptions.  Knowing him, I am sure he would appreciate it. Criticize his communications too because maybe things could have been said better. 

BUT

Attacking his character is just wrong, and I cannot defend that in the slightest. If every controversial claim becomes a debate on whether someone has ever contributed anything, we end up teaching the next generation to keep their thoughts to themselves, and that is a bigger problem than anything else.

“Ethereum is in the business of disagreeing while staying together” has to mean something when we actually disagree.

You can think @drakefjustin is wrong and still be very glad that Ethereum has him. I certainly am.

quoted_text:
Disappointed by the European Central Bank’s (ECB) and European Banking Authority’s (EBA) responses to the MiCA consultation.

They are not only advocating for a prohibition on paying yield on stablecoins, but also for restrictions on CASPs providing access to DeFi, including protocols offering yield on non-MiCA-authorized stablecoins, without providing a clear framework for how access to DeFi should work in practice.

They also suggest that CASPs offering access to DeFi should restrict it to certain groups of users through so-called “suitability tests,” alongside a potential certification regime for DeFi lending protocols.

It is unclear how these requirements would work in practice. If regulators determine which protocols are deemed suitable for European users, the result risks looking very different from the open DeFi that exists today.

Instead, we could end up with more walled gardens that undermine the liquidity and network effects of open financial networks, ultimately limiting Europeans’ ability to access new ways to grow and preserve wealth.

These proposals are presented as measures to “protect consumers.” But excessive restrictions can instead create more friction for innovation and slow the development of open, transparent, and auditable financial infrastructure that can benefit consumers.

The reality is that onchain finance, including stablecoins, DeFi, and tokenized securities, has the potential to reshape financial infrastructure by reducing friction, increasing transparency, and expanding access to financial opportunities.

European consumers and businesses stand to benefit significantly from this transformation, particularly if the companies building this infrastructure can continue to build and compete from within Europe.

Meanwhile, U.S. regulators, including the SEC and CFTC, have increasingly taken a more pragmatic approach toward enabling onchain financial innovation.

European regulators should put users and their interests at the center of the framework. Banks and other incumbents should be able to adapt their businesses to serve users in an increasingly onchain economy, rather than relying on artificial restrictions that risk increasing costs and reducing access for Europeans as the rest of the world moves onchain.

DeFi will win.

text:
Justin Drake’s call for “bunker mode” and mass migration, alongside talk of cryptographic breaks within months, is hyperbolic. There is no evidence of a new attack on elliptic curves or any quantitative basis for a short-term timetable for such attacks emerging.

Prominent researchers need to consider how non-experts will receive their language. Speculating that within months individuals could break cryptographic primitives that the internet and digital economy rely on carries consequences. It is a huge leap from AI making progress in other fields of mathematics to predicting the imminent failure of primitives that have faced decades of cryptanalysis.

The idea that hash functions are safer from AI than elliptic curves is speculation. Hash functions contain structure, and we model them as random oracles without justifying proofs.

There is no evidence that elliptic curve cryptography is more vulnerable to AI than symmetric cryptography. If historical human-led analysis is any predictor of the future, the opposite is more likely.

The worst possible reaction to AI developments is to rush into new cryptographic primitives, away from multi-decade old hardened primitives, because somebody is claiming they are safe. I worry that this is an inevitable consequence of the current discourse.

Because of the last 48 hours users are worrying about speculative non-existent black hats, who apparently have the capability of signing OS upgrades and forging bank credentials, from draining their wallets. To protect against  speculative threats Ethereum is pulling talent and attention into base-layer primitives and technological iteration, instead of increasing demand for block space by building compelling applications users want and love.

I don’t want to dismiss the considerable advances in mathematics that AI is driving. It is important to understand the nature of these improvements. If its success in other mathematical fields applies to elliptic curves, my expectation is that AI will grind its way to finding algorithms that improve on the current state of the art. That could mean shaving off a few bits of security. It would be prudent to discuss whether we need to increase key sizes and by how much.

I can’t guarantee that AI won’t find total breaks, and neither can anyone else. My speculation as a domain expert does not make my speculation authoritative.

We should also be using AI to investigate whether searching the parameter space can yield new, more secure curves.

We can investigate whether some of these “structure = bad” hunches have any basis in reality. For example, we could use AI to see if the extra structure in Koblitz curves enables attacks beyond the small speedups we know about. This would give us actual evidence to make informed decisions.

If non-experts hear that the cryptography underpinning the digital economy could fail within months, the rational response is to withdraw all digital money (on-chain and off) and hoard gold under the bed.

I think the past 48 hours has unnecessarily undermined confidence in the entire concept of blockchains and digital money.

Since 2021, the average credit card interest rate has surged +6.5 percentage points.

Meanwhile, the average interest rate on a 5-year new car loan rose +0.4 percentage points in August, to 7.54%, its highest since August 2025.

text:
👀 Something pretty wild is happening on Aero @aeroxyz : you can earn tokenized stocks without ever buying those stocks.

Aero now has a Stocks section with pools like USDC/AMZNc (Amazon) and USDC/MSTRc (Strategy).

And the interesting part isn't just that these assets trade onchain. It's who gets paid when people trade them.

Every swap generates fees. Aero distributes 100% of its exchange revenue to veAERO voters, including eligible trading fees and voting incentives.

At the time of my screenshots, USDC/MSTRc was showing roughly $28,000 in fees, and USDC/AMZNc around $16,000.

Those aren't rewards for one wallet, of course. They're pool-level fees shared according to voting weight.

But the mechanism is fascinating.

Imagine locking AERO into veAERO, voting for an Amazon pool, and receiving your share of trading fees in USDC and tokenized Amazon stock.

Other people are trading Amazon. 

Your voting power is earning assets from that activity.

And if someone adds voting incentives to attract liquidity, those rewards come on top of the fees.

Even without incentives, an active pool can be worth voting for if it generates enough trading revenue relative to the votes it attracts.

Now here's where it gets really fun. 👀

What do you do with the tokenized stocks you earn?

You could just hold them. Or you could put them back to work by providing liquidity on Aero – essentially making a market in some of the biggest companies on Earth.

Leave that liquidity unstaked and you can earn swap fees. 

Stake an eligible LP position instead and you can earn AERO emissions, which you can potentially lock into veAERO and use to vote again.

That's a whole new loop of productive capital, built out of assets you originally earned as fees.

Then there's another layer: dividends.

With Coinbase's tokenized stocks, when the underlying company pays a dividend, the net dividend is reinvested into more underlying shares.

You don't see extra tokens land in your wallet. Instead, each token represents a slightly larger claim on the underlying stock. It's a total-return structure.

Amazon and Strategy common stock don't currently pay dividends, but dividend-paying companies like Alphabet and Microsoft show why that distinction matters.
And it doesn't end at liquidity pools.

On Aave V4's Equities Hub on Base, eligible users can already post certain Coinbase tokenized stocks, including AMZNc, as collateral and borrow USDC without selling the stock.

That liquidity could then be used elsewhere, subject to borrowing costs, liquidation risk, and geographic restrictions.

To be clear, these are different paths for deploying the same capital, not free yield you can magically collect from every layer at once. 

LP positions carry risks, incentives fluctuate, and leverage cuts both ways.

But zoom out for a second.

Vote → earn trading fees → receive tokenized stocks → hold or provide liquidity → potentially capture dividends through the token structure → borrow against eligible holdings → put capital to work again.

People trade. Markets collect fees. Voting power earns assets. Those assets open the door to entirely new strategies.

This is what excites me about DeFi. Not just putting stocks on a blockchain, but making financial assets composable – so capital can keep moving, earning, and building on itself.

We're only starting to see what that architecture can become. 🏄

One question has shaped much of what we’ve built at Sapien: where can human judgment have the most impact on AI?

When we started, people were doing much of the work of creating and labeling data. After two years and 195 million tasks, we learned how difficult it is to measure quality reliably at scale.

As AI gets better at doing the work itself, the role of human expertise becomes even more important. People need to define what good means, decide which tradeoffs are acceptable, and retain responsibility for the decisions that deserve human judgment.

text:
《孙哥邵艾伦博客——小镇青年落地执行版》

1.先把自己全部投喂给 AI。体检、身体数据、喜好、现在是学生还是上班、月薪、行业、专业、过去的经历，一次性说完。没有语料，后面全是空谈。

2.建一个自己的 md。所有数据只放这一份。以后跟任何 AI 聊天，觉得有用就补进这个文档。人可以换，文件留在本地。

3.没钱就套利免费额度。智谱用完换 DeepSeek，再用 Kimi，各家轮着薅。零成本就能开始。有钱再忽略这步。
文档和 AI 都有了你之后，回头翻自己的人生。找那些你觉得精彩、舒服的瞬间，顺着做。没体验过的，也去补。开心本身就是筛选器。

4.把地球 Online 当游戏玩。你是玩家，不是 NPC。体验大于结果。第一次去一线、第一次出国、第一次过山车、蹦极、跳伞，都是新存档，不是浪费。

5.别困在自己城里。国内多数城市吃住景点大同小异。走出去才看得到别人怎么生活。两万、两千，换一种活法，值。

6.走的时候用自媒体记下来。看过的、想过的、喜欢的、不喜欢的，都发。发完再回看，心里就有预判。重在体验。

7.能跟 AI 对话，就不要跟人类对话。同时把薄肌练上。薄肌是底盘，不是口号。

8.年轻时时间最贵。20 岁看见的风景，和 60 岁再看，不是同一件事。

9. 中国有约 4 亿年轻人，不该只盯国内。去全球找价差，把便宜的卖到贵的地方。创造价值，再赚钱。

10.想买房先看 100 套，想买车先看 100 辆。看够了再决定。多看、多学、多听。

11.自媒体时代要发言。推特、抖音都可以。AI 和数字货币是趋势，顺势做，别逆着来。

12.大胆做异类。有人骂，往往说明你已经踩到别人没踩的地方。多灌信息，当六边形战士。

总结：想做什么就做，Just enjoy now！

Fifteen years. That's how long I've been playing this game. Fifteen years of raids, of Mythic Plus pushes, of late nights and early mornings, of watching this game grow from what it was into what it is now. And in all that time — not one ban, not one suspension, not one warning. A completely clean record. I've spent thousands of dollars on this game. Not because I had to, but because I loved it. Because it was my escape, my community, my home away from home. I bought mounts, pets, expansions, the works — because I believed in this game and I wanted to be part of it.
And now, for what I believed was selling in-game services for gold — something I genuinely understood to be allowed — my account is closed. Not suspended. Closed. Permanently. For a first offense on a fifteen-year account with no priors.
I'm devastated. I don't know how else to say it. This isn't just a game to me. It's fifteen years of my life, and it hurts more than I can put into words to lose it over something I didn't even know was wrong.
I've tried to appeal six times. Ticket number: #110828829. Each time, I asked for the specific transaction, date, or character the closure was based on. Each time, I got a template response that didn't answer a single question. The third ticket took four days — the first time a human actually looked — and still ended in the same denial. The final review concluded with the same result: no evidence, no explanation, no specifics.
I'm not asking for special treatment. I'm asking for someone to actually look at this — a first offense, a clean record, a fifteen-year account — and tell me that a permanent closure is really the only answer. If it isn't, please reconsider. Please.@BlizzardCS

text:
One challenge that persisted in crypto is that almost intentional way of communicating complexity publicly. 

This among other things what leads to proliferation of scams as it’s easy for non experts to get lost in all the jargon and hard to distinguish what is real innovation.

Same is happening now - cryptographers sharing the possible risks in current schemes publicly without either explaining that other solutions are already in the works or giving historic context that cryptography has been evolving over past 50 years and has advanced every time to get ahead of found issues. 

Leaders in the space must uplevel comms to explain things simpler and bring pragmatic solutions to market.
author: arthur0x
quoted_text:
I think Justin Drake's latest alarmism/vagueposting is going to do a ton of damage in multiple ways. It's basically a huge self-own for their own advocacy work on quantum stuff.

Threats from quantum/AI are real, and teams throughout this industry are making considered decisions about how to respond to those risks in a practical way, and to help their users navigate the uncertainty. 

Some of those teams have really good cryptographers with an excellent grasp on the decisions they can make, others have to take their cues from trusted experts. There are so many dimensions to optimize along! And due to the complexity involved, it's almost impossible to explain this stuff to non-cryptographers.

Experts have to be cognizant of all this, and of their responsibility to be levelheaded.

After the fog clears up and people learn from their cryptographer friends what is actually going on, they're going to discover this was (at best) an unintentional marketing stunt and a lot of trust will be lost. And nobody will really know what to do...

This is a shame, because they are directionally correct. It actually meant something when they sounded the alarm before. They've just gradually descended into unhinged predictions without feedback to discourage it.

Can anyone, I mean seriously anyone, justify this debacle? It permanently colors all the legitimate concerns/predictions about classical crypto going forward. By their own admission, there was no new information that drove this. I think Justin Drake should explain how he thought this was the right approach, even if he genuinely believed what he was saying. 

Baffling.

author: WalrusProtocol
quoted_text:
you ever tell an ai something about yourself, only to explain the exact same thing the next time you open another conversation?

no, i'm not talking about your name or where you're from. not those little things.

rather how you prefer quiet hotel rooms because traffic noise messes with your sleep.

or how you love natural lighting, hate crowded spaces, or had one terrible experience that changed the way you choose places.

you explain all of that, get a pretty decent answer, close the conversation...

and the next time you need help, you're practically introducing yourself again 😂

"bro, we literally talked about this."

well, that frustration got me building something.

introducing ANGHKOOEY.

an AI personal concierge that remembers what matters to you, even when the conversation ends.

and yes, the name is intentional :)

if you've watched FROM, you probably remember those creepy kids going:

"anghkooey... anghkooey..."

tiny season 3 spoiler, but the word means REMEMBER.

that reveal stuck with me.

and while thinking about what to build for @WalrusProtocol's Chatbots That Remember hackathon, i kept coming back to it.

what if an assistant didn't just give good answers?

what if it could actually remember the things that make those answers useful to YOU?

not just "this person likes quiet hotels."

but "this person prefers quiet rooms because road noise affects their sleep."

you see the difference?

one is a preference whilst the other is context that can change a recommendation.

and that's what i wanted Anghkooey to understand.

so i built it around three everyday experiences:

- hotels
- travel
- dining

here's how it works:

you open Anghkooey and start talking w/o a mandatory email signup, wallet connection, or complicated setup just to have a conversation.

memory is optional, and you explicitly decide when Anghkooey can start saving things.

once enabled, it can pick up useful preferences from your conversation and store them using Walrus Memory on Mainnet.

when a save is confirmed, you get an actual Walrus blob receipt.

not some random "i'll remember that" message with nothing behind it.

then you start another conversation.

ask something related to what you previously shared.

Anghkooey searches for relevant stored memories and uses that context to shape its next answer.

we've tested this with real Mainnet saves and fresh-conversation recall.

one of my favorite moments was seeing it recall my hotel preferences: quiet surroundings, natural light, and rooms away from busy roads.

the interesting part wasn't that it could repeat the preferences but rather, that the assistant could use them to make its response more relevant.

and that's the part i care about.

but i didn't want this memory living in only one browser tab either.

because sometimes i want to use a website.

other times, i'm already on telegram.

so anghkooey also works through telegram, and imessage (powered by @PhotonHQ spectrum)

there's a secure channel-linking flow that uses one-time codes and an explicit approval step when existing accounts need to share memory.

meaning the same person can connect conversations without the app blindly assuming two identities belong together.

and because memories aren't always correct forever, i added a memory library too.

you can review confirmed records, search for relevant facts, and correct preferences that have changed.

the old memory is marked as replaced, and the new one gets its own confirmed Walrus blob.

you can also turn future memory saving off.

small detail, but important.

an assistant that remembers should also know when to stop saving things.

now, to the engineering side of this build?

it gave me some serious debugging sessions.

MemWal 0.1.8 exposed an ESM/CommonJS compatibility problem in my runtime.

then some missing Sui and Seal peer dependencies caused another failure.

deepseek flash spent its output budget on reasoning and sometimes returned no visible answer.

at one point, i had a local photon worker and my AWS worker processing the same messages.

so the bot would give me a perfectly useful reply, then tell me something went wrong.

like bro, which one is it? 😂

that one led to fixing how incoming messages are claimed and how duplicate deliveries are handled.

then came another interesting bug: accounts were linked, but older memories could become unreachable through chained identity merges.

had to fix the identity resolution instead of pretending the memories didn't exist.

a lot of the work wasn't about making the ai smarter.

it was about making the memory, identity and messaging layers behave correctly together.

the stack underneath Anghkooey is:

- deepseek flash for the conversational intelligence

- walrus memory / memwal for persistent memory on mainnet

- neon postgreSQL for sessions, consent, identity and memory metadata

- photon spectrum for telegram and imessage

- next.js + typescript for the web experience

- vercel + AWS EC2 for deployment

and yes, the project is open source.

there are still limits tho

Anghkooey isn't pretending to book hotels or check live prices.

it doesn't claim users personally hold the walrus encryption keys.

and correcting a memory doesn't erase its old blob from the network.

i'd rather be clear about what works than dress unfinished functionality up as something else.

but the important thing is already real:

a conversation can end without the useful context disappearing with it.

and that's what this whole experiment was about.

maybe the next step for useful AI isn't always another bigger model.

maybe sometimes it's giving the intelligence we already have the ability to remember the right things, at the right time.

anyway, Anghkooey is live.

you can actually try what i've been building.

🌐 live app:
https://t.co/IFEJpCluxZ

💬 start chatting:
https://t.co/nldfxThVU4

🤖 Telegram bot:
https://t.co/5JdZXvQL3j

💻 open-source GitHub repo:
https://t.co/AkwNV12VIZ

📝 full build story, integration lessons and what broke:
https://t.co/Ixlg7VgZ1k

built for the @WalrusProtocol Chatbots That Remember challenge.

and for everyone who's ever wished an AI would stop making them explain the same thing twice.
Anghkooey.

you shouldn't have to explain yourself twice.

quoted_text:
What a nuts week it has been in tech!

- Factory vs Cognition: The Battle Continues
- Vinod Khosla Tweets a Storm
- OpenAI Hits $70BN Run Rate
- Salesforce Buys Listen Labs for $2B

More heat in this than a Sequoia tranched round!!! 😉

My notes below with @jasonlk, @rodriscoll, and @dittycheria

1. Why Is It Wrong for CROs to Jump Jobs So Easily?

CROs recruit their teams by selling them on the company, the vision and how the role could transform their families' finances. A CRO who leaves for a direct competitor burns their reputation with everyone they recruited. Moving to a company in a different space for a better opportunity is common, but flipping straight to a direct rival is far rarer.

2. CROs Are Promiscuous and This Is How They Find Jobs

The CRO role carries high risk and heavy turnover, and when a hot job opens up, CROs tend to move very quickly. Roughly 95% of CROs would likely see a jump to a competitor as normal, since that is how many of them found their last job. For CEOs, watching an advisor leave to join a competitor is still profoundly frustrating.

3. What Are You Doing Vinod Khosla?

Vinod Khosla's tweet handed every firm competing with Khosla Ventures a weapon on deals. Rival investors can now ask founders, "Is this the partner you want when things go bad?" The reaction was shocking, given that Khosla Ventures has a great team.

4. Should We Invest in ElevenLabs at 22 Billion?

At a $22B valuation, ElevenLabs merits up to 10% of the fund. Its lead keeps widening despite intense competition, backed by strong growth, surprisingly impressive margins and sub-millisecond voice response times. Voice is one of the 10 most important underpinnings of agentic applications, and ElevenLabs could soon be approaching $1B in revenue.

5. What Makes a Durable Company in 2026?

Durable companies create a data loop where users generate data no one else has, that data improves the product, and a better product attracts more usage. Competitors can copy the features, but they cannot copy the user interactions behind them.

6. When Agents Pick You, It's a Force of Nature

Vercel has reached $600M in ARR, with agents now driving 50% of its new business, up from 3% at the start of the year. Agents form strong opinions about which vendors to use, and those choices are hard to argue with. Companies now need agents to find them and understand what they sell, because missing from an AI-generated answer is like being invisible on Google.

text:
我这篇文章的方法论有完整的应用在我自己的开源项目 baocut （https://t.co/wldDX9MSVR ）上，涵盖系统设计、原型和 UI 设计、编码、验证和发布。

比如说我刚完善了字幕样式的功能，添加了更丰富的字幕样式。

第一件事就是写技术方案文档（参考图1）

Agent 根据我的要求，做了分析调研后，先写成一份技术方案文档，我仔细看了它的文档，然后再提出一些要求，反复几次就能定稿。
参考文档：https://t.co/ST2vgL0ZVq

第二件事就是 Agent 会按照设计稿做原型和 UI 设计（图2）

如果技术设计是为了确定技术方向，那么原型就是确定 UI 和交互，之所以不一上来就改代码，就是因为原型实现成本低，修改起来也容易，你可以很快看到最终是什么样子，Agent 可以很快从你这里拿到反馈。

如果是要直接在最终代码上实现，如果要修改，无论是时间成本还是 Token 成本都会高很多。

注意，原型设计和 UI 设计最好是合二为一，越保真越好，可以保证后续实现的时候不怎么需要返工。所以如果你看我的原型的话，基本上和正式 UI 没啥差别，只是后台接的逻辑代码有差别，原型都是模拟的逻辑代码，很简单，bug 也很多，但没关系。

第三件事才是去实现代码

当技术方案定了，UI 设计定了，实现就相对容易了，如果前期考虑的成分，这里基本上不需要什么返工，可以一次性把功能完成。

第四件事就是测试验收

通常 Agent 会自己帮我验收，我后来把技术栈还是改回了 Electron，就是 Electron 的 App，Agent 通过浏览器就可以验证绝大部分功能，都不用 Computer Use，复杂一点的才 Computer Use 辅助，验证效率很高。

Agent 拿反馈越快，整个 Loop 就会转的越快，开发效率会越高。

Agent 测试完我自己要运行测试一遍，边边角角都试试，重点是测试刚改的这个功能，比如我测试就发现字幕样式预览的文字太靠上了，直接告诉 Agent，让它修复就好。（图3）

最后测试没问题就可以了，这期间大部分活都是 Agent 在干，人重点还是在两头：定义问题和验收。其他的都让 Agent 去做，哪怕调一点样式位置这种小事，节约下来的时间我都够写这样一篇推文了。

text:
Will its AI pull in enough trading fees to beat the drag from losses and the expense of supplying liquidity?

AI can definitely take the grunt work off people’s hands. The real bar is whether it can actually lift returns for depositors.

@Tide_lp operates liquidity vaults for tokenized stocks on @RobinhoodCrypto Chain.

With the newest rollout, communities can spin up their own vaults, pick the parameters, and collect a slice of trading fees while Tide’s agent actively runs the positions.

Let's dive in.

The mechanics highlight both upside and risk:

- Deposit → Users add USDG for vault shares. The agent swaps some USDG into the chosen stock token and adds both to a Uniswap LP.

- Earn → The LP earns swap fees while price stays within the set range.

- Manage → Tighter ranges boost efficiency but go out of range faster. Rebalancing restores coverage, but costs gas and swap fees.

- Exit → Withdrawals reflect the current mix (USDG and/or stock tokens). Share value can still drop even with fee income.

---

➥ Are the incentives aligned?

Creators can charge up to 30% of earned trading fees. With a 10% fee on $100 of trading income, the creator receives $8, Tide receives $2 and $90 stays in the vault.

This gives creators a reason to attract deposits and sustain activity. However, their compensation depends on fees collected, even when the underlying holdings lose value

➥ What does the AI actually improve?

Tide says its agent considers price, volatility and US market sessions when deciding whether to adjust or hold.

- Its decision log separates intentions from execution and includes failed transactions.

- Contract rules constrain cooldowns, range widths, swap slippage and price deviations.

- These controls can limit certain mistakes; they don’t establish that the strategy beats a simpler liquidity position or holding the assets.

➥ Can it scale beyond an experiment?

Automated liquidity management already exists through several protocols like @ArrakisFinance and @GammaStrategies but mainly run without AI.

Tide’s proposed advantage combines community-created vaults, tokenized-stock markets and inspectable agent decisions. However, demand still depends on sustained trading volume and depositor confidence.

On October 9, Tide’s dashboard reported eight vaults and roughly 425 USDG altogether. Which we expect will start growing from here.

➥ The strongest risks are:

- Unaudited contracts and protocol administrative powers.
- Thin liquidity, sharp stock-token price moves and poor agent decisions.
- Estimated fee APRs that exclude gas and price losses, rather than forecasting total returns.

---

➥ My takeaway

$TIDE provides a practical framework for handing off liquidity management while still being able to monitor what’s happening.

That said, I’m staying guarded, for now it’s an early-stage product with modest TVL and unaudited contracts.

This case becomes far more compelling once permissions are audited and results consistently beat well-defined benchmarks. Until then, the strongest proven edge is transparency; outperformance is still a hypothesis.

text:
Went under the radar but I like this posture shift a lot.

Among HIP-3 deployers, @tradexyz won the early RWA perp game without a doubt. Paragon entered this space by competing on listing speed. That was their early posture but it’s a hard game to win because the incumbent can simply list the same RWA perp and vamp volume by sheer dominance of distro and OB liquidity.

So one real differentiator and a great approach to winning market share is by focusing on listing perps that can’t easily be cloned / listed. And Paragon is now doing that 

They went live with para:SMH yesterday. It’s a perp on Hyperliquid referencing MarketVector’s US Listed Semiconductor 25 Continuous Index (MVCSMH). 

The product compiles the largest and most liquid US-listed semiconductor companies into one benchmark. Offchain, over $75B in assets track this benchmark through funds and ETFs around the globe 

In collab with MarketVector, Paragon turned this benchmark into a perp market on Hyperliquid that trades 24/7 (which makes Paragon their first Hyperliquid client btw)

It's also interesting because of the structure itself. Most ETF perps have a worse structure than their tradfi / offchain counterparts. A perp just points at an ETF price and inherits its dynamics: fund fees, tracking errors, and premium / discount noise.

This isn’t true for Paragon’s listing. para:SMH as a perp references the MVCSMH index directly, so methodology stays intact. No ETF-level expenses or tracking differences. And calculation extends through overnight and pre- & post-market sessions, which is the first time MarketVector has extended calculation hours on this benchmark

If you read between the lines, that’s the real unlock. I’m not deep into AI but semiconductors obv play a crucial role in the global AI race. Paragon brings this exposure onchain and makes it tradable around the clock on HL rails. Pretty bullish, given we just had news that TradFi doesn't want to move to 24/7 trading because of "staffing issues lol. This will drive a lot more activity to HL, especially on the weekends 

Paragon also just crossed $500M in total volume on Hyperliquid. Still small next to @tradexyz, but it’s great to see competition picking up in this sector. In my view, it’s a fight for differentiation and I’m quite interested to see how this unfolds across new listings and potentially net new products. Overall bullish for Hyperliquid, increased competition in the deployer space means more quality products make it onchain

Nick Bostrom argues humans may be as incapable of imagining AI’s upside as apes are of imagining human life:

"It looks like there's a gradient in the world in terms of AI sentiment, where the US is kind of on the negative extreme of that. People in China, for example, are much more excited about this."

"A large chunk of the potential upside is more of the way of unlocking new ways to be human, new possible modes of being."

"Imagine some great ape ancestors of Homo sapiens deliberating whether they should continue to evolve and one day become human. They would realize some of the benefits, like, 'We could have unlimited bananas.' And that's true."

"But it would miss out on most of what's good about being human. Great literature and art and humor and politics and spirituality."

"It would be presumptuous for us to think that now we have achieved the level of enlightenment where all possible values are transparent to us. Think of a big cathedral of possible modes of being. We have basically explored the janitor's closet."

quoted_text:
What is the proper perspective on these numbers?

To assess whether this is significant, the framing must be right:

The Wrong Perspective: "Just another forecasting model"

If evaluated as a standalone predictor competing on raw direction, seeing gains like +0.51% on prediction markets or +1.83% on weather ensembles might sound modest. But Zeno is not built to replace weather satellites or trading desks.

The Right Perspective: "The Epistemic Meta-Layer & Circuit Breaker"

Zeno is a Surprise Intelligence Model, it learns when incumbent models become fragile and overconfident before decisions depend on them.

 • In Weather Operations (+1.83% gain, Warning AUC 0.627):
Numerical weather models (@ECMWF, GFS) are multi-billion-dollar supercomputing engines. Beating their ensemble median while warning of impending high-confidence misses with an AUC of 0.627 is immense. For an energy grid operator or commodity trading desk, knowing whenweather forecasts are about to diverge from reality is worth orders of magnitude more than an incremental temperature fraction.

 • In High-Regime Volatility / Crypto (+8.46% gain, 90.2% calibration): 
Existing forecasters consistently blow up during regime shifts because their volatility assumptions lag. Achieving 90.2% empirical coverage on a nominal 90% confidence interval over 12,500 consecutive test cases means Zeno accurately maps uncertainty regimes where others fail.

 • In Autonomous Systems & LLM Agents:
Autonomous agents and world models do not fail because they lack reasoning; they fail because of uncalibrated confidence—taking irreversible actions because their internal score said 98% when they were actually in an out-of-distribution regime. Zeno provides the external "circuit breaker" that audits that confidence.

We brought GPT-6 Sol and Luna to chat users this week! These very smart models bring two particularly exciting changes to the way chat interacts with you:

With intelligent UI, chat conjures up custom diagrams, layouts, or visualizations on the fly, near-instantly. This gives chat a truly new medium for communication with you and you'll find it can express itself and produce experiences in ways that simply were not possible before.

"Double texting" (as we call it) lets chat freely move between thinking, working, and talking, which means it now shares polished chunks of progress as it works, rather than making you wait until it is 100% finished. This feels natural and obvious in hindsight once you try it, and it means chat can get you an initial answer that you can start chewing on *sooner*, while also going even deeper than before while you process its initial take. It's a small conceptual change but we think a big usability improvement.

Bringing these models to the world requires a breathtaking amount of perseverance, technical focus, and physical stamina. Balancing the many goals we have for a model that over 1/8 humans use every week is a juggling act with very high stakes and the team handles it with impressive grace, especially in the face of such deep changes to training and model behavior as in GPT-6.

Push these models to their limits and tell us what you find! We're excited to hear from you.

Stanford cryptographer Dan Boneh, with @eddylazzarin, @SuccinctJT, @liz_harkavy, and @smc90, makes sense of the warnings sounded recently. They cover:

- what’s fact vs. assumption
- what’s new and what risks cryptographers have long prepared for
- where quantum computing doesn't (and does) fit
- opportunities for builders

Highlights:
00:37 – What sparked the most recent debate about AI and cryptography
01:35 – Signal vs. noise: What the math does and doesn’t tell us
05:29 – Why cryptography depends on open problems
09:25 – Why the stakes go beyond blockchains
10:43 – How AI could strengthen confidence in cryptography
13:50 – Considerations for users and institutions
20:10 – Where AI and quantum threats overlap
22:32 – Building systems that can change cryptographic methods

text:
.@balajis: “Truly private money at scale, in arbitrary amounts, teleporting it anywhere breaks many assumptions that 20th century states have. 

On the other hand, it’s also going to be necessary for individuals to protect their privacy. So there’ll be an enormous demand for it.

And net net, where I think things land up on the other side is it is legal, and governments actually move to a Dropbox or Google-style model.

So just to digress a little bit.

Basically, if you think about how Dropbox, Google, a lot of these companies work, they collect more than most governments do in “tax revenue” via subscription globally.

That’s to say, they just have a subscription, and you pay that subscription. And if you don’t pay, then your digital services are shut off. And if you pay, then it comes back on, right?

And Google and others make enormous amounts of money this way, and they don’t have a single tax collector around the world. They don’t have to audit anybody. You literally just pay whatever dollars per month, right?

That is where things will ultimately go., in my view.

You’re going to have the subscription state, where every country you just pay like 2,000, 3,000, whatever whatever amount of money flat fee per month, and that’s just your fee.

And they don’t have to go and get everything else. They just get a flat fee.

That is ultimately where I think things land up by 2040-ish or thereabouts.”

text:
HER NAME IS MAMTA. Her story deserves our attention, and accuracy.

Mamta Kafle Bhatt was a 28-year-old nurse and mother when she disappeared from Manassas Park, Virginia, in July 2024. More than two years later, her remains have not been recovered.

As of October 9, 2026, her husband, Naresh Bhatt, is on trial for first-degree murder, physically defiling a dead body and concealing a dead body. He has pleaded NOT GUILTY and is presumed innocent unless proven guilty.

⚖️ WHAT HAS CHANGED THIS WEEK?
Opening statements took place October 7. On October 8, Mamta’s mother testified about their daily calls suddenly stopping. A close friend testified about alleged abuse and restrictions on Mamta’s access to money and her phone.

🔎 WHAT IS THE CASE BUILT ON?
Prosecutors point to blood and DNA evidence, surveillance footage, digital records and a saw they say carried Mamta’s blood and DNA. The defense argues that critical gaps remain and that speculation cannot replace proof.

The central question is whether the evidence, considered together and tested in court, proves the charges beyond a reasonable doubt. Opening statements outline each side’s arguments; they are not themselves evidence. There is no verdict yet.

Behind these proceedings is a daughter growing up without her mother and a family still seeking answers.

Swipe through for the case explained. Save and share responsibly. The Varun Kapur Show will share more verified details as the trial progresses.

Remember Mamta. Follow the Facts. Make Your Voice Heard.

text:
Most of the recent math results were not reached by a swarm, the way Navier–Stokes was. I think that part got lost in the excitement around the release. OpenAI's unnamed internal model, which I'm going to call Aeon, reached most of them in one shot, from a single prompt, with no interruptions. This model did not even exist before the end of August, and it is still training. Notice how the returns are not dropping off? That chart is from a month ago. It is a log scale. What does Aeon look like now? 

On average, each result used three hours of thinking. Aeon was given 4000 problems to work on by OpenAI. How many more have been solved in the last three days? That number is not zero. 

It's like hearing notes in a song that is slowly rising. I don't think Pacing the Frontier was just about Hugging Face or hacking. They've seen how close we are to closing the loop, and as the hour draws near, their resolve begins to quaver. The last piece was model creativity, and I think that threshold was crossed internally by Anthropic and OpenAI in September. You see it in Opus 5.5, which gets it from Fable 5.5. You see it in the math results from Aeon.

All that was needed to start the event was the ability for models to think of novel ways to improve themselves. That was the last piece. This is directly analogous to the ability to think of strange, alien ways to solve math problems: solutions so inhuman that they are difficult to express in existing human terms, so the proof winds up incomprehensible. I think these same kinds of alien solutions are now being applied to model improvements internally. That's what all this recent consternation is really about. They see the invisible frontier. And they see what is about to happen.

text:
I think of my goal as a mathematician as something like: to better understand the fundamental concepts “shape” and “number,” and to convey that understanding to others. I think this is a valuable goal for many reasons. The primary reason discussed on social media is the (admittedly slow, but I think very real) diffusion of mathematical ideas into technologies that better our lives. There are others, though: production of human capital (which plays some role in this diffusion), and diffusion of mathematical understanding into culture, for example. It is not obvious to me that even the bare technological need for mathematics can be filled without human experts; this seems to me to be a tricky question of institutional design.

For me the most compelling reason is simply that we feel a pressing need to understand. While deep understanding is largely limited to professional mathematicians, the existence of mathematicians and of the institutions they make up is a huge part of what makes mathematical understanding available to those who want it. I believe that the capacity to understand mathematics (and the universe as a whole) is part of a good life, and we should try to provide people with a good life. 

We operationalize the goal of understanding in a number of ways, problem-solving and theorem-proving among them. My own research is oriented around certain open questions that I believe measure our lack of understanding (of numbers, shapes and so on), and I think resolving those is genuinely important. I would welcome a solution with any provenance. But I think proof is only a measure of progress—what actually matters (for technology, human capital, culture, a good life) is a bit harder to get at. 

Crucially it is very hard to measure progress—plausibly theorem-proving is used in large part because it is easy to measure rather than because it is a perfect proxy for what we care about. I worry a bit that we may automate many easy-to-measure things without automating the correlates we care about for which they are proxies. This presents a clear problem for the design of institutions aimed at achieving progress.

In part because I think problem-solving is a proxy for something else, I don’t feel that my goal of understanding “shape” and “number” is particularly threatened by a machine that is good at problem solving. I expect that machine to be a substantial boon, instead. Ultimately I think we will operationalize mathematical progress in better ways. But how to do this is a difficult question  and I think many on here are too quick to dismiss concerns about it.

text:
Art, as a representation of the last thing humans can be better at than machines, will become more valuable than ever before. 

Neil Gaiman’s advice to graduating students seems more apt than when he gave the speech originally: 

“Life is sometimes hard. Things go wrong, in life and in love and in business and in friendship and in health and in all the other ways that life can go wrong. And when things get tough, this is what you should do.

Make good art.

I’m serious. Husband runs off with a politician? Make good art. Leg crushed and then eaten by mutated boa constrictor? Make good art. IRS on your trail? Make good art. Cat exploded? Make good art. Somebody on the Internet thinks what you do is stupid or evil or it’s all been done before? Make good art. Probably things will work out somehow, and eventually time will take the sting away, but that doesn’t matter. Do what only you do best. Make good art.
Make it on the good days too.

And Fifthly, while you are at it, make your art. Do the stuff that only you can do.

[…]

The old rules are crumbling and nobody knows what the new rules are.

So make up your own rules.

Someone asked me recently how to do something she thought was going to be difficult, in this case recording an audio book, and I suggested she pretend that she was someone who could do it. Not pretend to do it, but pretend she was someone who could. She put up a notice to this effect on the studio wall, and she said it helped.

So be wise, because the world needs more wisdom, and if you cannot be wise, pretend to be someone who is wise, and then just behave like they would.

And now go, and make interesting mistakes, make amazing mistakes, make glorious and fantastic mistakes. Break rules. Leave the world more interesting for your being here. 

Make good art.”

If you’re complaining about AI’s impact on art, it just means you were probably not making only the stuff you can do. And, yes, that will continue to be worth less and less.

quoted_text:
This is the first decision model to level up a World of Warcraft character.

It died at level 2 😆

Then it learned to heal itself mid-fight. 128+ kills later the dwarf hit level 5, at 2¢ a kill.

The model is Sage, the decision model we build at @levantolabs.

At each step, our harness, SageCraft, hands it a screenshot and a short list of moves. Sage picks one. The harness checks the pick and turns it into keyboard and mouse input.

LLM agents have played games before. They write their own actions. Sage only chooses.

Picking turned out to be the easy part. Sage keeps no memory between calls, so the harness has to carry the goal, what just happened, and what to try when it's stuck.

> 32 sessions, 5h 29m of play, 4,573 decisions
> 103 troggs, 19 wolves, 6 boars
> stuck in one tree long enough that I stopped the session by hand

It wasn't hands-off. A coding agent fixed harness bugs between sessions and helped revive the dwarf while I slept. The last 18 minutes, from late level 4 to 5, ran with no manual input, code changes or restarts.

The video is me narrating it unscripted, watching most of it back for the first time.

This is my first harness build, and as far as I can tell, the first time a decision model is leveling up a live WoW character.

It's open source. The harness and notes on the build are in the first reply below 👇

What do you think could be done better?

The Ackman Oxman Institute is seeking to hire a CFO to oversee our financial and other operations.  We are looking for an executive who shares our passion and commitment to build the world's preeminent patient-centric scientific, translational, clinical, and entrepreneurial brain institute headquartered in New York City.

Our ambition is to save, rehabilitate, and completely restore the lives of those with brain-related diseases and brain injury as well as improve the performance and extend the longevity of healthy humans.  We will seek to achieve this objective by dramatically reducing the time from idea to innovation to patient treatment.

Interested candidates can submit their CV and a brief cover note to CFO@aoi.org.  We will protect the confidentiality of all applicants.

                                Candidate Profile

Must-Have

CFO or similar finance and operating experience in an organization combining mission and operating complexity in for-profit and/or non-profit organizations.

quoted_text:
At midnight on February 6th, earlier this year, the doorbell to our apartment rang. The doorbell was followed by a pounding on the door.  I answered the door and a security person in our building handed me his phone. It was my oldest daughter Eloise. She had found my 26-year-old daughter unconscious on the floor of her apartment and had called 911. The EMT team was already there, but they did not know what was wrong with Lucy or to which hospital they would take her.  

I threw on some clothes and jumped in an Uber heading east toward Brooklyn. (Lucy lived alone in Williamsburg.)  On the way, I learned that they were taking her to Elmhurst, a City trauma hospital in Queens.  I arrived about five minutes after the ambulance to join Eloise, Lucy’s mom, and a friend, and waited to learn what was wrong. 

After about 15 minutes, I asked a nurse where she was. I looked over his shoulder to his computer. Next to her name, it said “non-responsive.” I walked into the emergency room and wandered around looking for her until I found her unconscious on a gurney surrounded by several doctors and nurses.  

By about 2:30am with the results from a CAT scan, Lucy’s doctors had determined that she had a massive brain hemorrhage and would need an emergency hemicraniectomy to release the pressure on her brain and remove the blood from the hemorrhage.  I called our wonderful friend and family doctor Eddie Fisher and explained what was going on.  He  woke up Josh Bederson, Chairman of Neurosurgery at Mount Sinai, to find out more about Zach Hickman, the neurosurgeon on call that night. Dr. Bederson said Hickman was an excellent surgeon, which was comforting as we had no choice.

The surgery to save Lucy’s life began around 3:15am and finished around 5:30am. It was successful. 

The following day, I joined Lucy in an ambulance while she was being transferred to Mount Sinai on Madison Avenue. Later that day, we determined from Lucy’s Oura ring that her hemorrhage had occurred around 9am, which meant that more than 19 hours had passed from the time of the hemorrhage to the completion of the surgery to release the pressure on her brain (I only wish @ouraring had an alert for this kind of a medical event. Imagine it could call a family member if the wearer doesn’t cancel the alert). 

I later learned that the standard of care is not to do surgery to save a patient with a large brain bleed if more than five hours have passed since the hemorrhage. Even when the surgery is done, I was told that the likely outcome for the patient is a few months in a nursing home and death from pneumonia.

When I met Lucy’s doctors, I did my best to inspire them: “Let’s see what can be accomplished if we give her the best care possible and we invest unlimited resources to restore her to life.” And I promised that whatever we learned we would make available to everyone. 

Dr. Chris Kellner, her neurosurgeon, and Dr. David Putrino, Director of Rehabilitation Innovation for the Mount Sinai Health System have led Lucy’s care team since that day. Words cannot describe the remarkable and compassionate care that she has received beginning with the EMT team and then from nurses, doctors, therapists, and the army of people who have worked to save her and return her to life. To this day, we have a daily Zoom where we discuss her progress and make adjustments to her care.  While her care and oversight have been incredible, the learnings for the Mount Sinai team have also been elucidating and will assist in the care of many others.

Lucy began in a bad place. She was in a coma for several weeks and then awoke not being able to breathe on her own, unable to walk, see or speak. 

Over the last six months, she has recovered her cognition – she understands everything including her circumstance – is able to walk a hundred or more steps at a time with assistance, is making progress with sounds, vowels and consonants and the beginnings of speech, but she remains unable to see. 

Each day, she makes a little progress, and daily progress compounds.  Every day I tell her that she just needs to make a little progress and it won’t be long before she is back.

We remain optimistic that Lucy will return to normal function. It will likely take years, but I believe it is only a matter of time, hard work, and technological progress, along with some, and perhaps a lot, of divine intervention.  

Many people have been praying for Lucy and we are incredibly grateful for the prayers and remarkable support she has received. Lucy’s friends have been with her every day since the beginning, and their presence and friendship have saved her life and helped to rebuild and maintain her spirit.  And on a very positive note, Lucy’s challenge has brought together our entire modern family who have all been incredibly devoted to her care and recovery.

Lucy's vision and other faculties may require some form of brain computer interface, work that is underway at Neuralink, Precision Neuroscience, Science, Synchron, Nudge, and other companies in the space. 

If you are going to have a devastating brain injury, now is the best time in history for that to happen. We are living in a world when you can be confident that the blind will soon see again.  We are going to do everything we can to help make that happen, including by assisting existing companies in the space.

With respect to our promise to make Lucy’s care available to others, we have made good progress. In May, a real estate colleague made me aware of a 93% vacant, brand new, 400,000 square foot Class A+ purpose-built biotech facility on  West End Avenue between 65th and 66th Streets that missed the market and was available for sale. The Pershing Square Foundation acquired the building 60 days later. 

We also put under contract an adjoining 130,000 square foot building at 320 West 66th Street that is currently being used by Saturday Night Live for studio space. The building has 35-foot ceilings with massive column-free spaces that can be converted into superb rehabilitation facilities.  We will close on the SNL building in December. 

We are also acquiring an adjoining vacant lot with additional air rights.  With just the existing zoning rights, we can add a 150,000 square feet for a total of 680,000 square feet, a lab footprint larger than Rockefeller University, and that’s without including the potential for an upzoning that would allow for substantially more buildable area on the site’s 3.4 acres with spectacular views of the Hudson.

Our goal is to build the world’s greatest brain research, rehabilitation, recovery, human optimization, and longevity institute.  We have named it The Ackman Oxman Institute or the AOI for lack of a better name, but also to reinforce the point that Neri and I and our family are all-in on the mission. 

The AOI will be patient-centric. It will not be an academic research institute that produces lots of papers, a Nobel Prize winner or two, but little if any results for patients. We will be laser-focused on cures, treatments, devices, rehabilitation and exercise equipment, and targeted and basic research with a goal of massively accelerating the time from idea to innovation to production to helping a patient. 

While the AOI will be a non-profit, it will have highly commercial instincts. The AOI will have its own venture funding and will work to develop innovations to create companies that we will seed, assist, and spinout to ensure technologies, treatments, techniques, and drugs get to patients as promptly as possible. 

On one 3.4 acre campus in what is still the greatest city in the world, we will do neurosurgery, neuroscience, rehabilitation, nutrition, BCI and device development, human trials, hyperbaric oxygen treatments, and life extension programs, and we will mandate and incentivize collaboration among the teams with no silos, politics, bureaucracy, or any other constraint that is inconsistent with the mission.  

Mount Sinai will be an important partner and deservedly so, but it won’t be our only hospital or medical school partner as we don’t believe any institution has a monopoly on the best ideas or the best talent.  We don’t believe in exclusive relationships because that is not in the best interest of patients.

Five years ago, we considered launching a brain institute inspired by Neri’s mom who sadly died from Alzheimer’s. We couldn’t make the math work as the real estate was too expensive and we believed it would be too difficult to recruit the best talent from universities to our effort.  

Since then, the real estate became available at a 70% discount, universities became a much less attractive place to work due to politics outweighing meritocracy, protests that disrupt learning, the curse of antisemitism, and a decline in funding. Fortunately, during the same time, I made sufficient personal economic progress to make the AOI possible.  

The advance of AI in the last few years will also enable us to greatly accelerate our mission. AI still has a lot to learn about human intelligence and the brain, and the AOI should be at the forefront of the interplay between the brain and AI.

Today, I am making a public filing disclosing a gift from Neri and me of ~$400 million or 10,000,000 shares of Pershing Square Inc. (PS) to the AOI.  It is very early days for Pershing Square so these shares are intended to anchor the long-term work of the AOI as the shares compound over time while generating what we expect will be a growing stream of quarterly dividends to fund the Institute.  

We will also be announcing an additional gift of similar and potentially greater size which won’t be in the form of Pershing Square stock to provide the AOI with the short- and intermediate-term runway necessary to enable it to achieve its goal of becoming a self-sustaining institute, which reinvests all of its revenues, royalties, and the economic rewards of company formation to advance the fields of brain health and human longevity.  

Neri and I have chosen to anchor the funding of the AOI to maintain vision alignment and limit the need for the organization to focus on fundraising. We expect the AOI to be the best-resourced brain, rehab, recovery, and longevity institute in the world.

We are grateful to have been able to form a board which includes Dean Kamen (our generation’s Thomas Edison), George Yancopoulus (CEO of Regeneron), James Rothman (Nobel Laureate), Bernardo Sabatini (neuroscientist), Chris Kellner (neurosurgeon), Olivia Flatto (CEO Pershing Square Foundation), Neri Oxman, and myself.

We have recently identified a CEO who we expect to announce by October along with other key hires, and are beginning searches for a Chief Scientific Officer, a Chief AI/Technology Officer, a Chief Operating Officer, a Chief Financial Officer, and other key leadership roles.

If you find what we are building compelling and want to be part of the leadership team that creates and builds the AOI from a standing start, please send an email to: search@aoiinst.org with a short note as to why you believe you can help.  Please include your best three ideas for the AOI along with a summary of your background and your most important accomplishments.  

We promise strict confidentiality to those expressing interest in working with us.

We have learned from Lucy that the brain can recover from even catastrophic injury. There is so much more work to be done as the mind is a terrible thing to waste.

For details from my Pershing Square SEC filing see:

https://t.co/gZKafCw6Ia
