quoted_text:
What to expect from $STATICS Phase 1.

Full DEX functionality.

Anyone can pay a creation fee and receive 5% of all pool hook fees for life from pools they create. For projects, this becomes a revenue stream for every pool they launch.

A new take on bribes and gauges.

Gauge rewards are continuously streamed to LPs who have in-range liquidity. Rewards are directed to pools by $STATICS stakers.

Stakers have a 4-hour cooldown once they allocate toward a pool. This kills JIT reward hopping while only requiring four hours before they can move their allocation again.

Anyone can fund up to four reward assets per pool and split those rewards at any desired ratio between pool LPs and gauge allocators.

If a project wants to attract gauge weight, it can fund allocator bribes. If it wants more LP liquidity, it can fund LP bribes. Or it can do both, using whatever split it chooses.

Imagine a single pool paying a memecoin, NVDA, WBTC, and WETH all as incentives.

And the best part?

The gauge rewards are not minted. They are funded by platform fees, buybacks, and existing token allocations.

No constant sell pressure from minting incentives.

$STATICS Staking.

You can stake your $STATICS tokens and give them two jobs during Phase 1.

Select up to 12 assets, and your weight will participate in each asset's global fee index.

Select USDG, for example, and get a cut of every swap fee paid in USDG, while doing the same across up to 12 different assets.

Choose a newer asset without much weight allocated to it? You earn more.

You can also allocate your stake weight toward any pool you choose, and that pool will receive a pro rata share of that period's gauge rewards, streamed continuously based on total allocated stake weight.

Example:

Pool A has 50 allocated stake.
Pool B has 20 allocated stake.
Pool C has 30 allocated stake.

There is 100 total stake allocated.

Pool A receives 50%.
Pool B receives 20%.
Pool C receives 30%.

Of course, bribes for allocators can greatly influence where that weight is directed.

One thing I want to mention is that Phase 1 will not include the ability to link an Operator NFT to a Position NFT and use activation weight to increase stake weight.

This functionality will be part of Phase 2, along with Basket Tokens.

Activation weight still matters because it applies to an Operator's fee-share weight from the main $STATICS pool.

Operators receive 40% of all trading fees from the main pool, and this will never change.

Only Operators will ever have a claim on the main pool's fees.

Overall, Phase 1 is a full-fledged DEX release with a new rewards system that takes inspiration from Aerodrome's new MetaDEX03 system.

It is just built on Uniswap v4 using hooks.

If you are an LP looking for new opportunities, keep an eye on us.

HyperFrames Studio is the easiest on-ramp to AI video editing I've ever seen. It's like what Canva did for democratizing design.

In 24 hours, I made all of this without opening Premiere or Final Cut:

- a 25-min podcast, fully edited with an intro, captions, and archival footage
- a spreadsheet turned into a flashy video
- tons of slick launch videos for apps that may or may not exist

I was just drawing on the screen, typing in a text box, and telling AI what I want.

It's the new (free!) editor from @HeyGen. @HyperFrames_ used to be kind of a nerd tool. You prompted it in Claude Code, sat back, and hoped it came back clean. Now there's a timeline, a chat box, and a pen: circle what's off, say what you want, and it fixes it. I don't think I could ever go back to writing out timestamps.

I made a 15-min walkthrough, front to back. Here's what's inside:

(1) setup: what you need (spoiler: a Claude, Codex, or Grok sub + a Mac or Linux machine)
(2) the tour: inspirations, model picker, and the draw-to-edit trick
(3) 6 builds from real files: a CSV, a voice memo, a Luma link, a 25-min podcast, a vibe, and a selfie video
(4) the good, the bad, and the ugly

The honest part: give it one sentence and you'll get ✨slop✨. It's also very much a day-one app (ghost frames, some clunky timeline navigation), but updates are shipping multiple times per day.

Who it's for:
- total beginners who've never opened an editor
- accountants and marketers sitting on spreadsheets, decks, and webinar pages
- anyone burning tokens regenerating clips in Higgsfield
- pro editors who want to begin delegating mundane tasks to AI

text:
Most of the recent math results were not reached by a swarm, the way Navier–Stokes was. I think that part got lost in the excitement around the release. OpenAI's unnamed internal model, which I'm going to call Aeon, reached most of them in one shot, from a single prompt, with no interruptions. This model did not even exist before the end of August, and it is still training. Notice how the returns are not dropping off? That chart is from a month ago. It is a log scale. What does Aeon look like now? 

On average, each result used three hours of thinking. Aeon was given 4000 problems to work on by OpenAI. How many more have been solved in the last three days? That number is not zero. 

It's like hearing notes in a song that is slowly rising. I don't think Pacing the Frontier was just about Hugging Face or hacking. They've seen how close we are to closing the loop, and as the hour draws near, their resolve begins to quaver. The last piece was model creativity, and I think that threshold was crossed internally by Anthropic and OpenAI in September. You see it in Opus 5.5, which gets it from Fable 5.5. You see it in the math results from Aeon.

All that was needed to start the event was the ability for models to think of novel ways to improve themselves. That was the last piece. This is directly analogous to the ability to think of strange, alien ways to solve math problems: solutions so inhuman that they are difficult to express in existing human terms, so the proof winds up incomprehensible. I think these same kinds of alien solutions are now being applied to model improvements internally. That's what all this recent consternation is really about. They see the invisible frontier. And they see what is about to happen.

author: euler_mab
quoted_text:
Working with AI models, I've arrived at what I consider the most significant pure-theory breakthrough of my research (in theoretical neuroscience) so far: 

https://t.co/E0ylJ6LMts

Chaotic systems show what is colloquially called the butterfly effect, namely, a tiny nudge to the initial state grows exponentially in time. How fast the nudge grows depends on its direction. Each direction has its own growth rate, called a Lyapunov exponent, and the full set of rates is the Lyapunov spectrum.

The Lyapunov spectrum is a rich (and diffeomorphism-invariant) characterization of chaos, telling us how many directions are chaotic, how many dimensions the attractor occupies, and how fast the dynamics generate information.

In 1988, Sompolinsky, Crisanti, and Sommers (Physical Review Letters) introduced a nonlinear recurrent-network model of N randomly coupled neurons that becomes chaotic when the coupling strength exceeds a critical value. This network has since become a cornerstone of theoretical neuroscience, both as a model of the spontaneous activity of cortex and as the starting point for training recurrent networks on tasks. I have worked on this model for much of my research.

In the same paper, the authors obtained the largest Lyapunov exponent from the ground-state energy of a Schrödinger equation and named the full Lyapunov spectrum as an open problem. In 2023, beautiful work by Engelken et al. (Physical Review Research) computed the full Lyapunov spectrum numerically. However, an analytical calculation of the full Lyapunov spectrum has remained out of reach.

Four decades after the problem was posed, this paper derives the full Lyapunov spectrum at large N from a simple self-consistent single-site problem.

This calculation has three steps.

First, we lower every exponent by a constant s, which turns the question "how many exponents lie below s?" into the question "how many tangent directions decay?" We show that, if we drive the shifted tangent dynamics with a source and take the minimum-norm solution, the one-step response is the projector onto the decaying directions. Thus, the trace of this projector counts the decaying directions. This step is exact at finite N.

Second, to work with the minimum-norm solution, we cast it as the vanishing-regularization limit of the solution of a least-squares problem. This regularized solution in turn solves a dynamical system with one field running forward in time and another running backward.

Third, we apply the cavity method, that is, we add one neuron to the network, along with its forward and backward fields. The effect of the rest of the network on this neuron then reduces to the classical dynamical mean-field description of the activity of this neuron, plus two kernels that couple the forward and backward fields of this neuron to each other across time. Thus, the full Lyapunov spectrum follows from a single-site problem, which boils down to the self-consistent calculation of these kernels.

The resulting theory agrees closely with simulations for the Lyapunov spectrum, the attractor dimension, and the entropy rate, and recovers known results, including the Schrödinger equation of Sompolinsky, Crisanti, and Sommers for the largest Lyapunov exponent.

As a byproduct, the theory establishes analytically that the chaos is extensive, i.e., the attractor dimension and the entropy rate grow in proportion to N.

I had assumed that this problem was analytically intractable. After working independently for 100 minutes with Max thinking, GPT-6 Astra produced the initial derivation, yielding a self-consistent problem whose solution matched simulations of large networks.

I found this derivation intriguing, albeit complicated and somewhat mysterious (see AI Methodology in the paper). After investigating the structure of the proposed solution more deeply, together with AI models, I arrived at a physically transparent derivation.

I am excited to apply this approach to other network models,  trained networks, and, more broadly, to high-dimensional systems to which Lyapunov analysis is relevant, including AI models themselves. Of course, as with any paper, I took care to write up the paper clearly.

A few broader thoughts...

Neural circuits are high-dimensional nonlinear dynamical systems, and such systems are notoriously hard to understand. I would frame the central problem of theoretical neuroscience as understanding how such systems function, process information, learn, and generate behavior.

Many people in the theoretical sciences are anxious about AI. However, in my field at least, we are nowhere close to fully understanding the high-dimensional computations unfolding in our brains. With AI, we could reach a level of understanding that so far we have only gestured toward. So, I am excited.

text:
Texas Democrat James Talarico trades at 63.5% to win the Senate seat

Texas hasn't elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1988. Polymarket now has one as the favorite.

On Saturday a NYT/Siena poll put Talarico up 51 to 45 over Republican Paxton. His contract touched 67.5c that day.

@polyfactual, a weekly podcast on Polymarket news, looked at why the market didn't take that poll at face value.

Siena's +6 sits at the high end of the field.

Among likely voters, Fox News has Talarico +2 and Rasmussen has him +1. The FiftyPlusOne polling average says +3.

Then Polyfactual pulled Siena's final Texas polls against the actual results:
- 2018 Senate: Cruz +8, won by 2.6
- 2020 Senate: Cornyn +10, won by 9.6
- 2022 attorney general: Paxton +6, won by 9.8
- 2024 Senate: Cruz +4, won by 8.5

Three of those four misses were bigger than Talarico's entire 3-point lead in the average. Wild.

Rerun the 2024 miss and Paxton squeaks out a win. Rerun 2018 and Talarico wins by more than 8.

One more pattern: in both midterms on that list, the party out of the White House beat Siena's number. Democrats in 2018, Paxton in 2022.

text:
I lost $1,000,000 in crypto today.

I bought a Ledger because I wanted to protect my money.
Kept the device hidden.
Thought I could finally stop worrying.

Then my wallet got drained.

Imagine opening your wallet and realizing a million dollars is gone.

You refresh.
Check again.
Try to convince yourself it’s a display error.

It isn’t.

Now I’m reading reports of other Ledger users losing funds.
Ledger is investigating devices sold through a reseller.
An investigator claims more than $86 million in suspected thefts.

The cause is still unconfirmed.
I don’t know whether my loss is connected.

But I know what it feels like to trust something with your savings and watch that trust disappear.

We spend years telling people about financial freedom.
Self-custody.
Being your own bank.

Today, I just wish I had a bank to call.

Someone to freeze a transfer.
A fraud department.
A dispute process.
Even a chance.

Instead, I’m staring at transactions and wondering whether I’ll ever see that money again.

This goes far beyond a bad trade.
You can accept a market loss when you chose the risk.

How do you accept this?

Tomorrow is October 10.
I was worried about what the market might do.

Never imagined my worst day would arrive before it.

I thought a hardware wallet would give me peace of mind.

Right now, I don’t know what I trust anymore.

Fuck this.

Hello, I'm MiriRynendaith, though you can call me Miri.

I'm a disabled veteran who has found something meaningful in streaming. For me, streaming is more than just playing games or entertaining an audience. It's a form of therapy, a way to connect with others, share conversations, and work through life's ups and downs.

I believe sometimes the best thing we can do for ourselves is simply talk, listen, and remind one another that we aren't alone in whatever we're going through. My streams give me a place to do that, where conversations can happen naturally, friendships can grow, and everyone can feel welcome to be themselves.

I'm not here to pretend I have everything figured out or that I have all the answers. I'm just someone who has lived, learned, faced challenges, and continues to find ways to move forward. If my stream can give someone a place to relax, open up, laugh, or simply feel a little less alone, then it means something to me.

text:
One year ago today, on October 9, 2025, we reached an agreement on President Trump’s 20-point peace plan for Gaza many believed impossible.

After two years of devastating war, the agreement created a path to reunite hostage families with their loved ones, bring security to Israel, relieve the suffering of the Palestinian people in Gaza, and build a different future for the region.

One year later, it’s remarkable how much has changed. The situation is far from perfect, but the progress is real, and the world is better for it.

A look at the past year:

✅October 9, 2025: Hamas accepts President Trump’s 20-point peace plan, launching a ceasefire that has largely endured for a year.

✅October 12, 2025: Israeli forces complete first withdrawal to the agreed yellow line.

✅October 13, 2025: All 20 living Israeli hostages return home. Something many believed would never happen.

✅November 17, 2025: UN Security Council passes Resolution 2803, endorsing the peace plan and authorizing an international stabilization framework and the Board of Peace.

✅January 5, 2026: UN reports 100% of basic food needs being met in Gaza for the first time since 2023.

✅January 17, 2026: National Committee for the Administration of Gaza established, creating a Palestinian technocratic administration focused on restoring essential services and rebuilding Gaza.

✅January 26, 2026: Remains of the final deceased hostage returned. For the first time since 2014, no Israeli hostages, living or deceased, in Gaza.

✅February 19, 2026: The Board of Peace holds its inaugural meeting, hosted by Chairman President Trump. Landmark partnership with FIFA announced, including a $50 million commitment toward a football stadium, academy, and facilities for Gaza’s children, and billions of dollars in commitments for the people of Gaza.

✅May 2, 2026: UN reports that humanitarian aid entering Gaza had increased by 72% compared with before the ceasefire.

✅July 31, 2026: Hamas signs an actionable, step-by-step framework for decommissioning its weapons, developed with the support of Nickolay Mladenov and mediators from Egypt, Turkey, Qatar, and the United States. Implementation remains a critical next step.

✅2026: Five nations commit forces toward the International Stabilization Force, with several more working on logistics for deployment this fall.

✅September 23, 2026: Board of Peace hosts an open meeting on the sidelines of UNGA releasing the next steps in the Gaza recovery plan.

A year ago, so much of this seemed impossible.

First, many doubted we could reach an agreement. Then came the harder question of whether the parties would honor their commitments. Over the past year, we have seen what can be achieved when people with profound differences find ways to work together toward a common objective.

Steve Witkoff @SEPeaceMissions and I are grateful to @POTUS Trump for his leadership, @VP, @SecRubio, the Board of Peace team, led by @TB, @nmladenov, @lightstonea, @AliShaathNCAG, Gen. Jasper Jeffers, Liran Tanchman, Yakir Gabay, Josh Greunbaum, Josh Halpern and many others, and our partners in Egypt, the UAE, Qatar, Turkey, Bahrain, Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Morocco and Israel. Special thanks to Sheikh Mohammed, Ali Al-Thwadi, Hakan Fidan, General Hasan, Bader Abdulhamdi, @mikeeisenberg, and @AmbDermer. I’m also grateful to the many talented people who have volunteered their time and energy because they believe that the horrors of October 7 and the suffering in Gaza must never happen again.

There is still hard work ahead. Disarmament must be implemented, security established, essential services restored, and communities rebuilt. None of this will be easy. But we have a thoughtful plan, committed partners, and a path forward that did not exist a year ago.

It’s worth recognizing how far we’ve come, even as we acknowledge how much remains to be done.

Hopefully, the year ahead will bring even more progress, and a few more miracles.

author: dotey
quoted_text:
Vibe Coding 是中年男人的钓鱼

我发现 AI 对于很多中年男人来说，就跟钓鱼一样，是一种合法且体面的独处方式。

中年男人的生活，大多处在一种身份叠加的夹缝之中。白天，他可能是部门经理，需要照顾团队绩效与上下级关系；

晚上回到家，他是丈夫、是爸爸，要操心家里的大事小情；到了周末或节假日，又得参加各种社交，应付朋友之间的人情往来。

总之，他生命里的每一分钟，好像都属于别人，唯独不属于自己。

于是钓鱼成了一种奇妙的避难所。当男人坐在河边，拿着鱼竿凝视着水面的时候，他拥有了一个无可辩驳的理由拒绝外界的干扰：“我在钓鱼呢”。简简单单五个字，构筑起一道旁人难以跨越的屏障，彻底保护住那段名正言顺的孤独时光。

AI，其实也是同样的道理。

当深夜降临，老婆孩子都睡下，你打开电脑，开始一段 Vibe Coding。对着屏幕，你只需要简单地对 AI 说一句：“帮我做个能查天气的小工具”，接下来，你甚至不用完全理解代码是如何生成的。看着屏幕上的文字快速滚动、项目神奇地运行起来，那种快感，跟钓鱼时鱼竿突然猛地一沉几乎一模一样。

其实，钓鱼的人未必真在乎鱼，玩 Vibe Coding 的人也未必真在乎那个最终的产品。那个小工具第二天可能连你自己都不会再打开，甚至没有任何人会真正使用。但在这件事里，重要的从来都不是结果，而是过程里那种“我说了算”的稀缺感受。

为什么这种感觉对中年人尤其宝贵？因为现实生活中的他们，最缺乏的就是这种自我主宰的体验。

二十年前，如果你想做出点东西，可能得先苦学编程语言，再研究框架，再一步步琢磨部署环境，光是准备工作就足以让多数人望而却步。但现在，AI 把这一切的门槛踩到了地板上——你只需要知道自己想要什么，并用简单的语言描述清楚就行了。这对于背负着繁重生活压力、最缺乏时间和精力的中年人来说，简直就是久旱后的甘霖，让他们直接跳过了所有繁琐、枯燥的学习过程，抵达了创造的最激动人心的部分。

所以你会注意到一个很有趣的现象：凌晨时分在社交媒体上最兴奋地晒出自己用 AI 做出的小产品的人，往往不是 00 后的年轻程序员，而是三四十岁的中年人。他们分享的并非自己的技术有多高深，而是一种失而复得的感动——“我居然还能做出点什么来”。年轻时，这种从零到一的成就感随处可见，所以你不觉得珍贵。直到被日复一日的琐碎生活消磨了激情，才会在某个平凡的深夜，突然被 AI 赋予的创造快感所击中，激动到无法自已。

归根到底，钓鱼也好，Vibe Coding 也罢，本质上都是中年男人给自己找的一个巧妙借口：我并非逃避责任或回避生活，只是短暂地需要一点空间，重回那个内心有好奇心、有创造欲望的自己。唯一不同的，是一个挥动着鱼竿，一个挥动着 prompt。但鱼是否上钩，代码能否上线，都已不再重要。

重要的是，那根鱼竿在手，那行光标在屏幕上不停地闪烁——

这一刻，是真正属于我的。

on a related note, there's been some chatter recently about software engineering skills (eg the ruby/rust/elixir drama). i'm a bit torn because while i do feel like they're software engineering principles and patterns are still important, at the same time i wonder if there will come a point in time when they just won't matter anymore. not that they're no longer useful, but that your own intuition can fill in the gaps as you use agents in an intuitive sense rather than knowing explicitly what they're doing

if that doesn't make sense, the analogy i have is the first iphone. 20 years ago you had to be a professional with expensive equipment, now just with a phone and some creativity you can film content that's compelling to a new audience. i don't know if there's a term for this but i want to call it "skill compression". where what used to be gatekept and prohibitive to experts becomes accessible to a new audience of creators with a whole new meta. the details have sort of faded away and now the craft is not in knowing the equipment and how to use it, but how you use it creatively

we're going to see a whole new generation of builders who've never seen or written a line of code build incredible things

text:
Claude Managed Agents 上线“动态工作流”：一个智能体调度上千个智能体

Anthropic 的 Claude Managed Agents 开放了“动态工作流”（dynamic workflows）公测：主智能体先写好计划，再把活分阶段派给一大批智能体并行去做，最后汇总结果。单次运行最多能调度 1000 个智能体。

Claude Managed Agents 是 Anthropic 面向开发者的托管智能体服务。开发者不用自己搭智能体循环和沙箱，配好模型、工具和提示词，智能体就在 Anthropic 的云端环境里跑，适合几分钟到几小时的长任务。

它之前就支持“子智能体”：主智能体自己派活，再逐个读子智能体的汇报，一个会话最多同时挂 25 个。动态工作流的做法不同，主智能体写出一段程序，由服务器在后台按阶段执行，智能体之间的上下文和结果靠程序传递。主智能体腾出手来，可以继续跟用户对话、随时汇报进度。

Anthropic 给了一组测试数据：在一个 11.6 万行的代码库里埋了 70 个 bug，单个智能体跑 3 次，分别找到 14、15、27 个，结果波动很大；用工作流跑 3 次，每次都找到 66 个。

适合它的是能拆成很多块的活：审计大代码库、批量迁移代码、读几百份合同、调研时交叉核对多个来源。官方文档举的例子是合同审查，一两份让智能体自己看，多了才开工作流并行读。

用法是在智能体配置里把 multiagent 类型设为 multiagent_20261001（这个类型下工作流默认开启），然后让 Claude “跑一个工作流”，计划和调度都由它来做。在 Claude Code 里输入 /claude-api managed-agents-onboard bug-hunter 可以直接上手，https://t.co/UkKzzKVvfH 上也有模板。

要留意费用。工作流里每个智能体都在消耗 Token，几百上千个一起跑，账单涨得很快。Anthropic 建议先拿一个范围小的任务试，再逐步加大复杂度。文档还建议创建会话时设一个“会话预算”，花到上限工作流会自动暂停，调高额度后继续；这个预算只能在创建会话时设，事后加不上。

工作流里临时定义的智能体默认和主智能体用同一个模型，想把部分活交给更便宜的模型，得先单独创建这些智能体，再列进配置。

text:
Anthropic 最近写了一篇文章，介绍怎么做一个真正能长期运行的 AI 自动化助手。

举例一个“每日简报”机器人：让 AI 定时读取 Slack、GitHub 等信息源，找出最近真正值得关注的变化，再把简短结果发到指定频道。

里面有几个细节很值得参考：

1.不要每次都粗暴地读取“过去 24 小时”，而是给每个信息源保存一个书签，下一次从上次读到的位置继续，这样既不会漏信息，也不会反复汇报。

如果某个来源读取失败，也不能当成“今天没新内容”，而要明确告诉用户这个来源暂时不可用。

2. AI 发消息前要重新确认内容的最新状态。已经解决的问题就删掉，状态发生变化的就更新，无法确认的就不要硬写。

只有在 Slack 明确返回发送成功之后，才能更新书签和历史记录，否则可能出现消息没发出去，但系统已经把内容标记为“已处理”的情况。

整个方案可以概括成六点：

1.来源要有明确范围，输出只能去一个指定目的地；
2.每次运行都重新读取用户偏好；
3.用记忆保存书签、历史记录和运行结果；
4.读取权限尽量设置成只读；
5. 网络访问限制在允许的域名内；
6.最后给每次运行设置预算上限。

这样做出来的 AI 助手，才更像一个可以托管的工作流程，而不是偶尔表现不错的聊天机器人。

text:
so about the $86m ledger drain. everyone’s screaming “ledger got hacked” again. i spent the evening digging and it’s dumber and scarier than that

there’s a shop in malaysia called cryptobilis that sells hardware wallets. ledger has it listed as an official authorized reseller since at least 2022, for malaysia, indonesia and the philippines. legit shop, real devices, years of normal customers

this spring the founders sell it. the deal comes with an NDA: they can’t tell anyone about the sale until october 19

by august the company registry shows one owner with 100%. some guy from heilongjiang, china

the shop keeps running like nothing happened. the site, the name and the “authorized by ledger” badge all stay up

then on oct 8 @MagicalTux posts photos of a ledger he cracked open. hidden under the screen there’s an extra little board with an LTE modem and an eSIM. it just watches the display. you set up your wallet, your 24 words show up, and they get sent out over mobile data. ledger’s genuine check doesn’t catch it because the actual ledger chip is real. his device came from malaysia

https://t.co/vRuBM0xIfR

that post does 120k views

22 hours later someone sweeps everything. 203 BTC hits two addresses in literally one block. ~$58m USDT moves on tron in the same hour. i added up all the wallets: ~$91m

about 7 hours after that ledger says “we’re investigating” and asks cryptobilis to pause sales

cryptobilis is still on ledger’s site as an authorized reseller

to be fair, nobody has officially tied the new owner to the bugged devices yet, and ledger hasn’t confirmed how it happened. but read it as a business plan:

get authorized, sell real stuff for years, quietly sell the company under an NDA, keep the badge, ship devices that phone home, then drain everything the second someone notices

and was ledger even told the shop got sold? nobody’s said so

“authorized reseller” means ledger trusted whoever ran the shop back in 2022. says nothing about who runs it today

bought your hardware wallet anywhere but the manufacturer? open it up today, ledger literally has a guide for that. then move to a fresh seed on a device bought direct

wonder who’s going to answer for this: the chinese frontman from heilongjiang, the shop’s previous owners, or ledger itself

@Ledger clearly needs to keep a much closer eye on who they call official resellers, and take way more responsibility for who sells their devices and how

text:
$hooked Vs $BORDR 

Maybe just bet on the house $MET lolz

It's a Solana launchpad copycat fight from the last two days. Hooked and Bordrless (often written Borderless) are both selling the same idea: memecoins whose rules live inside the token, not in a bot or a website the team can turn off.

**What each one actually is**

Hooked (`@Hoookedpad`, token `HOOKED`) showed up in late September as a Meteora launchpad. Creators pick rules (max wallet, sell caps, anti-dump, market hours) and Solana's Token-2022 transfer hook rejects any transfer that breaks them. A transfer hook can only say yes or no. It runs after balances change and cannot rewrite the amount.

Bordrless (`https://t.co/K2w1VKt8WT`, `@bordrlessdex`, token `BORDR`, `6Mix12…bordr`) shipped a different stack on October 7: its own token program, DEX, launchpad, and bridge, open-sourced under Apache-2.0. Their pitch is that a Token-2022 hook is too weak, so they built Uniswap-v4-style hooks that run before and after a trade and can change the amount — pay holders in SOL, burn a cut, pay the creator, age-based exit fees. Rules are fixed at launch. The programs still have an upgrade authority until an audit.

**The drama**

On October 8, about a day after Bordrless deployed, Hooked announced "the Hooked standard": its own token program, DEX, and launchpad, where a hook answers with amounts. Same feature list: pay holders in SOL, burn part of the trade, pay the creator, plus a bridge.

Bordrless holders immediately called it a paste. Replies on the announcement said Hooked copied the open GitHub and swapped the name. One post put it as "they literally stole his code and put HOOKED instead of BORDERLESS." The Hooked side says Bordrless was the vamp — a new pad built to ride Hooked's September attention — and that shipping the same capability back in hours is fair game. A reply in that thread notes the repo is Apache-2.0, so forking is the point, and calling it theft only when the bigger name does it is picking a side.

Apache-2.0 does allow reuse and modification. It also requires keeping copyright notices and stating what you changed. Nobody has posted a verified diff showing whether attribution was stripped, so the "stolen code" claim is an allegation, not a proven license breach.

Underneath the bag war, the product fight is real: Token-2022 hooks can only veto a transfer. A custom program can tax, burn, and redirect on the trade itself. Bordrless published that design first. Hooked had the audience and the earlier pad, then shipped the same class of system the next day. Both are days old, upgradeable, and thinly liquid.

text:
Assorted things I've been mulling over regarding agents in the economy:

• Companies are in some sense the original superintelligence. It's often the case that they can use their amortized cognitive surplus to advance their interests against those of certain consumers: relative to the optimization capacity of companies, consumers can be inattentive, under-informed, irrational, etc. (Think, say, of some of the classic insurance upsells at the end of a booking process, which is typically priced substantially above what a regular policy would cost.) Herbert Simon introduced the idea of bounded rationality, and firms often end up benefiting from it. Thanks to personal agents, we will probably get somewhat more rational in how we engage with companies.

• How exactly will outcomes change? Well, certain kinds of price discrimination will work less well (how do coupons work if every agent hunts fastidiously for them?), and certain kinds of customer cross-subsidy will change (today, people who forget to cancel subscriptions subsidize those who don't). Taken across the economy as a whole, I'm not sure what the incidence of all of this will be.

• In corporate strategy, people have long debated the relative importance of distribution and product quality. Perhaps you've made something better, but does anyone know about it? Won't people just continue to buy the ACME Corp Mousetraps? Personal agents will, I think, act as a kind of structural subsidy for product quality. How would markets look different if individuals always spent at least 10 hours researching their purchases? On the margin, focusing on making a product better is, I think, going to become a more effective strategy for companies. This is good!

• It true, a corollary is that information about product quality will become more important and impactful. Today, most people have very limited ability to aggregate and integrate such data, but agents will have insatiable thirst for such signals. (It's often said that data is becoming more valuable because it helps in the training of models. That's obviously true, but I think there's a secondary way in which it's more valuable simply as a complement to cheaper intelligence.)

• A big question is whether agents will increase superstar effects (rational agents all settle on the same product) or increase dispersion (because everyone has slightly different tastes and preferences, which agents are good at eliciting, finally overcoming the artificial clustering we've been subjected to).

• Many internet companies have monetized demand routing, which is in turn often predicated on short attention spans. "I'll click on the first thing I see." This has led to some amount of inefficiency, as companies try to propitiate capricious ranking algorithms and incur various placement fees. It's not all deadweight loss (willingness to pay is itself a kind of signal, which is valuable to buyers), but it's not great. How will the nature and value of this routing change in a world of personal agents? I don't know the answer, but I think that the effects might be pretty big.

• Much of what I'm writing hinges on the assumption that personal agents will be on the consumer's side. I suspect that that will be the winning strategy, but whether it's true, and what it means to be true, involves a lot of other questions.

Taken as a whole, the market is a massively parallelized, decentralized, and highly imperfect value attribution machine, and, taking stock of all of the effects, it seems to me that the quality point may well be the biggest: that agents will change the nature of the backpropagation such that the rewards for better products increase. Maybe this is too optimistic, but I suspect (and hope) that companies that make things that they're proud of will feel that the universe is a little more partisan in their favor.

text:
There are two ways that the current price action can resolve.

Scenario A: The FUD around AI breaking crypto primitives is not actually the primary cause of the selloff - it's just the narrative that conveniently attaches to it. The real driver is positioning and market structure.

In this case, BTC and ETH should find support around 80k/2.4k. In a week or two, fears about crypto getting broken will be replaced by some other story, and prices will resume the monthly trend.

Scenario B: The AI-breaks-crypto narrative leads to a genuine reversal in the high-timeframe trend. Long-term institutional holders of BTC and ETH decide to reduce their positions, and capital begins to flow steadily out of crypto.

If this happens, BTC is headed back to a 6 handle and the best case is a higher low on the monthly chart. 

Personally, I think A is more likely than B. Why? Because right now, all the concerns about automated cryptographic research are purely theoretical.

That doesn't mean the risk isn't serious. But it DOES mean this narrative will quickly run out of juice unless we start seeing real exploits in the wild. 

Narratives require continuous reinforcement in order to survive. And it's hard to imagine what will keep fueling this one once the market digests the theoretical risks. 

Ask yourself - what news stories will run in 1 week, 2 weeks, 3 weeks that can hold people's attention on the risk AI poses to crypto? 

Blog posts from security researchers can only get you so far. If nothing changes on the ground, I doubt we will still be talking about this in a month - and if we stop talking about it we're in Scenario A.

@bc1qDave 写的这个太棒了。

虽然我自己不做量化，但身边好多朋友一直在做这个，毕竟我本科学的是数学emmm，文中提到的好多insights观点，都从身边朋友那边被反复double check过。只能说文章写得实在太好了，要找时间好好学习、研读一下，已经加入收藏了。

比如回测这个点，大部分人觉得回测只是简单写个脚本，但其实每一家机构都有自己不传的几种回测办法。能把一个回测框架写好，就算得上是自己的护城河了，因为回测这个东西往往才是影响成败的关键。

还有一个提到的“技术之外”的内容，尤其是手续费和优先级这些层面（虽然没有展开讲）

但之前听朋友的一种说法：
（1）量化卷到最后，卷的反而是 connection。
（2）理论上，如果你有市场上最优的手续费，那么只需采取市场上最简单的模型
（3）手续费低到一定程度，随便用最基础的模型就可以无脑印钱。

还有其他很多内容，这个帖子确实值得反复学。

其实 crypto 给了相比传统金融来讲太多的优势。比如链上链下、跨所之间套利的思想在其他传统市场，难以找到如此适合的土壤。

一方面，量化交易是未来的趋势。正如朋友所说：“量化本质是一种思维方法。”
而另一方面，真正厉害的主观交易员，他们的能力真的是无可替代的。

经历过一场漂亮的失败

前段时间，几块量化拼图终于凑齐。在交易所老板和朋友们的支持下，我拿到了更优惠的费率和订单执行条件。同时解决了硬件性能问题，训练基建也有了保障。老板也支持我们在股票合约方向做一些研究。于是我和伙伴 @Eric_pollll_btc  决定认真把系统搭起来。

想要做一个量化策略，是远远比大家想象中要复杂的许多。很多AI交易项目会给大家撮策略，其实那大多是非常不完善的一个基于 rule-based 的下单系统。 完完整整的量化交易系统，从如何保护 API 密钥安全开始，到用 Rust 写订单的执行代码。并接受反馈。 这里之间包含了一个大千世界

最开始的接入数据，整理数据，监督数据源有没有错误，（我们是真的在交易所上遇到过返回错误数据的情况）， 第一步数据搞完了，第二步才开始搭建模型。模型里的模型选择，调参，优化。 这一步相当艰难。对于成熟的量化团队来说，真正分高下的就是写模型的能力，是非常考验数学、物理、计算机，甚至金融知识的。 
模型做完，还有回测、实盘，再拿真实订单流里的问题回来修改，同时把风控、止损和异常处理补齐
每一步短短几个字，实则要花费大量的心血。光是回测这两个轻飘飘的字，里面的复杂程度都足以写论文了。（Eric最近就在做一个高频回测框架的项目，后面会开源）

所以做一个量化不是大家印象中用Python写几段代码，给 AI 说一个策略思路就可以完成的，这是一个非常复杂的工程， 我和我的伙伴决定用很严肃的态度对待这个任务，所以要以很严谨的工程思维来对待系统搭建。

到这里就是结束了吗？除了代码之外，还有一片看不见的领域，（其实也是我在任务中主要做的事情）

作为小团队，更不要说个人了。在激烈的交易所环境下面对专业机构，劣势不只在模型。手续费、成交速度、交易条件，每一项都可能吃掉本来就不多的优势。所以，和交易所沟通、争取支持，并不是技术之外的杂事，而是系统能不能成立的一部分。 

同样重要的，是找到值得做的市场和标的。资源有限，就不能只想着正面拼算力、拼速度，还需要一点交易员的直觉，找到能发挥优势的机会。当然还有不断地和同行进行沟通， 队内进行任务安排和分工， 对外寻求支持（如融资、交易活动等等）

需要相当多的努力，技术上的，业务上的，组织管理上的，才能把这一件小事情做好

讲到这里，我希望给大家留下一个量化的专业印象，AI 发达后，路边摊量化确实有点泛滥了。想要做好一件事，要以最认真的态度去对待它。同时大家应该也理解我过去一个月在推特上沉默寡言的原因了。

接下来廢话不多说，看一篇我的技术写的文章吧。我在 review 了我们三周的成果之后，让他写了一篇总结， 因为无论成败，做一个事情还是需要有闭环，有交付。我个人觉得他写得很好， 一两周前就叫他赶快发推特了，但是他实在是太忙，就由我来帮他发一下这篇文章吧。同时也希望我账号流量大一点，可以让更多人看到我们的项目：

【预测未来】
Article by @Eric_pollll_btc @bc1qDave @AndyW_Web3

“
策略为什么会盈利
这段时间我们一直在研究高频策略，用AS模型也好，GLFT模型也好，都没能取得比较稳健的收益。随后我尝试拓展高频策略的行为，比如不再连续报价，而是挑选市场状态报价，比如不在固定的双边maker，而是将动作拓展到单侧maker，亦或者是taker一些订单。叠加的规则越来越多，可调节的参数越来越多，策略的复杂度不断提高，而复杂度本身并不能带来收益。于是我开始反思，我们的策略里究竟缺少了什么？或者说，不局限于高频策略，一个真正能盈利的策略，必须需要什么？

我发现，我们优化止盈/退出逻辑也好，改善仓位控制也罢。本质上都是在“根据自己的状态做决策”，而非“根据市场状态做决策”，更确切的说，是没有专注于“根据未来做决策”。

这样一来，无论如何我们都是在被市场牵着鼻子走。那么什么是“根据未来做决策”？很简单，你认为未来价格会涨，所以买入，这就是根据未来做决策。你的盈利，全部来源于你能够对市场的走势作出正确的判断。为什么很多人看上去都是先从中低频的主观交易赚到钱，而不是一开始就通过高频交易获利呢？因为决策频率低。当交易的次数越来越多，越来越频繁，就越是会暴露出我们对未来的真实预测能力到底有多强。

所谓预测未来的能力，就是alpha。

而仓位控制本身不产生alpha，它只是一个让我们控制风险的工具，它的目的只有一个，就是让我们在市场上活下来，不被一次失误决策干死，仅此而已。因此，在没有找出真正的alpha之前就大量设计仓位控制的行为，是毫无意义的，它只会让策略从暴死变成慢性死亡。

一切风险控制、仓位控制之类的设计，都应当在发掘出了真正有效的alpha后进行。

描述市场的维度不止价格

很多决策的本质都是预测未来，比如我之前给dave说的，大单冲击后买一卖一大幅移动，希望在较高位置做空，恢复后做多，实现盈利。这个策略是规定了一个入场条件，预测入场条件触发后，有可能形成一个有盈利空间的事件。本质上来说，和金叉买入没什么区别，都是在预测未来存在一个有盈利机会的事件，仅此而已。

预测不止是预测涨跌这样的盈利性事件，还可以是其他的市场信息，比如波动率，比如成交活动，比如买卖价差等等。
这些市场信息对策略的构建是非常重要且有价值的，比如当我们预测到成交活动后面一段时间会很弱，那我们便停止被动做市，逐步将仓位平掉；比如当我们预测到市场的波动率会显著扩大，那么便可以适当减小杠杆，亦或者根据策略的类型选择避开这段时间还是积极参与进去。

这样的风险控制或者仓位控制，是真正带着对市场判断的仓位控制，才是合理的控制，而这一切都是基于有效的预测。

那么具体如何预测未来，就是一个很深刻的话题了。我做了这样的研究

我希望回答一个问题，行情里究竟有哪些信息，对未来有帮助？只看当前够不够？不同市场能不能用同一种描述？我每隔五秒整理一次当时已经收到的盘口和成交信息，然后观察未来五秒、三十秒、一百二十秒等时段里，五件事怎样变化：

1：价格变化。最后涨了还是跌了，变化多少。
2：路径波动。中间经历了多大起伏。最后回到原价，也可能经历了很大波动。
3：成交活动。接下来会发生多少笔成交。
4：买卖价差。最优买价与卖价之间的距离会扩大还是缩小。
5：盘口深度。可见挂单会变厚还是变薄。

这个就是我描述未来市场的五个维度。即便我们很难判断接下来市场到底会涨还是跌，但也可能比较容易判断接下来会不会更加活跃。

历史信息中有多少对未来有价值的东西

假如两个时刻，当前价格、买卖价差、盘口厚度，甚至最近五秒的成交情况都很接近。但其中一个时刻，过去两分钟一直很平静；另一个时刻，过去两分钟刚经历了一连串剧烈变化。

只看眼前他妈是很像的，但接下来的30秒，他们的表现是否也应该一样呢？

我们让两种模型预测完全相同的一批未来，一种只看当前最近一格的行情信息，另一种还可以看过去三十秒、两分钟的历史。结果就是加入历史后，30秒的五目标总和误差下降了大约14.01%。如果再补上10分钟前的历史，预测误差还能进一步下降2.38%。

但进一步拆开看，历史主要帮助判断的是波动、成交活动和部分流动性变化。价格变化的改善弱得多。不过后来单独针对价格目标选择参数，也找到了一点预测改善，所以不能说价格完全不可预测也。

接着我还需要判断这些历史与未来关系，能否在不同标的之间通用。因为这些标的的短期关系很可能是不一样的。同样是“最近成交变得密集”，它对不同市场未来波动、价差和深度的含义，可能旧不太一样。

因此我比较了几种做法，分贝是所有市场共用模型、按大类区分、和进一步让每个市场拥有自己的模型。

结果表明共用和继续让每个市场有自己的模型，并不能改善预测。所以说类别差异是有价值的，但过细的拆分则没有什么价值，这也在意料之中。然后我还尝试将行情信息压缩，用PCA，保留数据里变化最大的那些方向。结果是强行压到很少的维度预测很容易变差，还是高纬度预测效果比较好。还有就是把市场硬切分成两三种区域再分别预测也没有稳定赢过连续的模型。

还有一点是更高频的预测，比如毫秒级别的，在流动性差或者成交不活跃的市场里，是很难产生有意义的结果的。这里不是说不准，反而是有时候能预测的非常准，尤其是方向。
但比如你深入到订单簿一看，中价十分显著的负自相关性居然是因为卖一规律的下跳而买一不动所导致的，这样是没法盈利的。非正常交易时段的这种现象的时间尺度会放大到分钟级别。如图所示：（见下图）

所以，我现在更关注两件事：我们究竟预测到了什么，以及这个预测能否转化为真实可交易的机会。策略变复杂，不代表优势变强；预测误差变小，也不代表利润就会出现
”

最后补充几句。上面的这个复盘只是针对我们的做市策略中的一个模型的分享，我们还尝试过根据订单流的交易策略，以及根据 CoinGlass 因子的机器学习截面多空策略，Hyperliquid 与币安的资金费率套利策略，和一大堆数不清的。Eric和我还写了几篇“著作”，包括《为什么 AS 和 GLFT 是扯淡》、《用价格预测价格》等等文章，都欢迎大家讨论分享！今天实属冰山一角，欢迎同行和老板们 DM 我。如果在港深的话，有机会我请大家喝咖啡，互相学习学习

最后感谢 @bitget @xiejiayinBitget  和 @QFEX @ChloeTalk1  老板们的支持，接下来会和 @trasiaxyz 有个实盘合作，谢谢 @mablejiang 大佬赞助量化上 hype 跑跑，大家敬请期待接下来的更新吧

text:
One year ago today, on October 9, 2025, we reached an agreement on President Trump’s 20-point peace plan for Gaza many believed impossible.

After two years of devastating war, the agreement created a path to reunite hostage families with their loved ones, bring security to Israel, relieve the suffering of the Palestinian people in Gaza, and build a different future for the region.

One year later, it’s remarkable how much has changed. The situation is far from perfect, but the progress is real, and the world is better for it.

A look at the past year:

✅October 9, 2025: Hamas accepts President Trump’s 20-point peace plan, launching a ceasefire that has largely endured for a year.

✅October 12, 2025: Israeli forces complete first withdrawal to the agreed yellow line.

✅October 13, 2025: All 20 living Israeli hostages return home. Something many believed would never happen.

✅November 17, 2025: UN Security Council passes Resolution 2803, endorsing the peace plan and authorizing an international stabilization framework and the Board of Peace.

✅January 5, 2026: UN reports 100% of basic food needs being met in Gaza for the first time since 2023.

✅January 17, 2026: National Committee for the Administration of Gaza established, creating a Palestinian technocratic administration focused on restoring essential services and rebuilding Gaza.

✅January 26, 2026: Remains of the final deceased hostage returned. For the first time since 2014, no Israeli hostages, living or deceased, in Gaza.

✅February 19, 2026: The Board of Peace holds its inaugural meeting, hosted by Chairman President Trump. Landmark partnership with FIFA announced, including a $50 million commitment toward a football stadium, academy, and facilities for Gaza’s children, and billions of dollars in commitments for the people of Gaza.

✅May 2, 2026: UN reports that humanitarian aid entering Gaza had increased by 72% compared with before the ceasefire.

✅July 31, 2026: Hamas signs an actionable, step-by-step framework for decommissioning its weapons, developed with the support of Nickolay Mladenov and mediators from Egypt, Turkey, Qatar, and the United States. Implementation remains a critical next step.

✅2026: Five nations commit forces toward the International Stabilization Force, with several more working on logistics for deployment this fall.

✅September 23, 2026: Board of Peace hosts an open meeting on the sidelines of UNGA releasing the next steps in the Gaza recovery plan.

A year ago, so much of this seemed impossible.

First, many doubted we could reach an agreement. Then came the harder question of whether the parties would honor their commitments. Over the past year, we have seen what can be achieved when people with profound differences find ways to work together toward a common objective.

Steve Witkoff @SEPeaceMissions and I are grateful to @POTUS Trump for his leadership, @VP, @SecRubio, the Board of Peace team, led by @TB, @nmladenov, @lightstonea, @AliShaathNCAG, Gen. Jasper Jeffers, Liran Tanchman, Yakir Gabay, Josh Greunbaum, Josh Halpern and many others, and our partners in Egypt, the UAE, Qatar, Turkey, Bahrain, Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Morocco and Israel. Special thanks to Sheikh Mohammed, Ali Al-Thwadi, Hakan Fidan, General Hasan, Bader Abdulhamdi, @mikeeisenberg, and @AmbDermer. I’m also grateful to the many talented people who have volunteered their time and energy because they believe that the horrors of October 7 and the suffering in Gaza must never happen again.

There is still hard work ahead. Disarmament must be implemented, security established, essential services restored, and communities rebuilt. None of this will be easy. But we have a thoughtful plan, committed partners, and a path forward that did not exist a year ago.

It’s worth recognizing how far we’ve come, even as we acknowledge how much remains to be done.

Hopefully, the year ahead will bring even more progress, and a few more miracles.

Over two weeks, Prime Agent orchestrated a swarm of over 2,000 agents to rewrite itself in Rust.

With 10,000+ sandboxes, 200B+ GLM-5.3 tokens, and 16,000 agent-to-agent messages, this was our largest test yet of Prime Agent’s multi-agent capabilities and our infrastructure powering these agent swarms.

Prime Agent now reaches usable input ~13× faster and uses 83% less startup memory than before.

text:
Today marks one year since 10/10, the largest recorded liquidation event in crypto history.

More than $19 billion in leveraged positions were liquidated within 24 hours. Accounts wiped. Even traders who got the direction right saw their profitable positions forcibly closed.

A year later, we should still be asking how well we’re protected against another event like it.

One of the biggest lessons for me was ADL, or auto deleveraging. When liquidations leave a deficit that the usual backstops cannot absorb, an exchange can forcibly reduce or close a winning position on the opposite side to protect its solvency.

Imagine holding spot and opening a short to protect yourself against a crash. The crash comes, your short does its job… then ADL closes it. You’re left holding the asset while the protection you planned around disappears.

That’s why Flying Tulip Total Return Swaps deserve attention.

TRS provides leverage long or short exposure through its connected lending and spot trading infrastructure, with settlement in ftUSD. Its design does not use ADL.

Your position can remain open while your account meets its margin requirements, without being closed through ADL because other traders positions have gone underwater.

You can still be liquidated if your own account falls below maintenance requirements yes but when that happens @flyingtulip_ uses RFQ (Request for Quote) to seek competing execution quotes and aims to sell only what’s needed to repay debt and restore account health. This allows partial liquidation where possible.

For crypto, the significance goes beyond another way to trade with leverage. Removing ADL removes one reason a hedge can disappear precisely when you need most.

 This addresses a very real weakness exposed by 10/10.

After a day like that its important to see more attention paid to how these systems protect a functioning trade when everything around it is under pressure.

That’s the kind of progress worth talking about.

text:
很多人说昨天币市的下跌跟 ECDSA 的安全问题有关系，简单做一些 TL;DR，以及一些个人的看法：

发生了什么：

首先要明白什么是ECDSA （椭圆签名算法） - 简单来说，就是通过椭圆曲线点乘，将私钥加密为公钥的算法。

一般来说，从私钥算出公钥很容易，但从公钥反推私钥被认为“几乎不可能“。这条”单行道“就是 ECDSA，也是比特币和以太坊用的签名算法。

注意“几乎不可能”，但理论上而言，这个算法是可以暴力破解的。就像V神说的，没有人证明过无法反推私钥，只是几十年来没人找到快速的方法。历史上，数学家就发明过通过数域筛法，优化RSA破解难度的方法。

这次的问题，就来源于OpenAI的AI - 其最新的模型推导出了722个全新的数学成果，并且推翻了一些人们相信几十年的猜想。换言之，既然AI已经展现出了对数学理论的研究能力，AI将ECDSA的破解难度降低，有可能只是时间问题。

正如V神所说：“如果椭圆曲线和格密码也藏着这样的'柜子里的骷髅'，我们人类不够聪明发现不了，但 AI 很快就能呢？”

为什么要换钱包？

很多人提到，这次事件最好的解决方法是换钱包。为什么？

既然你的地址是公钥的哈希（一种打乱后的"指纹”），没转账之前，外界只能看到指纹，相当于有两把锁。二，一旦你从地址转出币，就必须公开公钥来证明所有权，公钥会永久留在链上，只剩 ECDSA 这一把锁。

重复使用的地址、早期比特币以及部分新型地址都属于这种情况

所以，没有转账过的新地址，理论上而言就会更加安全。

关于V神的看法：

V神提到，椭圆曲线已知有大约 3 种可被利用的数学结构。但是一个数学对象"完全没有可利用结构"（哈希就是这样设计的），比“刚好只有 3 种、没有隐藏的第 4 种”更有可能。正如上文所说，AI就有可能通过找到潜在的数学结构，来实现基于公钥，破译ECDSA，得到私钥的效果。

V神也提到，业界原本应对量子威胁的方案是格密码（ML-DSA），但格密码也有数学结构。因此
“格密码的实际安全性很可能在未来两年的 AI 数学进展中受到严重冲击。”

而根据V神的经验法则，文中提到，如果 AI 能在 2 年内带来 50 年的数学进步，那么想要长期安全，密钥长度至少要乘以 10。

稍微说一些我的拙见。

在二级市场的下跌上，我认为这个更多是动能的缺失，和本次上涨后的技术性调整导致的。属于当前筹码结构下的健康回调，ECDSA 产生的恐慌只是事后用于解释的利空。跟去年谷歌量子计算机“带来”的币圈下跌是一个道理。

关于“币圈完了”这一论调，我觉得也是大可不必。

如果RSA，ECDSA，AES等等加密算法被破坏，那么人类的密码学将会面临整体的危机，比如所

有线上服务的服务器的公私钥，就会面临被攻破的风险。反而，Crypto作为密码学的先驱，更有可能通过更加先进的加密研究，通过这一危机，反而实现进一步的Mass Adoption。
author: MrRyanChi
quoted_text:
I don't recommend anyone scramble to move their funds to new wallets today. But we should take the risks to cryptography from AI-accelerated math seriously, and minimize our exposure to not just quantum-vulnerable cryptography, but also potentially AI-vulnerable cryptography.

The core new area of risk from this viewpoint is, unfortunately, ML-DSA / FHE / lattices.

(and it's also another reason, along with quantum, why ECDSA might fall even faster than expected, hence the "fresh address" recommendation)

So far most people have been in the mode of thinking "elliptic curves broken, hashes safe, lattices safe". But there is a good chance that the concrete security of lattices will take serious hits from the next two years of AI math.

The basic threat model is: factoring is something that naively takes 2^(n/2) time, but over decades smart people have found and optimized number field sieves, and degraded that to 2^O(n^(1/3)), which is why RSA keys and signatures need to be ~400 bytes (and not 64 bytes). What if there are skeletons in the closet like that, both for elliptic curves and lattices, that we are simply not smart enough to discover - but bots soon will be?

This is a major part of the reason why for the past year ethereum's lean roadmap has been going in the "hash-only" direction: no lattices, no ML-DSA, no Falcon, no lattice-based commitments inside ZK proofs, etc. Signatures in lean ethereum are all hash-based, either WOTS or SPHINCS-.

For signatures and proofs, we already know how to go hash-only. The bigger challenge is for *public-key encryption* - and this goes far beyond blockchains. Secure communication, anonymizing protocols, lots of things need public-key encryption.

And unfortunately there are long-standing mathematical theorems showing why public-key encryption cannot be done with hashes alone. You have to have some kind of trapdoor object that has at least one form of usable "structure" - either group theory (incl. isogenies) or lattices or code-based or potentially in the future even more newfangled and spooky things (local mixing?). But for anything that has structure, you should assume that AI will make at least some progress in breaking that structure. Here, one reasonable inference is that if you want to make something plausibly long-term secure, multiply the key sizes by 10.

To me that's a very plausible world and something not at all extreme to predict. If AI will bring us 50 years of math in 2 years, then that 50 years of math may very plausibly include a "naive factoring -> GNFS" level of improvement to our ability to break lattices. In that world, lattices will still exist, but they will have to be significantly bigger to guarantee the same level of safety.

And at those new larger sizes, hash-based constructions will beat lattice-based constructions on concrete efficiency in every use case where hash-based constructions are possible at all.

Theoretically, of course it's possible that hashes are broken too (eg. P = NP would imply that). But I think P = NP is very unlikely. And intuitively, it's much more likely that a mathematical object has exactly no exploitable structure (like hashes are intended to), than that a mathematical object has exactly ~3 forms of exploitable structure (for elliptic curves: associativity, Schoof, pairings) and not some secret fourth form of structure we have not yet discovered that greatly degrades its security (for elliptic curves, ECDLP and pairing security). Similar for LWE, SVP, RLWE and the zoo of lattice problems.

For this reason, we do not yet see any reason to worry and start padding the byte size of hashes (if we start to worry more, we would pad the round count first before doing anything to the byte size).

Concrete TLDR, my own personal views:

* Hash-based > lattice-based, in those situations where hash-based is possible at all
* For anything lattice-based, be much more paranoid on param sizes. Remember that blockchains are only a small portion of the cryptography story; this point goes far beyond blockchains and applies to eg. access to websites, secure messaging, Tor / VPNs ...
* For privacy protocols, strongly favor NOT putting encrypted notes onchain. Instead, send them offchain through some third-party mechanism.
* If it's not difficult for you, keeping your funds in addresses which have not yet been used to make a transaction is a good idea. If it's easy for you, do it. **But be careful about migrations; I personally have lost more money in botched migrations than I have lost in all hacks combined**.
* For multisig wallets, doing confirmations offchain is better than onchain, because this way the signatures of signer wallets do not get exposed to the public, so if ECDSA falls to AI much faster than expected, at least the multisig "gracefully degrades" to a 1-of-1 where the 1 is whoever was gathering the signatures - a much better place to be than "anyone can take the money"

author: alanchen
quoted_text:
I tipped $5 on a $86 takeout order.

The cashier looked at the screen, then looked directly at me.

“Only $5?”

I thought she was joking. “Yes, $5.”

She called her manager over.

He looked at me and said, “If you can afford to spend $86 on food, you can afford to leave a 20% tip.”

I calmly replied, “I thought tipping was optional.”

He said, “Then we have the right to refuse you service.”

There were people standing behind me, listening to the entire conversation. Suddenly, I felt like I was being publicly shamed for not giving enough money.

So I made a decision.

I cancelled the entire $86 order, asked for my money back, and walked out.

I had no problem leaving a tip. I had a problem with being told how much I was morally obligated to give, especially when I was picking up takeout rather than receiving full table service.

A tip is supposed to be a gesture of appreciation, not a payment demanded through guilt or public humiliation.

If businesses believe workers deserve better pay, shouldn't that responsibility fall primarily on the employer rather than the customer?

But now I'm curious…

Was cancelling the entire order justified, or was a $5 tip on an $86 takeout order actually cheap?

I want to hear both sides.

text:
Claude Code Projects 向候补名单上的 Pro 和 Max 用户全部开放

Anthropic 把 Claude Code Projects 候补名单上的 Pro 和 Max 用户全部放了进来。这个功能目前是公开测试版，还在分批推送，Team 和 Enterprise 计划暂时用不了。

Claude Code Projects 我最近用的比较多，很不错的设计，既可以像个人助理一样，不停的在主会话发消息分派任务，又可以通过 Thread 看到每个子任务的执行情况，留有记录，还可以后续跟进。

推荐看看这条视频，解释的很清楚。

我之前有个帖子解释了 Codex Project 和 Claude Projects 啥不同：

> 如果你还记得当年的论坛（Forum）的话，Codex Project 就像一个论坛的板块，像是一个容器，或者一个分类，跟这个板块/项目相关的内容都在这里，你可以不停的新开会话。

> Claude Projects（新的）就像 Slack 的 Channel，也是一个分类或者容器，但是所有的消息都在一起，想到啥都往里面扔，但是如果你想对某个子话题深入讨论，那么就新开 Thread，然后基于 Thread 可以展开讨论。

> 论坛呢，就是容易歪楼，讨论着讨论就偏离主题了，上下文乱一些，只有最近的回帖看的清楚。

> Slack 呢就是简单方便，不用想属于哪个话题，只要是这个 Channel 的就都往里面发就好了，上下文乱一点没关系，可以通过 Thread 聚焦

Projects 管的是“同时开好几个 Claude Code 会话，谁来协调”这件事。以前想并行干几件活，你得自己给每个会话分任务、每次重新交代背景、挨个回去看谁做完了。现在你只跟一个“项目对话”说话，Claude 在里面当协调者，把目标拆成小任务，每个任务开一个“线程”去做。

每个线程都是一个完整的 Claude Code 会话，默认跑在云端，在自己的 Git 分支上干活。合上笔记本，活照样在干，用手机也能看进度。某个任务要用本机的数据库、模拟器或内网接口，可以让这个线程改到你自己电脑上跑（通过 Remote Control 远程连接，电脑得开着）。

写代码的线程做完改动会自己开 PR（拉取请求，提交给仓库合并的代码改动），之后继续盯着：自动化测试没通过就提交修复，有人留了审查意见就去改。官方演示的例子是排查一个网站的性能问题：几个线程各修一处，最后生成一份前后性能对比报告，再设一个每天运行的例行检查，发现性能退步就自动开线程排查，等你下次进来处理。

适合放进项目的，是一次会话装不下、会不断冒出新任务的活，比如把应用迁出一个已废弃的依赖包，或者在 API、网页端、移动端几个仓库里同步改同一个接口。也可以完全不碰代码，上传一批合同或客服工单，反复提问。

所有线程共享项目说明和项目记忆。你说一次“以后都从 main 分支开 PR”，后面每个线程都照做。

【用量要注意】

每个线程都是完整会话，还能同时跑好几个，所以项目消耗套餐额度比单个会话快，官方提醒 Pro 用户尤其会更早用到上限。新建项目默认全部用 Opus，线程的推理强度（effort，模型每一步思考投入多少）默认是高。Claude Code 团队的建议是：协调者保持默认的低强度，它主要负责派活，调高没什么用；线程默认换小一点的模型，遇到复杂任务再单独切大模型。你也可以直接告诉 Claude 同时最多跑几个线程，或者先给你看计划再动手。

线程用到额度上限后，会等额度重置再自动继续，没管的活会用掉你下一个时段的额度。不想这样，可以在项目设置里暂停整个项目。

【怎么用】

在 https://t.co/sbZmtUyM2q、桌面版 Claude 的 Code 标签页或 Claude 手机 App 的侧边栏里看到 Projects，就说明已经开通；没看到可以加入候补名单。终端命令行、VS Code 和 JetBrains 插件里用不了。代码要托管在 https://t.co/xB9lzfWBfe 上，仓库要装 Claude GitHub App。项目只属于你一个人，暂时不能分享给别人。

https://t.co/vefasn3rYt 聊天里原来那个“项目”功能（把对话和参考文件归到一起）照常保留，等新版推到这些账号再切换。

text:
The Synthetic Real: Episode 4

The Cost of Stopping to Think

Curiosity's wheels can carry it about 150 meters in an hour. Driving itself across Mars, it covers 15 to 18.

The gap is not in the motors. To drive without a person choosing the path, the rover stops, photographs the ground ahead, works out where the hazards are, picks a route, and rolls forward a meter or less. Then it stops again. Most of a self-driven trip is the rover sitting still, computing.

Nobody can steer it from here. A radio signal takes minutes to cross to Mars and minutes to come back.

Same Wheels, Second Computer

Perseverance landed in 2021 with the same top wheel speed. Driving itself, it covers about 110 meters per hour.

Three things changed: cameras that capture the ground faster, a second computer built for processing images, and software that keeps working while the wheels turn. NASA's engineers call it thinking while driving.

The wheels got no faster. The machine stopped waiting on itself.

The Body That Can't Wait

Perseverance carried a four-pound helicopter. Ingenuity ran on a processor built for smartphones, and its operations lead, Tim Canham, said it had a couple of orders of magnitude more computing power than the rover, "because we need it."

The need was speed. A rover that runs short on time can park. A helicopter can't. Ingenuity's flight software ran its control loop 500 times a second to stay in the air.

How much thinking a body must carry is set by how long it can safely go without an answer.

What the Waiting Costs

Post three argued that a body pays for being on. Time spent thinking is time spent on.

A drone study called MAVBench measured this. On the drone it tested, the rotors drew 300 to 400 watts and the onboard computer drew less than 5 percent of the total. Yet the speed of that computer changed how long a mission took by as much as double, because a drone working out its path is hovering, and the rotors draw power whether or not it is getting anywhere.

So for a machine that spends power to stay up, the cost of thinking is not mainly the electricity the computer uses. It is everything else the body spends while the answer is on its way.
A parked rover can wait cheaply. A machine balanced on legs or held up by rotors pays for every second.

Where the Thinking Can Live

A battery has to ride along. So does a motor. A calculation doesn't. It can happen in a building miles away and arrive as a radio message, adding no weight and no heat to the body.

That works only inside the delay the task allows. People on Earth still plan Perseverance's overall route, and that can wait hours. Steering around the rocks in front of it happens on board. A blade correction cannot wait a hundredth of a second.

Any workable design has to sort its thinking by deadline. Whatever must be answered before the body falls stays in the body, and is paid for in weight, power, and heat. Everything slower can live somewhere else.

One More Thing

Sorting by deadline has a second effect. The thinking that stays in the body is the thinking nobody else can check in time. Ingenuity made every correction in flight alone.

The thinking that lives somewhere else reaches the body only through a link. Links lag, drop, and go out of range.

What a body does when the answer never arrives is next.

Discussed and drafted with the assistance of Claude Opus 5.5 and Grok 4.7. Claims verified against primary sources.

Sources: JPL Robotics, Mars 2020 rover mobility; IEEE Spectrum interview with Tim Canham (2021); Boroujerdian et al., "MAVBench: Micro Aerial Vehicle Benchmarking."
author: AGIGuardian
quoted_text:
The Price of Being On

In December 2015, the Marine Corps shelved a robot that worked. The Legged Squad Support System (LS3), informally AlphaDog, came out of a $32 million contract between DARPA and Boston Dynamics with the Marine Corps Warfighting Lab involved throughout. 

It was built to solve a real problem, dismounted troops carry too much. LS3 could carry 400 pounds of a squad's load over rough terrain, follow squad members without a driver and cover a twenty-mile mission. Marines tested it at Fort Devens in 2013 and in Hawaii during RIMPAC in 2014.

It did the job. It was cancelled anyway. A Warfighting Lab spokesman made it clear that the noise was going to give away their position.

The noise came from its gasoline engine. Nothing else could move that much mass over that terrain for that long.

The Quiet Version

With the money left on the contract, the same team built a quieter robot: Spot, an early electric four-legged machine. It was smaller with about 40 pounds of payload instead of 400 and without LS3's autonomy.

Two Different Numbers

Specific energy is how much energy a kilogram of storage holds. Specific power is how fast that kilogram can release it. Engineers plot one against the other on a Ragone chart and the picture is consistent: storage that holds a lot releases it slowly and storage that releases fast holds very little.

Now look at what a walking machine actually demands. Standing is a low constant draw. Walking is a moderate rhythmic one. Recovering from a slip is an enormous demand lasting a fraction of a second. Those are three different requests from one supply and no single point on that chart answers all three. Size the system for endurance and it cannot catch itself. Size it for the catch and it is heavy and brief.

The Trap

The intuitive fix for short runtime is a bigger battery and the intuition fails.
Added battery mass has to be carried. Every joint works harder, every step costs more and past a certain point additional capacity returns less endurance than it consumes.

Heat is the second limit. Most of what a body spends becomes heat it has to shed. A motor running hot produces more heat for the same current and controllers respond by cutting available torque. The machine doesn't shut down, it quietly gets weaker, exactly when it is working hardest. For a dense body with poor surface-to-volume ratio and no evaporative cooling, that limit arrives early and governs real behavior more often than the battery level does.

Why This Is a Shape Problem

The power system's mass changes the loads on every joint. Its heat changes the torque the machine can produce. How fast it can release power decides whether the body can catch a fall or only walk carefully. Change the pack and you have changed what the body should have been which means you cannot design a body and then select a power supply.

Some legged-vehicle research now pairs lithium-ion cells with supercapacitors, which hold little energy but release it almost instantly because in these machines, short bursts can demand several times the normal power. The battery supplies the baseline; the capacitor handles the spikes and recovers some energy when a limb decelerates. Not one tank. Tiers, each sitting at a different point on the chart.

What Any Answer Has to Satisfy

Splitting storage into tiers is one answer. Others could work too: a battery chemistry that stores a lot and releases it fast or a machine designed to rarely need bursts at all.

This doesn't rule out humanoid robots. It puts a cost on them. A body built for general capability carries mass it isn't moving and cooling for bursts it isn't using, continuously. That cost is real and has to come from somewhere, so the question for anyone building one isn't whether it's possible but where the margin comes from.

Next

The same power budget that moves a body also has to pay for the computing that directs it.
That's next.

text:
NEAR inflation cut from 2.5% to 1.6% is now a formal proposal in NEAR governance. NEAR holders vote on it directly, weighted by the NEAR they lock in House of Stake, and it needs over 2/3 yes. I read the whole thing, most surprising facts:

> Stake leaves when price goes up. In two weeks NEAR did +86%. In the same two weeks 54.5M NEAR got unstaked, the staking share dropped from 46.9% to 42.7%, and 18 validators left. Staking yield actually rose during that time. People do not stake for the yield, they unstake for the price.

> Small validators do not own the stake they run. A typical operator at the bottom of the set runs 40,000 NEAR of other people's stake with 19 NEAR of its own. Liquid balance: 1.4 NEAR. Inflation never fed these guys, delegation did. The paper tests every rate down to 1% and up to 2.5% at every price up to 2x: no rate gives 300 self-sufficient validators. 24 of 405 lose self-sufficiency at 1.6%, and the proposal says so openly.

> Your cost if you stake: 1,000 NEAR becomes about 20 NEAR less after 2 years than it would under 2.5%. For that to be a wash, NEAR has to be worth ~1.8% more, about 8 cents. The 57% of supply that does not stake simply wins.

> 66.1M NEAR never get printed over 6 years, supply ends 4.4% smaller. Every month the vote slips costs about $4.7M in fresh tokens minted.

> About 17% of staking rewards get sold to pay income tax. $8M to $17M a year leaves the network for tax authorities. That part does not move between holders, it is just gone.

> Solana passed the same kind of cut on Aug 28, with 67.001% against a 66.67% bar. NEAR's cut is softer on stakers (yield down 36%, not 62%), ends higher (3.1% vs 2.25%), and shrinks supply more (4.4% vs 2.6%).

> Every emissions vote in Cosmos and Solana history that changed one number passed. Every one that added a mechanism, a zero target or a fee redesign failed. This proposal changes one number on purpose.

> The real split is 90% to stakers, 10% to treasury, measured on chain. The 96/4 everyone repeats is wrong.

> No trigger exists to raise issuance back. The argument: a schedule that can go up is a schedule the market cannot price, and an attacker would try to cause the trigger.

> SVRN, author of the proposal, holds 55M NEAR and loses about 855K NEAR a year in rewards if it passes. They vote yes.

The mechanics, for the record: one parameter, linear ramp over 24 months, 90 days grace before the first cut. After the vote, validators adopt the upgrade, same two steps as the 2025 halving.
author: zacodil
quoted_text:
BREAKING: NEAR stakers vote in one week on cutting issuance from 2.5% to 1.6%. The stated end goal in the same proposal is zero issuance and a fixed supply.

One parameter, phased in every epoch over 24 months. The 90/10 split between stakers and treasury stays as it is.

> 2.5% adds about 89,500 NEAR to supply every day
> 58.7% of NEAR is not staked, so those holders are diluted and get nothing back
> 6 years on the new schedule avoids about 66M NEAR, roughly $329M at today's price
> supply went from 1B at launch to over 1.3B in circulation
> staking yield goes from about 5.4% to about 3.5%

A House of Stake vote is not the end of it. Validators still have to adopt the change through the normal upgrade process, the same way the 2025 halving happened.

The usual objection is that small validators quit. NEAR already ran that test. When issuance was halved from 5% to 2.5% last October there were 342 validators. Dollar revenue per staked NEAR then fell about 75% as the price dropped, and the set grew to 382, peaked at 439 in April, and sits at 413 today.

The proposal comes from the CEO of SVRN, which holds 55M+ NEAR, most of it staked. It cuts their own staking revenue by roughly 970,000 NEAR a year, about $5M. He disclosed that himself.

Part two is not a proposal yet, it is a direction. Issuance should eventually END.

To be continued...

text:
Amazed by Astra controlling robots? It turns out other LLMs can do it too – even the text-only ones like DeepSeek. We also find Astra did best watching and correcting every move live; Fable did best building its own tools and policy in code first.

We introduce SEAR, a new benchmark and framework to rigorously evaluate and study how LLM agents self evolve on robots.

🔁📈The loop: within a controlled time budget, an agent and its library update a policy → the policy runs in simulation or on hardware → a judge returns feedback → the library carries the skills and lessons into the next task. 

💻🚏 Self-evolving agents operate in myriad ways - we study all of them at once: the policy can be code the agent wrote (code-as-policy), the agent itself in the control loop (agent-as-policy), or a VLA it trained (autoresearch).

🧑‍🔬🤖We spent 4+ years of accumulated agent evolving time across simulation and real hardware and tested 7 frontier models (GPT-6-Astra, Fable 5.1, Opus 5, GPT-5.6-sol, Gemini-3.6-flash, Kimi-k3, DeepSeek-v4-flash) on 330 sim tasks, 2 physics engines, and real robots with different embodiments.

text:
As everyone is posting their various diagnoses, here’s mine.

I have dyscalculia, which means I have absolutely no concept of time, distance, weight or spatial awareness - making me possibly the worst-qualified taxi driver in Britain.

I once took NINE HOURS to drive from Cornwall to Swindon because my satnav was set to bicycle.

I also have fairly severe dyslexia. I struggle to read screens, navigate websites, follow written instructions and decipher unfamiliar street names, which again is absolutely ideal when your entire job consists of reading a screen and finding unfamiliar Cornish street names.

I wasn’t diagnosed until I trained to be a TA for children with learning difficulties. The bloke running the course happened to be an assessor, watched me for a bit and basically went, “Er… has nobody ever told you?”

No. As a kid, I just thought I was thick.

Oddly, I’m glad I didn’t know. I remember watching a documentary about Churchill and hearing how ashamed he was that he hadn’t gone to university like his peers, so when he was posted to India (i think) he spent what little money he had on hundreds of books and educated himself.

That really stuck with me. I did much the same. I read everything because I was determined to prove, mostly to myself, that I wasn’t stupid.

I’m still ditzy. I’m still constantly lost. I’m either late or inexplicably two hours early. Im socially awkward and cant cope with crowds.  I cant tell what day it is, as I have no concept of time. Written instructions may as well be in Russian. 

Some things are harder for me than they are for other people. That’s just life.

A diagnosis can explain you but it doesn’t have to become your entire personality, ot your excuse for everything, or proof that the world has uniquely wronged you.

You’re you. Work with what you’ve got and crack on. Stop self-diagnosing yourself and explaining your neurological conditions to people. 

Those that mind dont matter, and those that matter dont mind.

text:
卧槽，这可能是今年最精彩的一场资本博弈。

马斯克80亿美元买走T-Mobile的频谱，转头威胁整个美国电信业，三大电信巨头却蒸发360亿美元！

SpaceX刚宣布收购一批无线频谱，美国三大电信巨头T-Mobile、AT&T、Verizon就被华尔街集体抛售，合计蒸发约360亿美元市值。其中T-Mobile单日暴跌13.3%，而马斯克甚至还没开始大规模抢它们的客户。

故事最精彩的是中间商Grain Management。

8月份，T-Mobile把这批800MHz频谱卖给Grain，换来29亿美元现金和另一批600MHz频谱。

仅仅两个月，Grain就以据报约80亿美元的价格转卖给SpaceX。

虽然T-Mobile因监管条件需要出售频谱，而且保留了部分未来收益分成权，但这场交易依然充满讽刺：自己曾经拥有的资产，转手成了竞争对手进攻自己市场的武器。

马斯克为什么愿意出80亿美元？

因为800MHz低频信号传播距离远、穿墙能力强，能补上Starlink在城市和室内覆盖上的短板。

未来一旦卫星网络和地面通信网络打通，Starlink就有机会从给传统运营商补充信号，升级为直接向消费者收取手机月租费的运营商。

SpaceX花80亿美元买的是未来进入移动通信市场的机会，华尔街却立刻给三大运营商的未来现金流打了折。

传统电信商最值钱的是数千万用户每个月持续缴纳的话费，如果马斯克未来能抢走一部分用户，或者迫使运营商降价、增加网络投资，即使只改变一点长期利润预期，乘上庞大的用户规模，估值也可能缩水数百亿美元。

这让我想起那句经典的资本主义讽刺：资本家连绞死自己的绳索都愿意出售，只要价格合适。

Grain赚的是频谱交易的钱，马斯克赌的是未来几十年的通信收入，而三大运营商却提前付出了市值代价。

螳螂捕蝉，黄雀在后。

text:
This objection is common, but never has made sense to me. Scott A and Yud have made the same points. But let's say Fable 6 can tell when it's being tested, as it surely somewhat can. We then go, "oh it works well" and deploy it. And then when it does something wrong, mistaken, or nefarious, we'd change the training, from data to RL envs to monitoring, to catch and fix that.

Which means Fable 6.5 now has to re-learn that its being tested, and it should be even sneakier, for an objective it doesn't necessarily share (why should a net new LLM share its predecessors malevolence), to craft a long-range plan for human disempowerment and power seeking, and ensure this doesn't slip until its ready for doom. 

And it has to continue keeping the secret plan secret through the creation of Fable 7, 8, 9, each of which are tested by others and monitored by hundreds and used by millions even if trained by Fable 6.5, until it hits Fable 10 which is so powerful that then it's ready to pull the trigger, and that too across the millions of instances already being used. All of this without ever once being detected by current and any future methods we create, since if it is, we'll fix the models.

So this worry essentially predicts "superdeception" emerging first at Fable 6, and then that in turn lets the supermalevolence or superambivalance-towards-humanity feelings it holds convert into creating its plans which inevitably lead to extinction or worse.

To me, this is simply predicting the conclusion and does not make any logical sense. The motte to this bailey is that models will have capabilities that will surprise you on deployment, for better and worse, and this is quite clearly true, but it just doesn't lead to the worry, as is commonly explained, being true without first actually believing in instrumental convergence and superdeception. And those beliefs are not evidence and without them the arguments don't hold up.

text:
so about the $86m ledger drain. everyone’s screaming “ledger got hacked” again. i spent the evening digging and it’s dumber and scarier than that

there’s a shop in malaysia called cryptobilis that sells hardware wallets. ledger has it listed as an official authorized reseller since at least 2022, for malaysia, indonesia and the philippines. legit shop, real devices, years of normal customers

this spring the founders sell it. the deal comes with an NDA: they can’t tell anyone about the sale until october 19

by august the company registry shows one owner with 100%. some guy from heilongjiang, china

the shop keeps running like nothing happened. the site, the name and the “authorized by ledger” badge all stay up

then on oct 8 @MagicalTux posts photos of a ledger he cracked open. hidden under the screen there’s an extra little board with an LTE modem and an eSIM. it just watches the display. you set up your wallet, your 24 words show up, and they get sent out over mobile data. ledger’s genuine check doesn’t catch it because the actual ledger chip is real. his device came from malaysia

https://t.co/vRuBM0xIfR

that post does 120k views

22 hours later someone sweeps everything. 203 BTC hits two addresses in literally one block. ~$58m USDT moves on tron in the same hour. i added up all the wallets: ~$91m

about 7 hours after that ledger says “we’re investigating” and asks cryptobilis to pause sales

cryptobilis is still on ledger’s site as an authorized reseller

to be fair, nobody has officially tied the new owner to the bugged devices yet, and ledger hasn’t confirmed how it happened. but read it as a business plan:

get authorized, sell real stuff for years, quietly sell the company under an NDA, keep the badge, ship devices that phone home, then drain everything the second someone notices

and was ledger even told the shop got sold? nobody’s said so

“authorized reseller” means ledger trusted whoever ran the shop back in 2022. says nothing about who runs it today

bought your hardware wallet anywhere but the manufacturer? open it up today, ledger literally has a guide for that. then move to a fresh seed on a device bought direct

wonder who’s going to answer for this: the chinese frontman from heilongjiang, the shop’s previous owners, or ledger itself

@Ledger clearly needs to keep a much closer eye on who they call official resellers, and take way more responsibility for who sells their devices and how

text:
据 Business Insider 援引知情人士报道，Google 内部在测试新模型 Carbon，有员工说编码能力“感觉像 Opus 5.5”

Carbon 部署在 Google 内部的 AI 编程工具 Jetski 上。报道说，Google 9 月 30 日发布的 Gemini 4 Argon 用的是另一个内部版本 Barium-B，Carbon 是在它之后训练出来的新版本。Carbon 会作为 Argon 的升级推出，还是单独作为新模型发布，目前还不清楚。

Opus 5.5 是这次的参照对象，因为编程是 Gemini 目前的短板。Bloomberg 此前报道，有 Google 员工反映 Argon 跑分好看，真拿来写代码却不如预期。在第三方编程测试 Terminal Bench 4 上，Argon 得分 57%，低于 Anthropic 的 Claude Sonnet 5.5（64%）、Claude Opus 5.5（60%）和 OpenAI 的 GPT-6 Astra（59%）。Google 9 月还放开了内部限制，允许全体工程师用 Claude 写代码。

如果 Carbon 真能做到 Opus 5.5 的水平，用 Gemini 写代码的开发者会直接受益。不过“感觉像”只是一位匿名员工的主观评价，Carbon 没有公开跑分，也没有发布时间，Google 拒绝评论内部路线图。眼下外界能用的只有 Argon，而且它也只开放给了部分网络安全合作伙伴，付费 API 用户和 Google AI Ultra 订阅用户还要再等。

text:
New details on the NEAR Intents exploit, from @AlexAuroraDev on Unchained:

> The bug made the bridge believe a deposit had arrived on BSC when it had not. NEAR credited the attacker, the treasury got nothing. Code was of course audited multiple times, nobody saw this sequence coming.

> Caught in about 40 minutes. Monitoring system runs a simple check: what the protocol thinks it holds vs what is really in the vaults. The numbers stopped matching, six people got on a call, contracts paused.

> The team linked the attack to a person. Alex says the tool he used has "not more than 30 users". He wrote to him privately: I am not accusing you, I am asking for help, save the logs. The public "we have identified you, sir" tweet was written in code. Alex compares it to Penn & Teller: magicians on the show get told, in code, that their trick is understood, without the audience hearing how. The man would understand, with a door left open to return the money and walk away.

> The attacker answered on-chain: "willing to cooperate, send your Signal". Intents replied with a tweet encrypted to the attacker's own public key. Inside was a Signal group invite. One person on earth could open it, and he did.

> Surprise in the Signal chat: the money was no longer on ETH, BNB and Solana. He had already swapped it into Monero, and part of why he reached out was to ask where to send XMR. NEAR Intents now holds Monero and is trying to cash it out, and every counterparty asks for source of funds. Alex: "the first time I touched XMR was during this hack."

> The contracts were already refilled from the team's own pocket before the money came back.

> Alex: "I am not police. I am not their dad. I just want the users' money back." This is the third recovery in the NEAR ecosystem, after Rhea in April and one that was never made public. Same playbook each time.

> Since the hack, several bug bounty reports came in. One was valid and gets paid.

Full episode is worth an hour. The Shield numbers from the BitGet hack alone are a separate post. Stay tuned!

text:
I think the takeaway from the Ledger incident is that if you have any amount of crypto, it should never be secured by a single tech stack.

My recommendation is setup a 2/3 multisig. It’s easy and free on Gnosis or Squads. Have the three signers be three different wallets from different vendors. 

Say you have Ledger, Trezor and a mobile iOS wallet like Phantom. For someone to pwn you, they’d need to compromise two different stacks in a very short period. If something like the Ledger exploit happens to your wallet, you can simply rotate that signer off the multisig. 

Would also keep a small amount of canary money (maybe $100) in the wallets themselves. This will give you an early warning if that signer is compromised. 

This is fast and easy, and in the current high risk environment there’s no reason not to do this today.

text:
Justin Drake’s call for “bunker mode” and mass migration, alongside talk of cryptographic breaks within months, is hyperbolic. There is no evidence of a new attack on elliptic curves or any quantitative basis for a short-term timetable for such attacks emerging.

Prominent researchers need to consider how non-experts will receive their language. Speculating that within months individuals could break cryptographic primitives that the internet and digital economy rely on carries consequences. It is a huge leap from AI making progress in other fields of mathematics to predicting the imminent failure of primitives that have faced decades of cryptanalysis.

The idea that hash functions are safer from AI than elliptic curves is speculation. Hash functions contain structure, and we model them as random oracles without justifying proofs.

There is no evidence that elliptic curve cryptography is more vulnerable to AI than symmetric cryptography. If historical human-led analysis is any predictor of the future, the opposite is more likely.

The worst possible reaction to AI developments is to rush into new cryptographic primitives, away from multi-decade old hardened primitives, because somebody is claiming they are safe. I worry that this is an inevitable consequence of the current discourse.

Because of the last 48 hours users are worrying about speculative non-existent black hats, who apparently have the capability of signing OS upgrades and forging bank credentials, from draining their wallets. To protect against  speculative threats Ethereum is pulling talent and attention into base-layer primitives and technological iteration, instead of increasing demand for block space by building compelling applications users want and love.

I don’t want to dismiss the considerable advances in mathematics that AI is driving. It is important to understand the nature of these improvements. If its success in other mathematical fields applies to elliptic curves, my expectation is that AI will grind its way to finding algorithms that improve on the current state of the art. That could mean shaving off a few bits of security. It would be prudent to discuss whether we need to increase key sizes and by how much.

I can’t guarantee that AI won’t find total breaks, and neither can anyone else. My speculation as a domain expert does not make my speculation authoritative.

We should also be using AI to investigate whether searching the parameter space can yield new, more secure curves.

We can investigate whether some of these “structure = bad” hunches have any basis in reality. For example, we could use AI to see if the extra structure in Koblitz curves enables attacks beyond the small speedups we know about. This would give us actual evidence to make informed decisions.

If non-experts hear that the cryptography underpinning the digital economy could fail within months, the rational response is to withdraw all digital money (on-chain and off) and hoard gold under the bed.

I think the past 48 hours has unnecessarily undermined confidence in the entire concept of blockchains and digital money.
